MODULE 3 — INTERNET, WEB, NETWORKING, TELECOM AND MOBILE
The Ultra-Comprehensive TCS InQuizitive 2026 Master Pack
Research cut-off for changing facts: July 28, 2026

This is one of the central modules of the entire preparation programme. It connects computing history, companies, science, engineering, business, current affairs, brands, personalities, visual clues and Indian technology. A question may appear to be about a logo, a song, a political policy, a failed company or a sports broadcast, but the hidden link may be the network that carried it.
Do not study this module as a glossary. Learn it as five interlocking stories:
1. Humans learned to transmit information over distance: telegraph, telephone, radio and satellites.
2. Computers learned to communicate: time-sharing, packet switching, ARPANET and TCP/IP.
3. Information became browsable: hypertext, the World Wide Web, browsers, search and online services.
4. Connectivity became personal and wireless: cellular networks, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and smartphones.
5. Networks became infrastructure: fibre, submarine cables, data centres, cloud platforms, content-delivery networks, internet exchanges and edge computing.
For every major term, person or product, prepare these eight angles:
• What came immediately before and after it?
• What does its name or acronym mean?
• Which institution, company or country is associated with it?
• Can you recognise its logo, device, sound or interface?
• Which popular story about it is false or oversimplified?
• What Indian connection could turn it into a TCS InQuizitive question?
The Internet and the World Wide Web are not synonyms.

The Internet is the global network of networks that moves data using the Internet Protocol suite. The Web is one service that runs on the Internet, primarily using HTTP or HTTPS to retrieve linked resources. Email, file transfer, internet telephony, multiplayer gaming and many messaging systems can use the Internet without being part of the Web.
PART I — FROM SIGNALS TO PACKETS

Long-distance communication existed long before electronics. Beacon fires, drums, semaphore towers, postal networks and optical telegraphs all encoded information into signals. Modern networking inherited three enduring problems from them:
• Encoding: How is meaning represented as a signal?
• Transmission: How does the signal cross distance?
• Routing: How does it reach the intended destination?

The telegraph converted messages into electrical pulses sent along wires. Samuel Morse is associated with a practical telegraph system and Morse code, although many inventors contributed to telegraphy. Morse code represents letters through combinations of short and long signals, conventionally called dots and dashes.

The famous first public message sent by Morse’s system between Washington and Baltimore in 1844 was “What hath God wrought”. The phrase came from the Book of Numbers and was suggested by Annie Ellsworth.
Why the telegraph matters to networking
• It separated communication speed from transportation speed.
• Telegraph offices formed switching and relay networks.
• Submarine telegraph cables created the first global electrical communications infrastructure.
• The word cable became both a physical medium and a metonym for a telegram.

Alexander Graham Bell received a celebrated United States telephone patent in 1876 and made the famous request, “Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.” Antonio Meucci, Elisha Gray and others are important in the contested history of voice telephony. Quiz questions may exploit the difference between “inventor of the telephone” as conventional shorthand and the more complex multi-inventor history.

Early telephones used human operators at switchboards. Automatic exchanges reduced dependence on operators. Almon Strowger, an undertaker who suspected that an operator was directing business to a rival, is associated with the automatic step-by-step telephone exchange and the Strowger switch.
Telephone numbering, dialling and exchanges introduced ideas that survive in networking:
• Signalling manages calls separately from the conversation itself.

James Clerk Maxwell’s equations predicted electromagnetic waves. Heinrich Hertz demonstrated them experimentally. Guglielmo Marconi built commercially significant wireless telegraph systems, while Jagadish Chandra Bose performed pioneering microwave and radio research and demonstrated wireless signalling in India. Nikola Tesla, Alexander Popov and others also appear in radio-history questions.

Radio eliminated the need for a continuous wire between sender and receiver. It introduced spectrum allocation, interference, antennas, modulation and broadcasting—concepts central to mobile communication.

Claude Shannon’s 1948 paper “A Mathematical Theory of Communication” created the mathematical foundation of digital communication. Its revolutionary move was to separate the technical problem of transmitting symbols accurately from the meaning of the message.
• Bit: a binary digit, representing one of two alternatives.
• Entropy: a measure of uncertainty or information content.
• Channel capacity: the maximum reliable information rate of a communication channel under specified conditions.
• Noise: unwanted disturbance that can corrupt a signal.
• Redundancy: extra structure that may help detect or correct errors.

The unit bit was suggested by John Tukey as a contraction of binary digit. Shannon adopted the term in his paper. Ralph Hartley’s earlier work connected information to logarithmic measures, and Harry Nyquist studied signalling rates and telegraph transmission.
Claude Shannon did not invent the first computer network. His role was deeper: he supplied the mathematical language through which communication, coding, compression and noise could be analysed.
Traditional telephone calls establish a dedicated path through the network for the duration of a conversation. Resources remain reserved even during silence.
• Natural fit for continuous real-time voice.
• A dedicated path can be vulnerable to failure.
• Scaling data communication through fixed circuits is costly.

Packet switching divides data into smaller units called packets. Each packet carries addressing and control information. Packets may share links with other traffic and may take different routes before being reassembled.
• Natural fit for bursty computer data.
• Supports many applications on common infrastructure.
• Delay and arrival order may vary.
• End systems or higher protocols must handle reliability when required.

Paul Baran at the RAND Corporation studied distributed communications networks for resilient military communication. He described dividing messages into “message blocks” and using distributed routing.

Donald Davies at Britain’s National Physical Laboratory independently developed packet-switching concepts and coined the term packet. His NPL network became an important early packet-switched network.
Leonard Kleinrock developed queueing theory relevant to data networks and led the UCLA group involved in ARPANET’s first connection.

Louis Pouzin led the French CYCLADES project. Its datagram approach and emphasis on intelligence at the network edges influenced later Internet architecture. The CYCLADES network did not become the Internet, but its design ideas mattered greatly.
Packet switching has no single uncontested inventor. Baran and Davies worked independently; Kleinrock supplied important theory and experimentation; Pouzin influenced datagrams and end-to-end design.
Networks by geographic or functional scale
A short-range network around one person, such as Bluetooth links among a phone, watch and earbuds.
A network within a room, building, school, laboratory or campus segment. Ethernet and Wi-Fi are dominant LAN technologies.
A LAN using radio rather than only cables, commonly Wi-Fi.
A network connecting buildings within a university, corporate campus or similar site.
A network spanning a city or metropolitan region.
A network spanning large geographic areas. Corporate leased-line networks and national backbones are examples.
A specialised high-speed network connecting servers and storage devices. Do not confuse it with a small area network.
An encrypted or logically private connection carried over another network, usually the public Internet. It can connect a remote user to an organisation or link sites securely.
All devices share a common backbone. Early coaxial Ethernet used bus-like arrangements. A break or termination problem could disrupt communication.
Devices connect to a central hub or switch. Modern Ethernet LANs commonly appear as stars. The central device is a critical point, but individual cable failures affect only one endpoint.
Each device connects to neighbours in a loop. Token Ring and FDDI are historically associated with ring concepts.
Devices have multiple interconnections. A full mesh connects every node to every other node; a partial mesh uses selected redundant paths. Mesh designs improve resilience but increase complexity.
Hierarchical arrangement of connected stars or branches. Enterprise networks often have access, distribution and core layers.
A real network may combine several topologies.
4. THE DEVICES THAT BUILD A NETWORK
Regenerates or amplifies a weakened signal so it can travel farther. It does not make sophisticated forwarding decisions.
A multiport repeater. An Ethernet hub sends incoming traffic out through all other ports. All connected devices share a collision domain. Hubs have largely been replaced by switches.
Connects network segments and filters frames using hardware addresses. A switch can be understood as a high-speed multiport bridge.
Forwards frames within a local network, primarily using MAC addresses. It learns which addresses are reachable through which ports. Each switch port normally creates a separate collision domain.
Forwards packets between IP networks using routing tables. Routers separate broadcast domains and choose paths toward destination networks.

A broad term for a device or service connecting unlike systems or serving as an entry and exit point. A home router is often the default gateway for local devices. Protocol gateways may translate between different systems.

Short for modulator-demodulator. It converts digital data into a form suitable for a transmission medium and reverses the process. Dial-up modems used audible tones over telephone lines. Cable, DSL and cellular modems use different signalling technologies.
Connects wireless devices to a wired network. A domestic “Wi-Fi router” usually combines a router, Ethernet switch, access point, firewall, DHCP server and sometimes a modem in one box.
Applies rules to allow or block traffic. Firewalls may inspect addresses, ports, connection state, applications or content.
Acts as an intermediary. A forward proxy represents clients; a reverse proxy represents servers. Proxies may filter, cache, secure, balance or conceal network relationships.
Distributes traffic across multiple servers or locations to improve capacity and reliability.
Caches content near users to reduce latency and backbone traffic. Akamai, Cloudflare, Fastly and major cloud providers operate extensive delivery infrastructure.
The hardware that connects a device to a network. It may have a Media Access Control address, commonly called a MAC address.
• Switch: forwards within a LAN using MAC addresses.
• Modem: adapts signals to a transmission service.
• Access point: provides wireless access to a network.
5. LAYERS: WHY NETWORKING IS DIVIDED INTO STACKS

A layered model divides a complex communication task into manageable parts. Each layer provides services to the layer above and relies on the layer below. This allows one technology to change without redesigning everything.
The International Organization for Standardization developed the seven-layer Open Systems Interconnection reference model.
Services used by applications, such as web, email and name resolution.
Data representation, encoding, compression and encryption concepts.
Establishes, manages and terminates communication sessions.
End-to-end delivery, segmentation, reliability and flow control. TCP and UDP are commonly discussed here.
Logical addressing and routing. IP operates here in the conventional mapping.
Frames, local delivery, MAC addressing and error detection. Ethernet and Wi-Fi have major functions here.
Electrical, optical and radio signals, connectors, frequencies and raw bits.
Top to bottom: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.
Bottom to top: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.
The practical Internet stack is often represented with four or five layers:
Do not claim that the Internet was designed strictly from the later OSI seven-layer model. OSI is an excellent teaching and reference framework; the Internet evolved around its own protocol suite.
As data moves down the stack, each layer adds control information:
Application data → transport segment or datagram → IP packet → link-layer frame → physical signals.
At the receiver, the process is reversed.
6. ADDRESSING: WHO ARE YOU AND WHERE ARE YOU?

A MAC address identifies a network interface at the link layer. Traditional Ethernet MAC addresses are 48 bits long and written in hexadecimal groups. Devices increasingly use randomised MAC addresses for privacy on wireless networks.
An IP address is a logical address used for routing across networks.
• Written as four decimal numbers from 0 to 255, separated by dots.
• Written as hexadecimal groups separated by colons.
• Consecutive zero groups may be compressed once using a double colon.
• Designed partly to provide a vastly larger address space and improve aspects of network operation.
127.0.0.1 is the familiar IPv4 loopback address, commonly called localhost. IPv6 loopback is ::1.
169.254.0.0/16 is used by IPv4 devices for automatic link-local addressing when a normal address service is unavailable.
A subnet divides an IP network into smaller networks. In CIDR notation, a slash followed by a number indicates how many leading bits identify the network.
192.168.1.0/24 means that the first 24 bits identify the network, leaving 8 bits for addresses within that subnet.
No difficult subnet arithmetic is required for most quiz questions, but recognise:
• /8 is a very large IPv4 block.

Network Address Translation allows multiple private devices to share one or a smaller number of public IPv4 addresses. A home router commonly translates internal private addresses and transport ports to an external address.
NAT prolonged the usable life of IPv4 but weakened the original idea that every endpoint could be directly addressed from every other endpoint.
An IP address identifies a host or interface; a transport port helps identify a service or application endpoint on that host.
465/587 — secure or submission-related email use, depending on configuration.
Port numbers are conventions, not magical restrictions. A service may run on another port, and encrypted protocols can have several deployment patterns.

IP provides addressing and packet delivery across interconnected networks. It is connectionless and offers best-effort delivery: packets may be lost, duplicated, delayed or arrive out of order. Higher layers add reliability when needed.
TCP establishes a connection and provides reliable, ordered delivery of a byte stream. It uses acknowledgements, sequence numbers, retransmission, flow control and congestion control.
The three-way handshake is commonly summarised:

Quiz trap: TCP does not guarantee that an application is correct or that the remote human received the message. It guarantees protocol-level ordered delivery between endpoints while the connection remains viable.

UDP sends datagrams without establishing a TCP-style connection and without built-in ordered retransmission. It has lower overhead and is useful where speed, timeliness or application-controlled recovery matters.
• QUIC as a modern transport foundation over UDP.

ICMP carries diagnostic and error messages. The ping utility commonly uses ICMP echo request and echo reply. Traceroute exploits changes in the IP time-to-live or hop limit and router responses to reveal a path.
ARP maps an IPv4 address to a link-layer address on a local network. IPv6 uses Neighbour Discovery mechanisms rather than ARP.
DHCP automatically supplies devices with configuration such as IP address, subnet information, default gateway and DNS server.
A common four-stage mnemonic is DORA:
DNS maps names to data such as IP addresses. It is a distributed hierarchical database, not simply one giant phone book on one server.
HTTP carries requests and responses for web resources. It is an application-layer protocol. Common methods include GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and HEAD.

HTTPS is HTTP protected by Transport Layer Security. It helps provide encryption, integrity and server authentication. The padlock does not prove that a site is honest; it indicates that the connection to the named site is protected under the certificate system.
TLS succeeded SSL. People often still say SSL certificate, but modern secure web connections use TLS. Certificates bind public keys to identities under a public-key infrastructure.
FTP transfers files but is not secure by default. FTPS adds TLS to FTP. SFTP is the SSH File Transfer Protocol and is technically different from FTPS.
SSH provides encrypted remote login and related services. It replaced insecure Telnet for many administrative uses.
SMTP is primarily used to send and relay email.
POP3 traditionally downloads messages to a client, often with simpler server synchronisation.
IMAP maintains mail on the server and synchronises folders and message state across devices.
NTP synchronises clocks across networks. Accurate time is vital for logs, security certificates, transactions and distributed systems.
SNMP monitors and manages network devices using managers, agents and management information.
SIP establishes, modifies and ends multimedia communication sessions such as voice-over-IP calls. The media itself is often carried separately using RTP.
RTP carries real-time audio or video data, commonly over UDP.
WebSocket establishes persistent, two-way communication between a client and server, useful for live chat, games, dashboards and collaboration.

Message Queuing Telemetry Transport is a lightweight publish-subscribe protocol widely associated with Internet of Things systems. Despite the expansion of its name, modern MQTT is not merely a conventional message queue.

QUIC was originally developed at Google and standardised through the IETF. It runs over UDP, integrates modern security and reduces some delays associated with establishing and recovering connections. HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics over QUIC rather than TCP.
8. ETHERNET: THE DOMINANT WIRED LOCAL NETWORK

Ethernet was developed at Xerox PARC by Robert Metcalfe and colleagues, drawing inspiration from the ALOHAnet radio network at the University of Hawaii. The name refers to the nineteenth-century concept of luminiferous ether, once imagined as a medium carrying electromagnetic waves.
Early Ethernet used a shared coaxial cable and Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection, abbreviated CSMA/CD.
• If the medium is free, transmit.
• Detect a collision if two devices transmit together.
• Stop, wait for a random interval and try again.
Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet largely eliminates collisions, but CSMA/CD remains a classic quiz association.
Digital Equipment Corporation, Intel and Xerox jointly promoted an Ethernet specification. DIX is formed from their initials.
• 10BASE-T: 10 megabits per second over twisted pair.
• Fibre variants support far higher speeds and distances.
• Speed evolution without abandoning the broad ecosystem.
• Adaptation from shared coaxial networks to switched twisted-pair and fibre systems.
PART II — THE BIRTH OF THE INTERNET

Early computers were expensive machines used by one job at a time. Time-sharing allowed multiple users to interact with a computer through terminals, making computing feel conversational rather than batch-based.

J. C. R. Licklider, a psychologist and computer scientist, envisioned interactive computing and a globally connected information environment. At ARPA’s Information Processing Techniques Office, he promoted networking among research computers. His phrase “Intergalactic Computer Network” became a favourite quiz clue.
Licklider did not build the Internet alone. His importance lies in articulating a vision, funding communities and encouraging interactive, networked computing.

The Soviet launch of Sputnik in 1957 shocked the United States. The Advanced Research Projects Agency, ARPA, was created in 1958 to pursue advanced research. It later became DARPA, returned for a period to ARPA and then again became DARPA.

ARPANET was not designed simply so that the United States could survive a nuclear attack. Resilience research influenced the era, particularly Baran’s work, but ARPANET’s immediate purpose centred on resource sharing and connecting research computers.
The first four ARPANET nodes in 1969 were:
• Stanford Research Institute, now SRI International.
The network used specialised packet-switching computers called Interface Message Processors, or IMPs. Bolt Beranek and Newman, usually BBN, built them using rugged Honeywell computers.
On October 29, 1969, UCLA attempted to log in to the computer at SRI.
The system transmitted L and O before crashing.
Therefore the famous first ARPANET message was “LO”. Leonard Kleinrock later compared it to “Lo and behold”, although that poetic interpretation was retrospective.
• Leonard Kleinrock: UCLA professor and queueing-theory pioneer.
• Charley Kline: student programmer who typed the first message.
• Bill Duvall: received the connection at SRI.
• Lawrence Roberts: managed ARPANET’s development at ARPA.
• Robert Taylor: promoted and funded networking at ARPA.
• Frank Heart: led BBN’s IMP team.
ARPANET initially used the Network Control Protocol, or NCP, for host communication. NCP was later replaced by TCP/IP.

Ray Tomlinson of BBN implemented network email across ARPANET in 1971. He selected the @ symbol to separate a user name from the host machine because it was uncommon in names and naturally meant “at”.
Tomlinson could not remember the exact first test message; accounts suggest it was an arbitrary string, not a grand historic phrase.
Email rapidly became one of ARPANET’s most popular uses, demonstrating a recurring lesson: users often decide what a network is for.

A major ARPANET demonstration occurred at the International Conference on Computer Communications in 1972. Robert Kahn organised it. The event exposed many computer professionals to packet networking.
11. FROM MANY NETWORKS TO AN INTERNET
The word internet can generically mean interconnected networks. The capitalised Internet refers to the global system based on the Internet Protocol suite.
Different packet networks used different technologies. How could they communicate without forcing every network to become identical?
Robert Kahn and Vinton Cerf developed a protocol architecture for interconnecting independent networks. Their 1974 paper described a protocol for packet network intercommunication.
The original Transmission Control Program handled several functions. The architecture was later divided:
• IP handled addressing and best-effort packet delivery.
This separation allowed applications needing speed rather than reliability to use alternatives such as UDP.

Many Internet functions are placed at the endpoints rather than requiring the network core to understand every application. The core moves packets; intelligent hosts perform reliability, security and application logic where appropriate.
A datagram is a self-contained packet routed independently. Louis Pouzin’s CYCLADES project strongly influenced datagram networking and Cerf and Kahn’s thinking.
In 1977, a celebrated demonstration linked packet radio, ARPANET and a satellite network using TCP, showing that heterogeneous networks could function as an internet.
ARPANET’s hosts were required to switch from NCP to TCP/IP on January 1, 1983. This coordinated migration is often treated as a defining birthday of the modern Internet.
The military portion of ARPANET separated as MILNET. ARPANET continued for research and was decommissioned in 1990.

The United States National Science Foundation funded supercomputing centres and the NSFNET backbone to connect researchers and institutions. NSFNET became a major successor backbone and helped spread TCP/IP beyond ARPANET.
• Regional networks connected to a national backbone.
• Network traffic shifted away from one government research network toward a diverse public and private infrastructure.
The NSFNET backbone was retired in 1995 as commercial networks took over backbone roles.
The Internet therefore has no single central machine and no single corporate owner. It is coordinated through standards, addressing systems, peering agreements, operators and institutions.
Develops and maintains many Internet standards through open technical working groups. Its informal tradition is captured by the phrase “rough consensus and running code”.
The RFC series documents protocols, practices, experiments and informational material. RFC 1, “Host Software”, was written by Steve Crocker in 1969.
Not every RFC is an Internet standard. The name Request for Comments survives even when a document is mature and authoritative.
Provides architectural oversight and guidance within the Internet standards ecosystem.
Founded in 1992 to support the open development, evolution and use of the Internet. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn were among its important founding figures.
Coordinates global protocol parameters, IP address allocation at the highest level and the DNS root zone. Jon Postel performed foundational IANA and RFC editorial work for many years.
ICANN — Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers

A nonprofit organisation created in 1998. It coordinates unique identifiers including domain-name and address-system functions through a multistakeholder model. ICANN is not “the owner of the Internet”.
IANA allocates large address blocks to five RIRs:
• ARIN — United States, Canada and parts of the Caribbean and North Atlantic region.
• LACNIC — Latin America and parts of the Caribbean.
• RIPE NCC — Europe, the Middle East and parts of Central Asia.

Founded by Tim Berners-Lee in 1994 to develop open Web standards. It is associated with HTML, CSS, accessibility and many Web technologies. The W3C and WHATWG have both played important roles in modern HTML development.
IEEE — Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
Standards body associated with Ethernet, Wi-Fi and many electrical and computing technologies. IEEE is pronounced “eye triple E”.

A United Nations specialised agency whose roots go back to the International Telegraph Union founded in 1865. It coordinates radio spectrum, satellite orbits and global telecommunications standards and development.

A partnership of standards organisations that develops cellular specifications including GSM evolution, UMTS, LTE and 5G systems. Its name still contains Third Generation even though its work extends far beyond 3G.
Industry organisation representing mobile operators and related companies. It organises Mobile World Congress.
END OF PARTS I AND II
PART III — THE WORLD WIDE WEB
The Web did not appear from nowhere. It combined several older ideas: linked documents, personal knowledge systems, networked computers, standard addressing and graphical interfaces.

In his 1945 essay “As We May Think”, American engineer and science administrator Vannevar Bush imagined a desk-like device called the Memex. It would store books, records and communications and allow users to create associative trails between items.

The Memex was never built as described, and it was based on microfilm rather than digital networking. Its importance lies in the idea that human thought proceeds through association rather than only through rigid indexes.

Theodor Holm Nelson coined the terms hypertext and hypermedia in the 1960s. His Project Xanadu sought a universal publishing system with persistent links, versioning and mechanisms for attribution and payment.

Nelson criticised ordinary Web links because they are often one-way and can break when a destination moves. His more ambitious idea of transclusion would include material from another document while maintaining its connection to the source.

Douglas Engelbart led the Augmentation Research Center at Stanford Research Institute. His team developed the oN-Line System, or NLS, featuring hypertext, windows, collaborative editing, outline processing and the computer mouse.

The 1968 demonstration later nicknamed “The Mother of All Demos” showed technologies that would take decades to become ordinary. Engelbart’s goal was not simply easier computing; it was augmenting collective human intellect.
Engelbart and William English built an early wooden pointing device. It was nicknamed a mouse because its cord resembled a tail. The patent described an X-Y position indicator for a display system.

Bill Atkinson created HyperCard for Apple. Released in 1987, it let Macintosh users organise information into stacks of linked cards and program interactions using HyperTalk. It helped popularise hypermedia thinking before the Web.
• Mother of All Demos and NLS — Douglas Engelbart.
• These systems inspired or paralleled the Web, but none was itself the World Wide Web.
15. TIM BERNERS-LEE AND THE BIRTH OF THE WEB

CERN, the European particle-physics laboratory near Geneva, hosted researchers from many institutions using incompatible computers and documentation systems. Information about experiments, people, equipment and software was difficult to connect and retrieve.

Tim Berners-Lee, a British software engineer working at CERN, proposed a system that combined hypertext with the Internet. His March 1989 proposal was titled “Information Management: A Proposal”. His supervisor Mike Sendall famously wrote “Vague but exciting” on it.

Belgian informatics engineer Robert Cailliau became a major collaborator and advocate. He co-authored a revised proposal, helped secure institutional support and later organised the first International World Wide Web Conference.
Describes the structure and links of a Web document.
Defines how a client requests a resource and a server responds.
Provides an address for a resource.
These worked over the already-existing Internet. Berners-Lee therefore invented the Web, not the Internet.
The first Web server and browser

Berners-Lee developed the first server, called httpd, and the first browser-editor on a NeXT computer. The browser was initially called WorldWideWeb and was later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion with the Web itself.
The NeXT computer carried a handwritten label warning people not to power it down because it was a server.
The first site was hosted at CERN and explained what the World Wide Web was, how to obtain a browser and how to set up a server. Its famous address began with info.cern.ch.

Nicola Pellow, a mathematics student working at CERN, wrote the Line Mode Browser. Unlike the NeXT browser, it could run on many text terminals. That portability was important in spreading access beyond one type of workstation.

CERN placed the Web software into the public domain on April 30, 1993, later issuing an open licence. This enabled people to use and improve the technology without paying CERN royalties. The open decision was fundamental to global adoption.
• Universality: any resource can link to another.
• Decentralisation: no central permission is required to publish a site.
• Open standards: protocols and formats should be implementable by many parties.
• Separation of layers: the Web can run over different networks and devices.
• End-to-end linking through globally understandable identifiers.
• Founded the World Wide Web Consortium at MIT in 1994.
• Became a leading advocate of open standards, net neutrality and personal control of data.
• Appeared in the opening ceremony of the 2012 London Olympics, typing “This is for everyone”.
• The first browser was not Mosaic; it was WorldWideWeb/Nexus.
• The first widely accessible cross-platform graphical browser was Mosaic, not the first browser of any kind.
• CERN did not own the Internet.
• The Web became successful because it used the Internet and was released openly.
• WWW is usually spoken as “double-u double-u double-u”; it has more syllables than “World Wide Web”.
16. URLS, URIS AND THE ANATOMY OF A WEB ADDRESS
Indicates the protocol or access method.
The domain name used to locate the server.
Optional explicit transport port. HTTPS conventionally uses 443.
Identifies a resource or route on the server.
Passes parameters, commonly as key-value pairs.
Points to a section within the retrieved resource. It is normally interpreted by the client and is not sent as part of the basic HTTP request to the server.

URI means Uniform Resource Identifier. URL is the familiar term for an identifier that indicates how or where a resource can be accessed. In ordinary use, Web address and URL remain acceptable, while technical standards increasingly use URI or more specific terms.
Characters that cannot safely appear directly in a URL may be represented by a percent sign followed by hexadecimal values. A space is commonly encoded as %20, although form data may use a plus sign.
Forward slashes separate path components. Backslashes are not the standard Web path separator.
Computers route using numerical IP addresses, but humans remember names more easily. DNS translates hierarchical names into records such as IP addresses and mail-server locations.
Represented conceptually by a dot at the end of a fully qualified domain name.
In example.com, example is the second-level label beneath .com.
In quiz.example.com, quiz is a subdomain.
A complete name leading to the DNS root. Technically it may be written with a final dot, such as www.example.com.
1. An application asks a recursive resolver.
3. If necessary, it asks a root server where to find the relevant top-level-domain servers.
4. It asks the TLD server where to find the authoritative server for the domain.
5. It asks the authoritative server for the requested record.
6. It returns and caches the answer for the permitted time.

There are 13 named root-server identities, labelled A through M. This does not mean only 13 physical machines exist. Anycast allows each identity to operate through many instances distributed around the world.
Maps a name to an IPv4 address.
Maps a name to an IPv6 address. It is called quadruple-A because IPv6 addresses are four times the length of IPv4 addresses.
Makes one name an alias of another canonical name.
Specifies mail-exchange servers for a domain.
Stores text. It is widely used for domain verification and email-security mechanisms such as SPF and DMARC.
Supports reverse lookup from an IP address to a name.
Start of Authority record containing essential administrative information about a DNS zone.
Identifies the host and port providing a named service.
States which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain.
Time to live tells resolvers how long an answer may be cached. A lower TTL enables faster changes but causes more frequent queries.
Operates the authoritative database for a top-level domain. For example, a registry manages the records for all names under its TLD.
A retail organisation accredited to register domain names for customers.
The person or organisation that registers the domain.
Coordinates the global domain-name system and accredits registrars under its policies.

Registering a domain corresponding to another party’s trademark or identity, often to profit from confusion or resale. The Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy, or UDRP, provides a process for many disputes.
.com, .org, .net and newer forms such as .app, .shop and .technology.

Two-letter domains such as .in for India, .uk for the United Kingdom and .jp for Japan. Some became globally marketed because their letters had commercial meaning, such as .tv for Tuvalu and .io for the British Indian Ocean Territory.
.edu, .gov and .mil have eligibility rules in their principal United States context. Other sponsored domains serve defined communities.
IDNs allow scripts beyond basic ASCII. Behind the scenes, Punycode represents many internationalised labels in an ASCII-compatible form beginning xn--.
• DNS is distributed, not one server.
• Thirteen root-server letters do not mean thirteen physical root machines.
• A domain registrar does not necessarily operate the TLD registry.
• A URL can contain an IP address, but domain names are usually more usable.
HTML marks the structure of content using elements such as headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, tables and forms. It is a markup language, not conventionally a programming language.
Early HTML grew from Berners-Lee’s requirements and ideas influenced by SGML. HTML5 later became the umbrella term for modern semantic elements, multimedia, graphics and application capabilities.

Cascading Style Sheets control presentation: layout, typography, spacing, colour, responsive design and visual adaptation. Håkon Wium Lie proposed CSS while working at CERN; Bert Bos was another central contributor.
Cascading refers to the rules that determine which style wins when browser defaults, external stylesheets, document rules and user preferences conflict.

Brendan Eich created JavaScript at Netscape in 1995 under intense time pressure, famously in about ten days. It was first called Mocha, then LiveScript, and finally JavaScript as part of a marketing relationship with Sun Microsystems.
JavaScript is not a simplified version of Java. The languages differ in design, type systems, runtime and history.
ECMAScript is the standardised language specification underlying JavaScript. ECMA International standardises it through Technical Committee 39, or TC39.
The Document Object Model represents a document as a tree of objects that scripts can inspect and modify. It enables dynamic pages that react to users and update without full reloads.
Extensible Markup Language uses custom tags to represent structured data. It became influential in document exchange, web services and configuration.

JavaScript Object Notation is a lightweight text format for structured data. Douglas Crockford helped popularise and specify it. JSON resembles JavaScript object syntax but is language-independent as a data interchange format.

AJAX means Asynchronous JavaScript and XML. Jesse James Garrett popularised the term in 2005. It describes Web applications that exchange data in the background and update part of a page without reloading the whole document. Modern AJAX often uses JSON rather than XML.
Lou Montulli created browser cookies at Netscape. A cookie is a small piece of data a site asks the browser to store and return with later requests.
First-party cookies are associated with the site being visited. Third-party cookies are set or read in a third-party context and became central to cross-site advertising and privacy debates.
Web Storage provides browser-side key-value storage. Unlike cookies, data is not automatically attached to every HTTP request.
The first browser and editor, written by Tim Berners-Lee for NeXT.
Text-based browser written by Nicola Pellow, important because it worked across many systems.
Created by Pei-Yuan Wei. It was an influential graphical browser for Unix and inspired features in later browsers.

Developed at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications by a team including Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina. Released in 1993, it combined graphics and text in an approachable interface and helped bring the Web to a mass audience.
Andreessen and Jim Clark founded Mosaic Communications, later renamed Netscape Communications. Netscape Navigator rapidly dominated early commercial Web browsing.

Microsoft licensed Mosaic-related technology from Spyglass and developed Internet Explorer. It bundled Internet Explorer with Windows and distributed it without a separate charge. Netscape’s market share collapsed.

The browser conflict became central to the United States antitrust case against Microsoft. Courts found that Microsoft had maintained its operating-system monopoly through anticompetitive conduct, although the company was not ultimately broken into two firms.
Netscape released browser source code through the Mozilla project. Mozilla was originally an internal Netscape codename blending Mosaic and killer, and its mascot became a red dinosaur.
Firefox emerged from the Mozilla project as a streamlined browser. Earlier names included Phoenix and Firebird before trademark issues produced Firefox.
Apple introduced Safari in 2003. Its WebKit engine was derived from KHTML and KJS, open-source technologies associated with the KDE project.
Google launched Chrome in 2008. Chromium is the open-source browser project on which Chrome is based. Chrome introduced a strong multi-process architecture and the V8 JavaScript engine.
Google forked WebKit to create the Blink rendering engine. Chrome, Chromium, Opera, modern Microsoft Edge and many other browsers use Blink.
The original Edge used Microsoft’s EdgeHTML engine. Microsoft later rebuilt Edge on Chromium, reflecting Chromium’s enormous influence over Web compatibility.

Opera originated at Norwegian telecom company Telenor before becoming an independent browser company. It was known for early innovations including tabs, speed dial and mobile compression. Opera moved from its Presto engine to Chromium/Blink.
Founded by Brendan Eich and Brian Bondy. Brave emphasises tracker blocking and privacy and uses Chromium as its technical base.
Built on Firefox ESR and designed to route traffic through the Tor anonymity network. Tor originally grew from United States Naval Research Laboratory onion-routing work.
Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge are browsers. Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo are search engines. A browser may use a search engine in its address bar, which causes the two categories to be confused.

Created by Alan Emtage at McGill University. Archie indexed filenames on public FTP servers and is often described as the first Internet search engine. Its name came from archive without the letter v.
Search tools for Gopher information spaces. Their names formed playful references to Archie Comics characters.

A menu-driven distributed information system created at the University of Minnesota. It competed with the early Web but lost ground partly because the Web’s hypertext and open publishing model proved more flexible.
Associated with Matthew Gray’s World Wide Web Wanderer, an early crawler designed initially to measure Web growth.
One of the first search engines to index the full text of Web pages rather than only titles or addresses.
Developed from Carnegie Mellon University research led by Michael Mauldin. Its name refers to Lycosidae, the wolf-spider family.

Jerry Yang and David Filo created “Jerry and David’s Guide to the World Wide Web”, a hand-organised directory. It became Yahoo. The official corporate expansion “Yet Another Hierarchically Organized Oracle” was a backronym or playful elaboration; the founders also liked the ordinary word yahoo.
Created at Digital Equipment Corporation. It became famous for speed, scale and advanced searching before losing leadership during the portal era and Google’s rise.
Used the fictional English valet Jeeves, created by P. G. Wodehouse, as a natural-language-search identity. It later became Ask.com.
Founded by Robin Li and Eric Xu. Its name comes from a line in a classical Chinese poem about searching hundreds of times for one’s beloved.
Its name is commonly explained as “Yet Another iNDEXer”. It grew into a major Russian search and technology company.
Larry Page and Sergey Brin’s Stanford project was initially called BackRub because it analysed backlinks. PageRank evaluated the Web’s link structure, treating links partly like academic citations.
PageRank is both a reference to Web pages and a pun on Larry Page’s surname.
Automated programs follow links and discover resources.
The engine analyses and stores information about content.
Algorithms order results in response to a query using relevance, quality, context and many other signals.
The engine presents results, snippets, rich answers, advertisements and specialised verticals.

A site can publish a robots.txt file giving crawler instructions. It is a voluntary convention, not an access-control or security mechanism. Sensitive data should not rely on robots.txt for protection.
A sitemap lists resources that a site wants search engines to discover. XML sitemaps are especially associated with machine-readable crawling support.
Search engine optimisation aims to improve unpaid visibility. Search engine marketing often refers to paid search advertising, although usage varies.
• Google was not the first search engine.
• Yahoo began as a human-curated directory, not primarily an algorithmic full-text engine.
• Archie searched FTP filenames rather than the modern Web.
• PageRank is only one historical component of Google’s much larger ranking systems.
21. FROM STATIC PAGES TO WEB APPLICATIONS
Sites largely consisted of documents written and uploaded by publishers. Users followed hyperlinks and read information, with limited interaction.
Darcy DiNucci used the phrase Web 2.0 in print before it was popularised by Tim O’Reilly and the Web 2.0 conferences. It came to describe participatory platforms featuring:
• Services that improved through user participation.
Web 2.0 was not a formal new version of HTTP or HTML.
Weblog was coined by Jorn Barger. Peter Merholz jokingly split it into “we blog”, helping popularise blog as noun and verb.
RSS has been expanded as RDF Site Summary, Rich Site Summary and Really Simple Syndication in different versions. It lets users subscribe to feeds of updates.
Ward Cunningham created WikiWikiWeb. Wiki comes from the Hawaiian word wiki, meaning quick. A wiki lets users collaboratively create and edit linked pages.

Podcast blends iPod and broadcasting, although podcasts do not require an Apple device. Ben Hammersley used the term in a 2004 newspaper article. Dave Winer and Adam Curry were important in developing and popularising enclosure-based audio distribution.
Streaming plays media as data arrives rather than requiring a complete download first. RealNetworks, Microsoft, Apple, YouTube, Netflix, Spotify and others shaped different stages of internet media.

Applications such as Gmail and Google Maps demonstrated that browser software could behave more like desktop applications through background requests, dynamic interfaces and large-scale server infrastructure.
PWAs use Web technologies and capabilities such as service workers, manifests, caching and install-like experiences to provide reliable and app-like behaviour.

Software as a Service delivers applications through networks, often by subscription. Salesforce helped popularise enterprise SaaS; Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 brought browser and cloud collaboration to mass audiences.

Web3 is an imprecise term usually associated with blockchains, decentralised applications, tokens and user-controlled digital assets. It should not be confused with Web 3.0 as Tim Berners-Lee’s older vision of the Semantic Web.
The Semantic Web sought machine-readable meaning through structured data, ontologies and linked data. Technologies include RDF, OWL and SPARQL.
HTTPS uses TLS to protect traffic between a client and server. It provides:
• Authentication of the server’s domain through certificates.

A certificate authority signs a digital certificate binding a public key to a domain or organisation under defined validation rules. Browsers and operating systems maintain trusted root-certificate stores.
Well-known organisations include DigiCert, Sectigo and Let’s Encrypt. Let’s Encrypt, operated by the nonprofit Internet Security Research Group, accelerated free automated HTTPS deployment.
Phishing impersonates a trusted party to steal credentials, payments or data. Spear phishing targets a specific person or organisation. Smishing uses SMS; vishing uses voice calls.
A fraudulent website may still use HTTPS. The certificate shows that the browser has an encrypted connection to the displayed domain, not that the business behind the domain is ethical.
XSS occurs when untrusted script executes in another site’s security context. It can steal sessions or alter pages.
CSRF tricks an authenticated browser into making an unwanted request to a site.
Untrusted input changes a database query. Parameterised queries are a central defence.
CSP lets sites restrict the sources from which scripts, styles and other resources may load, reducing some injection risks.
Browsers restrict scripts from one origin accessing data from another origin. An origin is generally defined by scheme, host and port.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing lets a server explicitly permit certain cross-origin browser requests through HTTP headers.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, or WCAG, are organised around four broad principles: content should be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. The acronym POUR helps remember them.
• Interfaces that do not depend on colour alone.
A page should not require one company’s private browser feature. Standards allow different browsers, devices and assistive technologies to interoperate.

W3C historically published HTML and many Web standards. The Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group, or WHATWG, developed a continuously updated HTML Living Standard after browser vendors sought a more implementation-driven approach. Modern Web standardisation reflects cooperation and occasional tension between these communities.
A tiny remote resource whose loading reveals information to a server.
Infers identity from characteristics such as fonts, screen size, hardware and browser behaviour.
A browser signal expressing a tracking preference. It lacked universal enforcement and broad industry compliance.
Reduces local history and cookie persistence after a session. It does not make the user invisible to websites, employers, internet providers or network administrators.
Only communicating endpoints possess the keys needed to read message content. The service provider may still observe metadata unless specifically protected.
Data about communication, such as sender, recipient, time, size, location or device. Metadata can reveal patterns even when content is encrypted.
PART IV — TELECOMMUNICATIONS AND MOBILE NETWORKS

The PSTN is the global collection of interconnected telephone networks. Historically it was circuit-switched and analogue at the edge, although core transmission became digital and modern voice increasingly uses packet technologies.
The physical connection between a subscriber and a local exchange, traditionally a pair of copper wires.
Switches calls among subscribers and toward other exchanges.
A high-capacity link between exchanges or network centres.
Control messages establish, manage and release calls. Modern telephone networks separate signalling from the voice path.

The ITU E.164 recommendation defines the international public telephone-number format. A country calling code follows the plus sign, such as +91 for India.

Many countries use a domestic trunk prefix, often 0, before an area or mobile number. It is normally omitted after the international country code because it is not part of the global subscriber number.
25. DIAL-UP, ISDN, DSL AND CABLE INTERNET
A dial-up modem converted computer data into audible signals compatible with ordinary voice circuits. It called an internet service provider and occupied the telephone line.
The sequence of tones and noise represented call progress, negotiation, carrier detection, speed and error-control training. It was not random interference.
Baud measures symbols per second. A symbol can encode more than one bit, so baud and bits per second are not always equal.

Integrated Services Digital Network carried digital voice and data over telephone infrastructure. Basic Rate Interface commonly provided two 64-kilobit-per-second bearer channels and one signalling channel, remembered as 2B+D.
Digital Subscriber Line technologies send high-frequency data over copper telephone lines while allowing voice service on lower frequencies.
Asymmetric DSL offers higher downstream than upstream speed, matching typical consumer use.
Very-high-bit-rate DSL supports higher speeds over shorter copper distances.
A Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexer aggregates customer DSL connections at the provider.
Uses cable-television networks, commonly through DOCSIS standards. A neighbourhood may share capacity over part of the access network.
FTTC — fibre to the cabinet or curb, followed by another medium for the final segment.

A powerful transmitter covering an entire region would use scarce radio spectrum inefficiently. Cellular systems divide territory into smaller coverage areas called cells. Frequencies can be reused in sufficiently separated cells, multiplying capacity.

Cell diagrams are often drawn as hexagons because hexagons tile neatly and approximate coverage planning. Real radio cells are irregular because buildings, terrain, antennas, power and interference alter propagation.
As a subscriber moves, the network transfers the connection from one cell or base station to another.
4G LTE — eNodeB or evolved Node B.
A tower commonly uses directional antennas to divide coverage into sectors, often three 120-degree sectors. One visible tower may therefore host several logical cells and multiple operators.

The same spectrum channel can be used in non-adjacent cells where interference remains acceptable. Smaller cells can increase capacity, but they require denser infrastructure and careful coordination.
These terms describe progressively smaller coverage contexts, though exact power and radius definitions vary. Femtocells are often installed indoors for a home or small office.
27. SIM, IMEI, IMSI AND MOBILE IDENTITY
Subscriber Identity Module. It stores subscriber credentials and enables authentication to a mobile network. The SIM evolved from full-size cards to mini, micro and nano formats.

An integrated SIM places secure subscriber functionality within a system-on-chip or closely integrated secure hardware.
International Mobile Subscriber Identity. Identifies the subscriber within mobile-network systems. It includes country and network information plus a subscriber identifier.
International Mobile Equipment Identity. Identifies the device equipment rather than the subscription.

A subscriber uses a visited network outside the home operator’s normal coverage. The visited and home networks authenticate, route and settle charges under roaming agreements.

Spectrum is divided into frequency bands and licensed or unlicensed uses. Lower frequencies generally travel farther and penetrate buildings better; higher frequencies can offer greater bandwidth but often require denser coverage.
Governments may assign commercial licences through auctions. Spectrum is not sold as physical property in the ordinary sense; operators receive defined rights under licence conditions.
Frequency Division Duplex uses separate frequency ranges for uplink and downlink.

Frequency Division Multiple Access gives users separate frequency channels.
Time Division Multiple Access gives users time slots.
Code Division Multiple Access separates users through spreading codes over shared spectrum.
Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access divides spectrum into many orthogonal subcarriers and allocates groups to users. It is central to LTE downlink and 5G.
Multiple Input Multiple Output uses multiple antennas and signal paths to increase capacity, reliability or coverage.
Shapes and directs radio energy toward a receiver rather than radiating equally in all directions.
A retrospective label for pre-cellular mobile radio telephone systems. Car-phone services relied on a small number of high-power channels and manual or automatic connection to the telephone network.
Pagers received short alerts or numeric/text messages. They became cultural symbols of doctors, emergency workers and 1980s–1990s business communication.
First-generation cellular networks were analogue and primarily carried voice.

Qualcomm commercialised code-division techniques through IS-95, often called cdmaOne. Later CDMA2000 evolved the family toward 3G.

GSM commonly used removable SIM identity from an early stage. Many CDMA markets historically tied subscriber identity more closely to the device, though later systems could also use removable modules.

On December 3, 1992, engineer Neil Papworth sent the text “Merry Christmas” from a computer to Vodafone executive Richard Jarvis’s Orbitel 901 handset. Phones could not initially send SMS text directly in the same way.
The original payload fit into spare signalling capacity. Standard GSM text commonly allows 160 seven-bit characters. Longer messages are split and reassembled.
Friedhelm Hillebrand is associated with analysing typical postcard and telex message lengths and helping settle on 160 characters within the technical constraints.
Multimedia Messaging Service carries images, audio, video and longer content through operator systems. It differs from ordinary internet messaging apps.

Improved data rates through more efficient modulation and coding. It is sometimes labelled 2.75G.
The ITU’s IMT-2000 framework defined a family of third-generation capabilities rather than one universal air interface.
Universal Mobile Telecommunications System, commonly using WCDMA radio technology and evolving from GSM.
Time Division Synchronous Code Division Multiple Access, strongly associated with Chinese development and deployment.

LTE Advanced later met fuller IMT-Advanced requirements through technologies such as carrier aggregation.

Early LTE phones often moved temporarily to 2G or 3G for voice because LTE networks were originally deployed as data systems.
Combines multiple radio carriers to create a wider effective channel and increase throughput.
LTE does not expand to Long-Term Evolutionary. The correct expansion is Long Term Evolution.
5G NR is the 3GPP radio technology for fifth-generation systems. The ITU framework is called IMT-2020.
Higher data capacity and dense broadband use.
Industrial control and other demanding communication scenarios.
Very large numbers of low-power connected devices.

NSA deployments use 5G radio alongside a 4G LTE core and control anchor. They allowed operators to launch 5G faster.
SA uses a 5G core and enables fuller support for capabilities such as network slicing and lower-latency service architecture.
Sub-6 GHz provides broader coverage and better penetration. Millimetre-wave bands offer large bandwidth but shorter range and weaker penetration, requiring dense small cells.
Mid-band, including frequencies around 3.3 to 3.8 GHz in many countries, became especially important because it balances coverage and capacity.
Creates logically separated networks with different performance and policy characteristics on shared infrastructure.
Uses large antenna arrays to serve multiple users and steer beams efficiently.
3GPP Release 18 begins the phase commonly called 5G Advanced, extending positioning, energy efficiency, extended reality, satellite integration and automation.
6G remains a research and standardisation programme, not an established mass-market commercial generation as of July 2026.

A phone shares its mobile-data connection with other devices through Wi-Fi, USB or Bluetooth.

Associated with the transistor, information theory, Unix, C, lasers, communications satellites, charge-coupled devices and many Nobel Prize-winning advances. It belonged historically to AT&T, later Lucent and Alcatel-Lucent; Nokia acquired Alcatel-Lucent.
Founded as Galvin Manufacturing Corporation. Its Motorola car-radio brand combined motor with the popular audio suffix -ola. It later became the corporate name.

Founded by Lars Magnus Ericsson in Sweden. A major telecom-equipment and network company. Sony Ericsson was a handset joint venture; Sony later bought Ericsson’s share.

Named after the Finnish town and river area associated with its nineteenth-century industrial operations. After selling its phone business to Microsoft, Nokia focused on network infrastructure and later acquired Alcatel-Lucent.

Chinese telecom-equipment and consumer-electronics company founded by Ren Zhengfei. Its name is difficult to translate exactly but is often associated with Chinese achievement. Wi-Fi is a family of wireless local-area-network technologies based principally on the IEEE 802.11 standards. It connects devices over radio to an access point or directly to one another.
Wi-Fi is not the Internet. A Wi-Fi network may provide Internet access, local-only communication or no external connection at all.

Wi-Fi does not officially expand to Wireless Fidelity. Early 802.11 work drew on wireless LAN developments including NCR and AT&T’s WaveLAN. Vic Hayes chaired the IEEE 802.11 working group and is often called the father of Wi-Fi.

The original 1997 standard, supporting low data rates.

The login or acceptance page presented on hotel, airport, café or campus Wi-Fi. A captive portal does not itself mean that all wireless traffic is encrypted.

46. INTERNET EXCHANGE POINTS, PEERING AND TRANSIT
An Autonomous System, or AS, is a network or group of networks under one administrative routing policy. It receives an Autonomous System Number, or ASN.
Border Gateway Protocol exchanges reachability information among autonomous systems. It is often called the routing protocol of the Internet.
BGP chooses paths based on policy as well as technical reachability. It does not simply select the geographically shortest route.
Two networks exchange traffic directly, often without payment when benefits are roughly balanced. Public peering occurs at an Internet exchange; private peering uses dedicated links.
One network pays another to carry traffic toward the rest of the Internet.
An IXP is shared infrastructure where networks interconnect. It reduces cost, latency and dependence on distant transit paths.
A network accidentally announces routes in a way that attracts traffic it should not carry.
Incorrect or malicious route announcements redirect traffic toward the wrong network.
Resource Public Key Infrastructure lets networks cryptographically authorise which autonomous systems may originate their IP prefixes. It helps reject some invalid BGP announcements.

The same IP address is announced from multiple locations. Routing directs users toward a nearby or topologically favourable instance. DNS root servers and content-delivery networks commonly use anycast.
47. DATA CENTRES, CLOUD AND CONTENT DELIVERY
A facility containing servers, storage, network equipment, power systems and cooling.
Cloud providers group data centres into geographic regions and separate availability zones to reduce correlated failure. Exact definitions differ by provider.
Complete applications delivered over a network.
Shared provider infrastructure offered to customers.
Cloud-style infrastructure dedicated to one organisation.
Coordinates private systems with public cloud services.
Processes data closer to users or sensors rather than only in distant central data centres. It reduces latency, bandwidth use and dependence on a remote connection.
A CDN stores or serves copies of content from distributed locations near users.
Founded by MIT professor Tom Leighton and student Danny Lewin, building on algorithms for distributing Web content. The name comes from a Hawaiian word meaning intelligent or clever.
Provides CDN, DNS, security and edge-computing services. Its 1.1.1.1 public DNS resolver became a recognisable product.
A cache stores frequently needed data closer to where it will be used. Browser cache, DNS cache, proxy cache and CDN edge cache operate at different layers.
The system must retrieve it from another source.
48. PERFORMANCE: DO NOT CONFUSE THESE TERMS
The theoretical or configured capacity of a link, commonly measured in bits per second.
The useful rate actually achieved after protocol overhead, congestion, radio conditions and system limits.
The rate of useful application payload, excluding retransmissions and protocol overhead.
Time taken for data to travel from source to destination. Round-trip time measures there and back.
Variation in packet delay. Voice and video are highly sensitive to jitter.
Packets fail to arrive. TCP may retransmit, while real-time applications may conceal or tolerate limited loss.
Mbps means megabits per second. MB/s means megabytes per second. Eight bits make one byte, so 80 Mbps has a theoretical maximum of about 10 MB/s before overhead.
Download moves data toward the user. Upload moves data from the user. Consumer services are often asymmetric.
Communication can flow in both directions, but not simultaneously.
The utility measures reachability and round-trip response using ICMP in common implementations. A low ping time does not guarantee high bandwidth.
Shows routers or hops along a path by eliciting expiry responses. Some hops may not reply or may appear misleading because of filtering and asymmetric routes.
QoS prioritises or manages traffic classes to control delay, loss and bandwidth. It cannot create capacity that does not exist.
Occurs when offered traffic exceeds available capacity or buffers. Packets wait, latency rises and packets may be dropped.
TCP senders infer congestion from loss or delay and adjust transmission. Algorithms evolved from work by Van Jacobson after severe Internet congestion in the 1980s.
Oversized or poorly managed buffers prevent packet loss but create extreme latency under load. Modern queue-management approaches seek a better balance.
A distributed denial-of-service attack overwhelms a target using traffic from many sources. Botnets of compromised computers, routers and IoT devices may participate.
A famous botnet that exploited insecure Internet of Things devices. In 2016 it generated massive attacks, including one against DNS provider Dyn that disrupted access to major websites.
A component whose failure can disable an entire system. Redundancy reduces such dependence, but common software, shared power or configuration can create hidden correlated failures.
A service may be running yet appear unreachable when names cannot be resolved.
Incorrect routing announcements can make networks unreachable or send traffic through unsuitable paths.
Expired certificates or incorrect time can prevent otherwise functioning encrypted services from connecting.
Some of the largest outages result from routine configuration changes rather than exotic attacks.
50. NET NEUTRALITY AND THE DIGITAL DIVIDE
The principle that Internet access providers should treat lawful traffic without unjust discrimination based on source, destination, application or payment.
A provider does not count a selected service against the user’s data allowance. Supporters call it affordable access; critics argue that it lets gatekeepers favour certain platforms.
Unequal access to useful connectivity due to:
Policies and funds seek to extend communication to high-cost or underserved areas where ordinary market incentives may be insufficient.
