PART VII — INDIA’S TELECOM AND INTERNET STORY
The East India Company and William Brooke O’Shaughnessy

William Brooke O’Shaughnessy, an Irish physician and scientist working in India, conducted telegraph experiments and helped build the first major Indian electric-telegraph network. An experimental line connected Calcutta with Diamond Harbour in 1850–1851.

Following successful trials, a rapidly expanding system linked Calcutta, Agra, Bombay, Madras and Peshawar. Telegraphy became strategically important to administration, commerce, railways and military control.

Telegraph lines helped British authorities transmit information during the uprising of 1857. Rebels also recognised their strategic value and cut lines. The technology’s role is therefore both a communications milestone and a reminder that networks shape political power.
Postal and telegraph services were administered together for much of their history. The telegram became a standard form of urgent official and personal communication.
BSNL ended its public telegram service in India in July 2013 after demand collapsed under telephones, mobile messaging and the Internet. The final day became a nostalgia-driven news event.
• O’Shaughnessy also pioneered intravenous-fluid research and introduced cannabis preparations into Western medicine.
• Calcutta–Diamond Harbour is the classic early Indian telegraph route.
• The telegraph predates the telephone and Indian radio broadcasting.
The first formal telephone exchanges in India opened in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1882. The systems began with a small number of subscribers and manual operators.

A trunk call connected different local telephone areas. Users often booked calls through operators and waited for a circuit. Categories such as ordinary, urgent and lightning reflected priority and price.
STD allowed callers to dial long-distance calls directly without booking an operator. STD booths became a defining symbol of Indian communication before mass mobile adoption.
Public Call Offices offered local, STD and ISD calling. Their signs—STD/ISD/PCO—were ubiquitous in towns, railway stations and markets.
International Subscriber Dialling allowed direct international calls. India’s country calling code is +91.
The Department of Telecommunications, or DoT, operates within the Ministry of Communications. It handles policy, licensing, spectrum administration and related telecom responsibilities.
The Telecom Commission was renamed the Digital Communications Commission, reflecting the shift from traditional telephony toward digital connectivity.
Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited was created in 1986 to provide services in Delhi and Mumbai. Its name means metropolitan telephone corporation.
Videsh Sanchar Nigam Limited was created in 1986 for international telecommunications. Videsh means foreign or overseas communication. It launched public Internet service in India in 1995.
The Tata Group acquired a controlling stake in VSNL during privatisation in 2002. The company was renamed Tata Communications in 2008.
Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited was incorporated in 2000 to take over telecom service operations from the Department of Telecom Services and Department of Telecom Operations, except in Delhi and Mumbai.

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India was established in 1997 as an independent regulator. It makes recommendations and regulates tariffs, interconnection, quality of service and consumer matters under the legal framework.
The Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal adjudicates disputes and appeals in the telecom and broadcasting sectors.
The Wireless Planning and Coordination Wing of the DoT manages radio-frequency spectrum and wireless licensing responsibilities.
The Centre for Development of Telematics was established in 1984 as an autonomous telecom research organisation. It became famous for developing digital exchanges suitable for Indian conditions.
54. SAM PITRODA AND THE TELECOM REVOLUTION

Born in Titlagarh, Odisha, Sam Pitroda trained in physics and electrical engineering and worked in telecommunications in the United States. He became a central adviser in India’s 1980s technology missions.
Imported exchanges were expensive and often unsuitable for dust, heat, unreliable power and dispersed rural demand. C-DOT designed digital switching systems adapted to Indian conditions.
RAX systems connected villages and small towns. They had to be rugged, maintainable and economical at relatively small subscriber capacities.
Pitroda advised Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and became associated with missions in telecommunications, literacy, immunisation, drinking water, dairy development and oilseeds.
Public call offices converted connectivity into a small-business service. Instead of waiting years for a private home telephone, citizens could pay for calls at a neighbourhood booth.

Pitroda did not single-handedly invent India’s telephone system. His distinctive role was institution-building, indigenous digital-switching development and policy advocacy during a critical transformation.
55. ERNET AND THE ARRIVAL OF THE INTERNET
The Education and Research Network began in 1986 as a collaborative project involving the Department of Electronics and leading educational institutions.
• National Centre for Software Technology, later connected to C-DAC.
ERNET connected academic and research users and helped build Indian expertise in networking, email and Internet protocols before mass public access.

The National Informatics Centre built NICNET, a satellite-based government informatics network connecting central, state and district administrations. It supported e-governance long before the phrase became routine.

VSNL launched commercial public Internet service in India on August 15, 1995. Early users connected through dial-up modems, faced high prices and often struggled with congestion and limited access numbers.
The date was symbolically chosen as Independence Day.
VSNL’s service was marketed as Gateway Internet Access Service, commonly GIAS. Shell accounts and TCP/IP accounts offered different levels of connectivity.
• Rediff, founded by Ajit Balakrishnan, became an early Indian portal and email provider.
• Sify grew from Satyam Infoway and became a major early ISP and portal.
• IndiaWorld, founded by Rajesh Jain, was acquired by Satyam Infoway in a landmark dot-com-era transaction.
• Indiatimes grew from the Times Group.
• Naukri.com, founded by Sanjeev Bikhchandani, became a landmark Indian Internet business.
.in is India’s country-code top-level domain. Registration expanded substantially after liberalised policies in 2005.
The National Internet Exchange of India was established to improve domestic Internet routing and manage key Internet resources.
• Supporting Internet adoption and related programmes.
• Serving as the national Internet registry function through IRINN for IP resources in India under APNIC’s framework.
Without domestic peering, traffic from one Indian network to another might travel through foreign transit points, increasing latency and cost. IXPs let networks exchange local traffic locally.
India supports domain names in multiple scripts. Examples of internationalised country-code domains correspond to Bharat in Devanagari and other Indian scripts.
India’s first commercial mobile call was made on July 31, 1995 between West Bengal Chief Minister Jyoti Basu in Calcutta and Union Communications Minister Sukh Ram in New Delhi.
The call used Modi Telstra’s MobileNet service. Modi Telstra was a joint venture between India’s B. K. Modi group and Australia’s Telstra.
• Public Internet and mobile service both arrived in 1995.
• Jyoti Basu and Sukh Ram are the two personalities.
• Calcutta, not Bengaluru or Mumbai, is central to the first-call story.
Calls were expensive, handsets costly and incoming calls were initially charged. Mobile phones were status symbols rather than universal utilities.
A major policy transition made the caller, rather than the recipient, pay for ordinary mobile calls. Free incoming calls helped accelerate adoption.
Prepaid service lowered barriers by removing credit checks and monthly bills. Small recharge denominations matched irregular incomes and made mobile access mass-market.

Sunil Bharti Mittal founded Bharti and entered telecom after earlier ventures including bicycle parts and push-button phones. Airtel became one of India’s largest mobile operators and expanded across Africa.
• Earlier brand styling included Airtel with a distinctive red identity.
• “Express Yourself” became a famous campaign line.
• A. R. Rahman composed a celebrated Airtel signature tune.

The undivided Reliance group launched a mass-market CDMA service under the “Monsoon Hungama” campaign in 2003. The business later belonged to Anil Ambani’s Reliance Communications and eventually entered insolvency.

Reliance Industries built an all-IP 4G network and commercially launched Jio in September 2016 after an employee trial phase. Free introductory voice and data offers triggered explosive adoption and severe industry price competition.
• Affordable smartphones and JioPhone feature phones.
Vodafone India and Idea Cellular merged in 2018 to form Vodafone Idea, branded Vi. The merger responded to intense competition and sector consolidation.
Idea’s ownership roots included the Aditya Birla Group, Tata and AT&T-related partnerships under earlier names such as Birla AT&T and Batata. Corporate ownership changed over time.

Mumbai’s mobile service passed through brand identities including Max Touch, Orange and Hutch before Vodafone acquired Hutchison’s Indian interests. The Hutch pug and “Wherever you go, our network follows” became iconic advertising.
Operated Tata Indicom CDMA and Tata Docomo GSM services. NTT Docomo’s name combines Do Communications over the Mobile Network and the Japanese word dokomo, meaning everywhere.
An operator with strong roots in Tamil Nadu that expanded nationally before entering insolvency amid intense competition and debt.
Norway’s Telenor entered India through Unitech Wireless. The brand became Uninor and later Telenor India before Bharti Airtel acquired its operations.
Sistema Shyam offered CDMA services under Russia-linked MTS branding. Its wireless business was acquired by Reliance Communications.
Earlier BPL Mobile in Mumbai; later renamed Loop. Its attempted sale to Airtel did not complete before closure.
India moved toward licence frameworks allowing operators to offer different access technologies under unified conditions.
Licences and spectrum allocated in 2008 at prices linked to older benchmarks became the subject of allegations of arbitrary procedure and lost public revenue.

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s presumptive-loss estimates became politically explosive. The Supreme Court cancelled 122 licences in 2012, citing an unconstitutional and arbitrary allocation process.
In 2017, a special CBI court acquitted all accused in the criminal trial because the prosecution failed to prove the charges. These two facts are not contradictory:
• The Supreme Court invalidated the administrative allocation.
• The criminal court found the prosecution had not established individual criminal guilt beyond the required standard.
Avoid reducing the issue to one slogan. Questions may distinguish spectrum policy, licence cancellation, presumptive loss and criminal acquittal.
India increasingly used auctions for commercial mobile spectrum. Different bands offer different coverage and capacity characteristics.

Adjusted Gross Revenue determines licence-fee and spectrum-charge obligations. A long dispute concerned whether AGR included only telecom revenue or broader company revenue. Supreme Court rulings produced major liabilities for operators.
60. MOBILE NUMBER PORTABILITY AND CONSUMER SYSTEMS
National mobile-number portability allows a subscriber to retain the same number when changing operator, including across service areas under current arrangements.
A Unique Porting Code authorises a port request. Users traditionally request it through a prescribed SMS format, subject to eligibility rules.
The National Customer Preference Register lets users limit unsolicited commercial communications. Earlier usage made “Do Not Disturb” the common phrase.
The short code 1909 became associated with telecom commercial-communication preferences and complaints.
A Department of Telecommunications citizen platform supporting services related to lost or stolen phones, connections issued in a user’s name and device authenticity.
The Central Equipment Identity Register enables blocking of a stolen device’s IMEI across networks, subject to process.
Telecom Analytics for Fraud Management and Consumer Protection helps users inspect mobile connections issued in their name.
NOFN was conceived to connect gram panchayats with broadband fibre. It was later renamed BharatNet.

A flagship rural-broadband infrastructure project intended to provide middle-mile connectivity to gram panchayats. Service delivery to homes and institutions still requires last-mile operators, Wi-Fi, fibre or other access networks.
Bharat Broadband Network Limited was created as the project’s special-purpose vehicle and later merged into BSNL.

The Universal Service Obligation Fund financed rural telecom expansion through levies on operators. Under the Telecommunications Act, 2023 framework, it was recast as Digital Bharat Nidhi with a broader digital-connectivity purpose.
Laying fibre to a gram panchayat does not automatically mean every household receives high-speed service. Backhaul, active equipment, power, maintenance, pricing and local last mile all matter.
The National Knowledge Network connects universities, laboratories, libraries, healthcare institutions and government research organisations through high-capacity links.
• NKN focuses on knowledge and research institutions.
• BharatNet focuses on rural broadband infrastructure to gram panchayats.
MTNL and BSNL were early Indian 3G launchers. Private operators followed after spectrum auctions.

Broadband Wireless Access auctions in 2010 allocated spectrum including the 2300 MHz band. Infotel Broadband won pan-India spectrum and was acquired by Reliance Industries, becoming a foundation of Jio’s network.
Bharti Airtel launched India’s first commercial 4G service in Kolkata in 2012 using TD-LTE. Jio’s 2016 national launch drove mass 4G adoption.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi formally launched 5G services in India on October 1, 2022 at the India Mobile Congress in New Delhi.
Airtel initially emphasised non-standalone 5G layered on its 4G network. Jio emphasised standalone 5G with a new 5G core.
India’s principal 5G auction bands included low-band 700 MHz, mid-band 3300–3670 MHz and high-band 26 GHz, alongside other spectrum.

5Gi was an Indian radio-interface proposal developed through institutions including IIT Madras, IIT Hyderabad and the Centre of Excellence in Wireless Technology. It included a low-mobility-large-cell concept for rural coverage. Elements were harmonised into global 3GPP specifications rather than becoming an isolated incompatible network.

BSNL pursued an Indian-developed 4G stack involving a consortium led by Tata Consultancy Services with C-DOT supplying core technology and Tejas Networks supplying radio equipment, alongside other partners.
• Reduces dependence on a small set of foreign network vendors.
• Builds domestic telecom intellectual property and manufacturing.
• Creates a foundation intended to be upgradeable toward 5G.
• Links TCS, C-DOT and Tejas—three highly quizable Indian technology institutions.

An Indian optical and broadband equipment company founded by technologists including Sanjay Nayak. Tata Sons acquired a controlling stake through Panatone Finvest. Tejas became central to the BSNL radio-access rollout.
C-DOT developed the packet core and related network elements. The project revived its historic role in indigenous telecom systems.
TCS acts as systems integrator, coordinating deployment, software, equipment and network implementation at national scale.
A domestically integrated stack may still contain globally sourced semiconductor components. Indigenous design, intellectual property, system integration and manufacturing are different claims.
India released the Bharat 6G Vision document in 2023, setting ambitions for research, standards, intellectual property and affordable global connectivity.
An industry, academic and research platform intended to coordinate the Indian 6G ecosystem and connect it with international alliances.
India established an indigenous 6G test bed involving academic institutions to support research and validation.
India does not have commercial 6G service as of July 2026. Vision documents, patents and test beds are preparation for the 2030-era standards cycle.

The Indian National Satellite System combines telecommunications, television broadcasting, meteorology, search and rescue and other services. It transformed long-distance communication and national broadcasting.
Ariane Passenger Payload Experiment was India’s first experimental geostationary communication satellite. Launched in 1981 by an Ariane rocket, it helped build experience in satellite communications.

A photograph shows the APPLE satellite’s antenna test model being transported on a bullock cart to avoid electromagnetic interference from vehicles. It symbolises frugal ingenuity but is often miscaptioned as the operational satellite being taken to the launch pad.
A family of Indian communication satellites supporting broadcasting, broadband, mobile communication and strategic services.
GSAT-3, launched in 2004, was India’s first satellite dedicated primarily to educational services.
GSAT-9, launched in 2017, provides communication services to participating South Asian countries. Pakistan did not participate.

Navigation with Indian Constellation, formerly IRNSS, is a regional satellite-navigation system rather than an Internet constellation. It provides positioning and timing over India and surrounding regions.

Operators require spectrum, landing rights, licences and security approvals. Debates include whether satellite spectrum should be auctioned or administratively assigned under global coordination practices.
67. INDIAN SUBMARINE CABLES AND GLOBAL GATEWAYS
India’s major cable landing hubs include Mumbai and Chennai. Other landing points and planned systems increase geographic diversity.

Through the VSNL inheritance and later investment, Tata Communications operates a major global subsea and terrestrial network. Its TGN, Tata Global Network, became one of the world’s extensive privately owned fibre systems.
Reliance Communications acquired FLAG Telecom, gaining a global undersea-cable network. The business later passed through restructuring and ownership changes.
Bharti participated in systems including i2i, connecting India and Singapore, and invested in new international capacity.
Google-backed systems such as Blue-Raman and other consortium cables have expanded routes toward India and surrounding regions.

Cable diversity matters because many Indian routes historically concentrated through a limited number of landing cities and westward corridors. More routes improve resilience and reduce latency to Asia, Africa, Europe and the Middle East.
68. INDIA’S DIGITAL PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE AND CONNECTIVITY
This topic belongs chiefly to Module 8, but the network layer must be understood here.

The Unified Payments Interface is a real-time payment system operated by NPCI. It depends on mobile connectivity, bank systems and interoperable APIs.
Provides authenticated digital documents and issuer–requester exchange.
Digital platform used to manage India’s COVID-19 vaccination programme.
Open Network for Digital Commerce uses open specifications to connect buyers, sellers, logistics and service providers across platforms.
An umbrella expression for digital identity, payments, data exchange and consent-based public infrastructure. The exact list evolves and should not be treated as one legally fixed product.
Digital public infrastructure multiplies the value of mobile broadband. Conversely, weak devices, poor coverage, language barriers and low digital literacy can turn nominal access into exclusion.

MODULE 4 — TECHNOLOGY COMPANIES, PERSONALITIES, BRANDS AND PRODUCTS
The Ultra-Comprehensive TCS InQuizitive 2026 Master Pack
Research cut-off for changing corporate facts: July 28, 2026
This module is not a directory of companies. It is a map of the modern technology industry and the stories from which quiz questions are built.
For every important company, you should be able to answer eight different kinds of questions:
• Origin: Who founded it, where, when and to solve what problem?
• Name: What did the name originally mean, and what earlier name was rejected or replaced?
• Product: Which product made the company famous, and which product actually made it profitable?
• Pivot: What did it begin as, and what did it later become?
• Ownership: Which parent owns it, and what major brands has it acquired or sold?
• Failure: Which celebrated launch failed, and why?
• Identity: Can you recognise its old logos, mascots, slogans, headquarters and founders?
• Rivalry: Which competitor, lawsuit, platform war or business-model change shaped it?
The deepest preparation method is to learn companies as connected family trees rather than isolated entries. For example:
Hollerith census machines → Tabulating Machine Company → Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company → IBM → System/360 → IBM PC → sale of PC division to Lenovo → acquisition of Red Hat.
Fairchild Semiconductor → Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore → Intel → x86 processors → IBM PC ecosystem → Microsoft DOS and Windows → Wintel.
Xerox PARC → graphical user-interface research → Apple Lisa and Macintosh → Microsoft Windows → modern desktop computing.

A founder creates the organisation. Several people may be recognised as co-founders, but corporate origin stories are frequently disputed. A person who joined soon after launch may be popularly called a founder even when legal records use a different description. Use the company’s own formulation where possible.

Alphabet is the parent company; Google is its largest operating company; Google Search is a product. Meta is the company; Facebook is an app. One 97 Communications is the listed company; Paytm is the consumer brand. Alphabet, Google and Google Search are therefore not interchangeable answers.

A subsidiary is legally controlled by another company. A division is an internal business unit rather than a separate ownership relationship. YouTube is a Google subsidiary or business; AWS is a division of Amazon; Instagram and WhatsApp belong to Meta.

An acquisition occurs when one company purchases another. A merger combines organisations, although the word may conceal the fact that one side gained effective control. A consolidation may create a new corporate entity.

A spin-off creates an independent company from an existing business. Examples include PayPal’s separation from eBay and IBM’s spin-off of Kyndryl. A split may produce two successor companies, as Hewlett-Packard did with HP Inc. and Hewlett Packard Enterprise.

An initial public offering sells shares to the public with underwriters and newly issued or existing stock. A direct listing places existing shares on an exchange without the conventional IPO process. Spotify and Coinbase became famous direct-listing examples.

A product performs a task. A platform lets other people build, sell or operate on top of it. An ecosystem links hardware, software, services, developers, advertisers, suppliers and users so that each reinforces the others.
A product may become more valuable as more people use it. Social networks, marketplaces, payment systems and communication platforms often benefit from network effects.

A vertically integrated company controls several layers of the supply chain. Apple designs operating systems, chips, devices, services and stores. Samsung spans components and consumer products. Amazon combines marketplace, fulfilment, cloud infrastructure, devices, advertising and media.
A company expands into adjacent products at the same broad layer. Adobe moved from PostScript into creative applications, documents and digital experience software.
A moat is a durable competitive advantage, such as a brand, patent portfolio, network effect, switching cost, data advantage, distribution system or scale economy.

A killer app is so useful that customers purchase the underlying hardware or platform to use it. VisiCalc helped sell Apple II computers; Microsoft Office strengthened Windows; gaming franchises sell consoles.
PART I — THE SIX PLATFORM EMPIRES
1. IBM — FROM CENSUS CARDS TO HYBRID CLOUD AND QUANTUM
• Full name: International Business Machines Corporation.
• Foundational figures: Herman Hollerith, Charles Ranlett Flint, Thomas J. Watson Sr.
• Current chairman, president and CEO as of July 2026: Arvind Krishna.
• Visual identity: the striped IBM wordmark designed by Paul Rand.

IBM’s deepest root is Herman Hollerith’s punched-card tabulation system for the 1890 United States Census. Hollerith founded the Tabulating Machine Company in 1896. Financier Charles Ranlett Flint combined that company with the International Time Recording Company and Computing Scale Company in 1911 to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, usually shortened to CTR.

Thomas J. Watson Sr., previously associated with National Cash Register, joined CTR in 1914. He brought the word THINK as a corporate mantra. In 1924, CTR adopted the more internationally ambitious name International Business Machines.
IBM did not become important through one invention. It repeatedly dominated successive eras:
• IBM 701: IBM’s first commercial scientific computer.
• IBM 650: a widely produced early computer.
• IBM 1401: one of the defining business computers of the punched-card transition.
• IBM System/360: announced in 1964; a compatible family that could serve commercial and scientific customers.
• IBM 305 RAMAC: associated with the first commercial hard-disk system.
• IBM Selectric: typewriter using a replaceable golf-ball-shaped typing element.
• IBM PC Model 5150: introduced in 1981; helped establish the IBM-compatible PC standard.
• Deep Blue: defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match in 1997.
• Watson: question-answering system that defeated champion contestants on Jeopardy! in 2011.
• IBM Quantum: one of the most visible corporate quantum-computing programmes.
IBM researchers are associated with major developments including:
• Dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, associated with Robert Dennard.
• Relational-database theory, associated with Edgar F. Codd.
• The scanning tunnelling microscope, developed by IBM researchers Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer.
The IBM PC became an industry standard partly because IBM moved quickly and used external components:
• The architecture was documented and extensible.

Competitors reverse-engineered the BIOS using clean-room methods, producing IBM-compatible clones. The standard became larger than IBM itself. Microsoft and Intel captured much of the ecosystem’s long-term strategic power.
• IBM sold its personal-computer division to Lenovo in 2005.
• It sold its x86 server business to Lenovo in 2014.
• It acquired Red Hat in 2019, one of the largest software acquisitions in history at the time.
• It separated its managed-infrastructure-services business as Kyndryl in 2021.
• IBM did not invent the personal computer, although its PC standard transformed the market.
• IBM’s OS/2 lost the desktop operating-system war to Microsoft Windows despite beginning as a Microsoft–IBM partnership.
• IBM’s workplace culture produced the saying that nobody was fired for buying IBM, reflecting trust and institutional dominance.
• IBM’s original company was not founded in 1924; that was the renaming year. The corporate ancestor dates to 1911, while Hollerith’s company dates to 1896.

Paul Rand designed the famous striped IBM logo. The stripes suggest speed and dynamism while retaining the block-letter identity. THINK predates the ThinkPad laptop brand, which originated at IBM and later passed to Lenovo with the PC division.
• Founders: Bill Gates and Paul Allen.
• First customer: MITS, maker of the Altair 8800.
• Name: microcomputer plus software; originally written Micro-Soft.
• Chairman and CEO as of July 2026: Satya Nadella.

The January 1975 issue of Popular Electronics featured the Altair 8800. Gates and Allen contacted MITS and offered a BASIC interpreter before they had finished building it. They developed Altair BASIC using simulation because they did not initially possess the Altair hardware.
Bill Gates used the spelling Micro-soft in a July 1975 letter. The company began in Albuquerque because MITS was located there, later moving to the Seattle region.

When IBM developed its personal computer, Microsoft obtained an operating system related to QDOS or 86-DOS, adapted it and licensed PC DOS to IBM. Crucially, Microsoft retained the ability to license MS-DOS to other manufacturers. As IBM-compatible clones spread, Microsoft’s software became the common layer across competing hardware.
• Intel supplied the dominant processor architecture.
• Versions of BASIC for many microcomputers.
• Windows 95, with the Start button and major consumer launch campaign.
• Windows NT, the technological foundation of later professional Windows systems.
• Microsoft Office: Word, Excel, PowerPoint and later Outlook and other services.
• Internet Explorer browser war against Netscape.
• Investment and partnership relationships with OpenAI.
• Microsoft AI led by Mustafa Suleyman.
• Integration of AI across Azure, Windows, Microsoft 365, GitHub and developer tools.
• Bill Gates: co-founder; software strategist; later philanthropist through the Gates Foundation.
• Paul Allen: co-founder; suggested the Microsoft name; later investor and philanthropist.
• Steve Ballmer: employee number 30; CEO from 2000 to 2014; known for energetic presentations.
• Satya Nadella: joined Microsoft in 1992; became CEO in 2014; shifted emphasis toward cloud, subscriptions, openness and AI.
• Charles Simonyi: associated with applications including Word and Excel.
• Ray Ozzie: creator of Lotus Notes; later Microsoft chief software architect.
• Activision Blizzard, bringing Call of Duty, Warcraft, Diablo, Overwatch and King’s Candy Crush under Microsoft Gaming.
• Microsoft Bob: simplified home interface featuring virtual rooms and assistants.
• Zune: media player competing with Apple’s iPod.
• Windows Phone: admired in some respects but unable to overcome the iOS–Android application ecosystem.
• Clippy: Office Assistant; became a cultural icon despite widespread annoyance.
• Internet Explorer: once dominant, later replaced by Microsoft Edge.
• Windows Vista: criticised for performance and compatibility problems.
• Tay: chatbot taken offline after users manipulated it into producing offensive output.
• Microsoft versus Apple over graphical-interface elements.
• Microsoft versus IBM in the OS/2 and Windows divergence.
• Microsoft versus Netscape in the browser war.
• United States antitrust case alleging maintenance of operating-system monopoly power.
• Microsoft versus Sony and Nintendo in consoles.
• Microsoft versus Google and Amazon in cloud, search, productivity and AI.
• Early Microsoft logos used stylised disco-era lettering.
• The 1987 wordmark had a distinctive cut in the first O, nicknamed the Pac-Man logo.
• The modern four-square symbol echoes Windows.
• Clippy is officially Clippit, though almost everyone calls it Clippy.
• Xbox’s identity centres on a stylised X inside a sphere.
• Microsoft was founded in Albuquerque, not Seattle or Redmond.
• MS-DOS was not written entirely from nothing for IBM; Microsoft acquired and adapted an existing system.
• PowerPoint began at Forethought and was acquired by Microsoft.
• Hotmail’s name highlighted HTML through the original styling HoTMaiL.
• GitHub is owned by Microsoft; Git itself was created by Linus Torvalds and is not a Microsoft invention.
3. APPLE — DESIGN, INTEGRATION AND THE CONTROLLED ECOSYSTEM
• Original founders: Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne.
• Incorporated as Apple Computer, Inc. in 1977.
• Renamed Apple Inc. in 2007 to reflect expansion beyond computers.
• Announced successor: John Ternus, due to become CEO on September 1, 2026; Cook is due to become executive chairman.

Steve Wozniak designed the Apple I after participating in the Homebrew Computer Club. Steve Jobs recognised its commercial potential. Ronald Wayne helped formalise the partnership and designed an early company logo but sold his stake shortly afterwards.

The Apple I was sold as an assembled circuit board rather than a complete modern computer. The Apple II, introduced in 1977, brought colour graphics, expansion slots and consumer-oriented packaging. VisiCalc, the pioneering spreadsheet, became its killer application.

Jobs said he had returned from an apple farm and thought the name sounded fun, spirited and unintimidating. It also appeared early in alphabetical listings. The name later produced a decades-long trademark conflict with the Beatles’ Apple Corps.

Apple’s Lisa introduced a commercial graphical interface but failed because of price and performance. The Macintosh, launched in 1984, packaged the mouse and graphical interface into a more focused product.
The famous 1984 advertisement, directed by Ridley Scott, positioned Macintosh as a liberating challenger to conformity. The target was widely understood as IBM’s dominance.
• Jobs left Apple in 1985 after a power struggle.
• He founded NeXT, which built advanced workstations and the NeXTSTEP operating system.
• He also acquired the computer-graphics group that became Pixar.
• NeXT technology became the foundation of Mac OS X and, through that lineage, modern Apple operating systems.
• Newton MessagePad, an early personal digital assistant.
• Apple silicon: A-series mobile processors and M-series Mac processors.
• Steve Wozniak: engineering designer of Apple I and Apple II.
• Steve Jobs: product vision, marketing, design integration and business strategy.
• Ronald Wayne: short-lived third founder; designed the ornate first logo.
• Mike Markkula: early investor and executive who helped professionalise the company.
• John Sculley: former Pepsi executive; Apple CEO during Jobs’s departure.
• Jony Ive: industrial designer associated with iMac, iPod, iPhone and many other products.
• Tim Cook: supply-chain and operations specialist who became CEO in 2011.
• John Ternus: hardware-engineering leader announced as Apple’s next CEO from September 2026.
Apple generally buys smaller companies and absorbs their technology rather than maintaining every acquired brand.
• NeXT: operating-system foundation and Jobs’s return.
• Beats Electronics: headphones and streaming assets.
• AuthenTec: fingerprint-security technology associated with Touch ID development.
• Lisa: highly innovative but too expensive.
• Newton: ambitious handwriting and mobile concept ahead of available technology.
• Power Mac G4 Cube: admired design but costly and commercially weak.
• AirPower charging mat: announced but cancelled before release.
• Butterfly keyboard: thin mechanism associated with reliability complaints.
• Apple versus Microsoft over GUI similarities.
• Apple versus IBM in the early PC era.
• Apple versus Samsung in smartphone-design and patent litigation.
• Apple versus Google over mobile platforms.
• Apple versus Epic Games over App Store rules and commissions.
• First logo: Ronald Wayne’s detailed illustration of Isaac Newton beneath an apple tree.
• Rob Janoff designed the bitten-apple silhouette.
• The rainbow-striped apple became strongly associated with Apple II and early Macintosh culture.
• Later logos became monochrome and material-dependent.

Rob Janoff has explained that the bite made the shape recognisable as an apple rather than another round fruit. Popular stories connecting it to byte, Alan Turing or forbidden knowledge are attractive quiz myths but are not the accepted design explanation.
• The computer for the rest of us.
• Apple was not founded by only Jobs and Wozniak; Ronald Wayne was the third founder.
• The first Apple logo was not the bitten apple.
• Macintosh did not invent the graphical interface or mouse.
• Pixar was not founded by Jobs from scratch; he acquired the Lucasfilm computer-graphics group that became Pixar.
• iPhone was not the first smartphone, but it transformed the modern smartphone market.
4. GOOGLE AND ALPHABET — SEARCH BECOMES AN INFORMATION EMPIRE
• Founders: Larry Page and Sergey Brin.
• Stanford project began: 1990s; company formally incorporated in 1998.
• Google name: a play on googol, the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.
• CEO of Google and Alphabet as of July 2026: Sundar Pichai.
• Mission language: organise the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful.

Early search engines often ranked pages heavily through text matching and directory organisation. Page and Brin used the link structure of the web as a signal of importance. The system associated with PageRank treated links partly like scholarly citations.
The name PageRank is a pun: it refers both to ranking web pages and to Larry Page’s surname.
• The first server casing famously used Lego bricks.
• Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim wrote an early cheque for Google Inc. before the company had completed all formal arrangements.
• The first Google Doodle placed a Burning Man figure in the logo to show that the founders were away.
• Yoshka became Google’s first company dog.
Google’s search service was free to users. Advertising became the financial engine through products including AdWords and AdSense. The company’s great strategic combination was:
• Massive user attention and intent data.
Alphabet was created as a holding company so that Google’s core internet businesses could be distinguished from other ventures.
Important Alphabet businesses or projects have included:
• X, the moonshot factory formerly called Google X.
• DeepMind, integrated closely into Google’s AI structure.
• Keyhole, whose technology contributed to Google Earth.
• Motorola Mobility, later largely sold to Lenovo while Google retained significant patent interests.
• Wiz, whose acquisition was completed in 2026 to strengthen Google Cloud security.
Google’s willingness to close services has generated the phrase Google graveyard.
• Google Glass consumer edition, although enterprise and research strands continued in different forms.
• Google versus Yahoo and earlier search engines.
• Google versus Microsoft in browsers, productivity, cloud and AI.
• YouTube versus traditional television and competing video platforms.
• Advertising and search antitrust cases in multiple jurisdictions.
• Privacy controversies over data collection, Street View, cookies and targeted advertising.
• The Google wordmark uses primary colours with a green L, signalling rule-breaking according to a common company interpretation.
• The company has hidden numerous search easter eggs.

• Android versions were historically named after desserts in public, including Cupcake, Donut, Eclair, Froyo, Gingerbread, Honeycomb, Ice Cream Sandwich, Jelly Bean, KitKat, Lollipop, Marshmallow, Nougat, Oreo and Pie.
• Alphabet is the parent; Google is the operating company.
• Google did not create YouTube, Android, Waze or DeepMind; it acquired them.
• Gmail launched on April 1, 2004, leading some people to suspect an April Fools’ joke.
• PageRank is not named only because it ranks pages.
• The word Google is based on a misspelling or playful adaptation of googol, not an acronym.
5. AMAZON — FROM ONLINE BOOKSTORE TO INFRASTRUCTURE OF COMMERCE
• President and CEO as of July 2026: Andy Jassy.
Bezos reportedly considered categories suitable for internet retail and chose books because:
• No physical store could stock the full catalogue.

Cadabra, from abracadabra, was rejected after it was heard as cadaver. Bezos chose Amazon after the world’s largest river, suggesting enormous scale. The initial A also placed it early in alphabetical lists.
Amazon expanded from books into a broad marketplace. Key innovations included:
• One-Click purchasing, protected by a famous patent.
AWS transformed Amazon from retailer into infrastructure provider.
The strategic insight was that computing infrastructure could be rented on demand like a utility. AWS became central to startups, enterprises and internet services.
Andy Jassy helped create and lead AWS before succeeding Bezos as Amazon CEO in 2021.
• Amazon Studios or MGM-related media businesses.
• Project Kuiper, subsequently branded Amazon Leo for satellite connectivity.
• Amazon-designed chips including Graviton, Trainium and Inferentia.
• Kiva Systems, whose warehouse robots became strategically important.
• Fire Phone: ambitious hardware tied too closely to Amazon services; sold poorly.
• Amazon Auctions: failed to displace eBay.
• Dash buttons: physical ordering buttons later discontinued.
• Haven healthcare venture with Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan.
• Several experimental retail and device projects.
• The arrow in Amazon’s logo points from A to Z, suggesting wide selection, and forms a smile.
• Bezos’s repeated phrase Day 1 describes maintaining startup urgency and avoiding institutional stagnation.
• Amazon versus Barnes & Noble in books.
• Amazon versus eBay and Walmart in commerce.
• AWS versus Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud.
• Amazon versus publishers over e-book pricing.
• Labour, marketplace-power, seller-data and antitrust controversies.
• Alexa versus Apple Siri and Google Assistant.
• Amazon was founded in 1994 but the public website launched in 1995.
• AWS is not merely Amazon’s internal server department; it is a major external cloud platform.
• Amazon did not begin with the ambition to sell only books forever.
• Andy Jassy, not Bezos, is the current CEO as of July 2026.
6. FACEBOOK AND META — THE SOCIAL GRAPH BECOMES A FAMILY OF APPS
• Founding figures commonly listed by Meta: Mark Zuckerberg, Dustin Moskovitz, Chris Hughes and Eduardo Saverin; Andrew McCollum is also frequently included in broader historical accounts.
• Original form: TheFacebook, initially limited to Harvard.
• Founder, chairman and CEO as of July 2026: Mark Zuckerberg.
TheFacebook began as a university social network using real identities and institutional email addresses. It expanded from Harvard to other universities, then beyond education.
The core asset was the social graph:

News Feed, introduced in 2006, changed Facebook from a set of profiles into a continuous personalised information stream. Initial user resistance faded, and the feed became a dominant social-interface pattern.
Facebook created powerful targeted advertising based on:

The corporate rename separated the company from the Facebook app and signalled a strategic bet on the metaverse, virtual and augmented reality, and future social platforms. Zuckerberg linked meta to the Greek idea of beyond.
• Mark Zuckerberg: product founder and controlling shareholder through dual-class voting structure.
• Eduardo Saverin: early business and financial role; later legal dispute dramatized in The Social Network.

• HTC First, associated with Facebook Home.

• The company introduced an all-capital FACEBOOK corporate wordmark before the Meta rename to distinguish the parent from the app.
• Meta’s loop-like symbol evokes an infinity sign and a three-dimensional form.
• The thumbs-up Like button became a defining social symbol.

PART II — THE SEMICONDUCTOR AND HARDWARE DYNASTIES
7. INTEL — THE COMPANY INSIDE THE PC
• Founders: Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore.
• Early employee and leader: Andy Grove.
• Current CEO as of July 2026: Lip-Bu Tan.

Noyce and Moore left Fairchild Semiconductor to establish Intel. The company’s first major business was semiconductor memory. Its 1103 DRAM became commercially important before microprocessors defined Intel’s public identity.
• 4004: first commercially available general-purpose single-chip microprocessor; developed for Busicom.
• 80286, 386 and 486: expanded PC performance and capabilities.
• Pentium: branding replaced the expected numerical 586 name because numbers were difficult to trademark.
• Core family: became central to laptops and desktops.
• Robert Noyce: integrated-circuit co-inventor, Fairchild founder and Intel co-founder.
• Gordon Moore: Intel co-founder and Moore’s Law.
• Andy Grove: operational leader; famous management phrase Only the Paranoid Survive.
• Ted Hoff, Stan Mazor, Federico Faggin and Masatoshi Shima: Intel 4004 team.
• Pat Gelsinger: former Intel engineer and CEO before Lip-Bu Tan.
• Lip-Bu Tan: semiconductor investor and executive who became CEO in 2025.
IBM’s choice of the Intel 8088 linked Intel to the rapidly expanding PC-compatible ecosystem. Backward compatibility became a formidable moat: customers could run old software on newer processors.

Intel marketed a component directly to consumers, persuading buyers to care which processor was inside a computer. Manufacturers received cooperative advertising support for displaying the Intel Inside logo and sonic identity.
• Intel initially treated the 4004 as a calculator-chip project rather than recognising the full future of microprocessors.
• It missed the leading position in smartphone processors as ARM-based designs dominated mobile devices.
• Manufacturing delays weakened its process-technology leadership.
• Nvidia gained enormous advantage in AI accelerators.
• Apple moved Macs from Intel processors to Apple silicon.
• Pentium floating-point division bug: a rare calculation error became a major public-relations crisis.
• Intel’s original name proposal Moore Noyce sounded like more noise, unsuitable for electronics.
• The company initially bought rights to the Intel name from another business.
8. AMD — THE SECOND SOURCE THAT BECAME A PRIMARY RIVAL
• Founder: Jerry Sanders and colleagues from Fairchild Semiconductor.
• Current chair and CEO: Lisa Su.
• Core businesses: CPUs, GPUs, adaptive computing and data-centre chips.

Jerry Sanders famously said real men have fabs, reflecting the period’s belief that serious semiconductor companies owned manufacturing plants. AMD initially produced logic chips and became a second-source supplier, manufacturing compatible processors so customers were not dependent on one supplier.
IBM wanted more than one source for PC processors. Intel licensed AMD to manufacture compatible chips, but the relationship later deteriorated into years of legal disputes.
• Radeon graphics, acquired through ATI Technologies.
• Xilinx acquisition, adding field-programmable gate arrays and adaptive computing.
AMD extended x86 to 64-bit computing while maintaining compatibility. Intel ultimately adopted the compatible approach. The architecture is commonly called x86-64 or AMD64.
Lisa Su became CEO in 2014 and is strongly associated with AMD’s revival through:
AMD no longer follows Jerry Sanders’s old vertically integrated manufacturing model. It spun off manufacturing operations that became GlobalFoundries and now operates primarily as a fabless designer.
9. NVIDIA — FROM GRAPHICS CARDS TO AI INFRASTRUCTURE
• Founders: Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.
The founders met at a Denny’s restaurant and believed graphics would become a major computing workload. Nvidia developed processors designed to handle many graphical calculations in parallel.
Nvidia popularised the term graphics processing unit with the GeForce 256. A GPU contains many processing units suited to parallel operations.
CUDA allowed programmers to use Nvidia GPUs for general-purpose computing rather than graphics alone. This became strategically decisive for:
Deep-learning researchers discovered that GPUs could train neural networks much faster than conventional CPUs for suitable operations. Nvidia built an ecosystem of:
• Quadro or RTX professional graphics lineage.
Nvidia proposed acquiring Arm from SoftBank, but regulatory opposition caused the deal to collapse. The story is useful for questions about semiconductor neutrality and architecture licensing.
Jensen Huang is visually associated with his black leather jacket. Nvidia’s name has been linked to the Latin invidia, meaning envy, and the eye logo reinforces the visual-computing identity.
• Nvidia does not fabricate most of its leading chips itself; it relies on foundries such as TSMC.
• A GPU is not simply a faster CPU. Its architecture is optimised for highly parallel workloads.
• CUDA is proprietary to Nvidia and is a major software moat.
10. ARM — THE ARCHITECTURE COMPANY INSIDE BILLIONS OF DEVICES
• Original expansion: Acorn RISC Machine; later Advanced RISC Machines.
• Business model: licenses processor architectures and designs rather than manufacturing most chips itself.
• Owner: SoftBank Group, with Arm also publicly traded after its 2023 listing.
Acorn needed a processor for new computers and developed a reduced-instruction-set architecture. The first ARM chips were notable for efficiency and simplicity.
Companies including Apple, Qualcomm, Samsung and MediaTek developed chips based on Arm architecture or instruction-set licences.
• Joint venture involving Acorn, Apple and VLSI Technology.
• Apple’s Arm-based A-series and M-series processors.
• Arm is an architecture and intellectual-property company, not mainly a chip foundry.
• ARM originally referred to Acorn, not Advanced, RISC Machine.
• Apple helped establish the independent Arm company and used Arm technology in the Newton.
• Founders include Irwin Jacobs and Andrew Viterbi.
• Core fields: wireless communications, modems, mobile processors and patent licensing.
Qualcomm championed Code Division Multiple Access, a cellular communication technology that allowed users to share spectrum through coded signals.
Snapdragon systems-on-chip combine components such as:
• Licensing patents essential to wireless standards.
This licensing model has produced major legal and regulatory disputes.

Andrew Viterbi is associated with the Viterbi algorithm, important in digital communications. Qualcomm’s history therefore connects academic information theory, telecommunications standards and consumer devices.
12. TSMC — THE FOUNDRY THAT REWIRED THE CHIP INDUSTRY
• Full name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company.
Traditional semiconductor companies both designed and manufactured chips. TSMC focused on manufacturing chips designed by customers without competing with them in branded end products.
• Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm and many startups could focus on design.
• Electronic-design-automation and architecture firms completed the ecosystem.

Chang previously worked at Texas Instruments and recognised that many designers needed trusted manufacturing capacity. His foundry model became one of the most important business innovations in technology history.
TSMC’s advanced manufacturing role makes Taiwan central to global technology supply chains. Questions often connect:
• United States and Japanese fabrication investments.
TSMC does not usually create the consumer brands printed on the device. An Apple, Nvidia or AMD chip may be designed by that company and manufactured by TSMC.
13. ASML — THE MACHINE MAKER BEHIND THE MOST ADVANCED CHIPS
• Founded: 1984 as a joint venture involving Philips and ASM International.
• Critical technology: extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, lithography.
Chip patterns are projected onto light-sensitive material on silicon wafers. Smaller features require increasingly advanced optics, light sources, materials and precision control.
ASML is the only commercial supplier of the most advanced EUV lithography machines. Each system depends on a highly specialised network including:
• ASML does not manufacture chips; it manufactures tools used by fabs.
• EUV uses a wavelength around 13.5 nanometres.
• The machines are among the most complex and expensive industrial systems ever produced.
• Export controls on ASML equipment are central to semiconductor geopolitics.
14. SAMSUNG — FROM TRADING COMPANY TO ELECTRONICS AND CHIP GIANT
• Samsung group founded: 1938 by Lee Byung-chul.
• Original business: trading, including groceries and dried goods.
• Name meaning: three stars in Korean.

Samsung is a chaebol: a large family-influenced Korean conglomerate with businesses across multiple industries. Samsung Electronics is the technology company most users know, but Samsung Group includes other companies.
The Galaxy brand spans smartphones, tablets, watches, earbuds and computers. Samsung became the principal global Android-hardware rival to Apple.
Samsung is unusual because it may both compete with and supply components to another company. It has supplied displays or memory for firms that compete with Galaxy products.
The Galaxy Note helped popularise very large smartphones and stylus input. The Galaxy Note 7 was recalled after battery fires, becoming one of the most famous hardware-quality crises.
• Samsung did not begin as an electronics firm.
• Samsung Group and Samsung Electronics are not identical.
• The name refers to three stars, explaining older star-based logos.
15. SONY — ELECTRONICS, MUSIC, FILM AND PLAYSTATION
• Founders: Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita.
• Original name: Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo, or Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation.

Sony combined ideas including Latin sonus, meaning sound, and the American expression sonny boy. The short international name was easier to pronounce globally than the original Japanese corporate name.

Sony considered or used names such as Soundabout, Stowaway and Freestyle in different markets before Walkman became the global identity. Grammarians objected to the invented English, but the brand prevailed.

Sony and Nintendo worked on a CD-ROM add-on relationship. The partnership broke down publicly, and Sony developed PlayStation as its own console. The failed alliance created one of Nintendo’s strongest future competitors.
The company’s image-sensor business places Sony inside many phones made by other brands.
• Betamax lost the consumer videotape format war to VHS despite technical strengths often attributed to it.
• MiniDisc remained important in some markets but did not become the universal successor to cassette and CD.
• The 2011 PlayStation Network breach became a major cybersecurity crisis.
• Sony did not invent the Compact Disc alone; it developed the standard with Philips.
• PlayStation grew partly from a failed Nintendo relationship.
• The Walkman was not the first portable audio device, but it transformed personal listening culture.
16. HP, HPE AND AGILENT — THE GARAGE FAMILY TREE
• Founders: Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard.
• Famous birthplace: Palo Alto garage, often called the birthplace of Silicon Valley.
• First successful product: HP 200A audio oscillator.
Hewlett and Packard reportedly used a coin toss to decide whether the company would be called Hewlett-Packard or Packard-Hewlett.
Walt Disney Studios purchased HP oscillators for work connected with Fantasia, providing a famous early customer story.
• Agilent Technologies was spun off in 1999, taking test, measurement and related businesses.
– HP Inc.: personal computers and printers.
– Hewlett Packard Enterprise: servers, storage, networking and enterprise services.
• HP acquired Compaq in a controversial deal led by Carly Fiorina.
• HPE later acquired companies including Aruba Networks.
• HP’s acquisition of Autonomy produced enormous write-downs and years of litigation.
HP Inc., HPE and Agilent are separate companies descended from the same original Hewlett-Packard.
17. DELL — DIRECT SALES AND THE PC SUPPLY CHAIN
• Origin: University of Texas dorm room.
Dell sold computers directly to customers and built them to order. Advantages included:
• Ability to use newer components quickly.
• Michael Dell and Silver Lake took the company private in 2013.
• Dell acquired EMC in 2016 in one of the largest technology deals of its time.
• VMware later separated from Dell and was eventually acquired by Broadcom.
• Dell’s fame came as much from supply-chain and direct-sales strategy as from a single invention.
• The company began with upgrading and selling PCs rather than designing a wholly new computer architecture.
18. LENOVO — A CHINESE COMPANY INHERITS THE THINKPAD
• Name Lenovo: Le from Legend plus novo, suggesting new.
• IBM personal-computer division, including ThinkPad, in 2005.
The ThinkPad brand originated at IBM. The name referenced IBM’s THINK culture and the idea of a notepad. Early ThinkPads became known for black box-like design and the red TrackPoint pointing stick.
Lenovo did not invent ThinkPad or Motorola. It acquired both businesses through major cross-border deals.
PART III — ENTERPRISE SOFTWARE, NETWORKING AND THE INVISIBLE CORPORATE STACK
