Artificial intelligence, or AI, is the broad field of building computer systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as perception, language understanding, reasoning, prediction, planning, learning and decision-making.
AI is an umbrella term. It includes rule-based systems as well as systems that learn from data.
• AI is broader than machine learning.
• Not every AI system uses a neural network.
• A system can appear intelligent in one narrow task while having no general understanding.
2. AI, machine learning and deep learning
Machine learning, or ML, is a subset of AI in which systems improve task performance by finding patterns in data rather than relying only on manually written rules.
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning based on neural networks with many processing layers.
Artificial intelligence → machine learning → deep learning.

A spreadsheet rule that flags every payment above a fixed amount is automation or rule-based logic. A fraud model trained on past transactions is machine learning. A neural network trained on millions of images is deep learning.
3. Narrow AI, general AI and superintelligence
Narrow AI, also called weak AI, is designed for a limited task or domain. Search ranking, spam filtering, face matching, speech recognition and chess engines are narrow AI.

Artificial general intelligence, or AGI, is the proposed ability of a machine to perform across a broad range of intellectual tasks at roughly human-level flexibility. There is no universally accepted test or agreed point at which AGI has been achieved.
Artificial superintelligence is the hypothetical idea of systems exceeding humans across most cognitive domains.
Quiz trap: “Weak AI” does not mean low-performing AI. A narrow system may outperform every human at one task while remaining unable to do unrelated tasks.
Symbolic AI represents knowledge through explicit symbols, facts, rules and logical relationships. Expert systems are a classic example.
Statistical AI learns patterns from data using probability, optimisation and machine-learning models.

Symbolic systems can be interpretable and precise in well-defined domains but struggle with messy real-world variation. Statistical systems handle patterns and uncertainty well but can be opaque and data-hungry.
Neuro-symbolic AI attempts to combine learned representations with rules or reasoning structures.

Alan Turing proposed the “imitation game” in his 1950 paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence.” A human evaluator communicates through text with an unseen human and machine and tries to distinguish them.

Passing a Turing-style conversation test would demonstrate convincing conversational behaviour under the test conditions. It would not automatically prove consciousness, truthfulness, emotions or general intelligence.
The term “Turing Test” became the popular name later; Turing himself discussed the imitation game.
The term “artificial intelligence” is strongly associated with the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence.

John McCarthy coined the term for the proposal. Other major participants and organisers included Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester. Allen Newell and Herbert Simon presented influential work related to the Logic Theorist.
Dartmouth 1956 → John McCarthy → naming of AI as a research field.
An expert system encodes specialist knowledge using a knowledge base and an inference engine.
MYCIN, developed at Stanford in the 1970s, is a famous medical expert-system project. It recommended antibiotics for certain bacterial infections but was not deployed as an ordinary clinical product.
XCON, used by Digital Equipment Corporation, configured computer orders and became a major commercial expert-system success.
Expert systems helped drive an AI boom, but maintaining large rule bases was expensive and brittle. Their limitations contributed to periods called AI winters.
An AI winter is a period of reduced funding and enthusiasm after expectations exceed technical results.
There is no single universally agreed list of exact start and end dates, but major downturns are commonly associated with the 1970s and late 1980s/early 1990s.
Supervised learning uses labelled examples. Each training example includes input data and a known target.
• Classification predicts a category, such as spam/not spam or disease/no disease.
• Regression predicts a continuous value, such as house price or future demand.
The word “supervised” refers to labelled targets, not necessarily a human watching every training step.
Unsupervised learning works with data that has no target label and seeks structure.
• Dimensionality reduction: represent data with fewer variables.
• Association discovery: find items that co-occur.
K-means is a famous clustering algorithm. Principal component analysis, or PCA, is a famous dimensionality-reduction technique.
Semi-supervised learning combines a small labelled dataset with a larger unlabelled dataset.

Self-supervised learning creates training signals from the data itself. A language model may learn by predicting masked or next tokens. A vision model may learn by reconstructing missing image regions or matching different views of the same object.
Self-supervised learning became important because unlabelled text, images, audio and video are far more abundant than carefully labelled examples.
In reinforcement learning, an agent interacts with an environment. It takes actions, receives rewards or penalties and learns a policy intended to maximise expected cumulative reward.
• Environment: world with which the agent interacts.
• Action: choice available to the agent.
• Policy: strategy mapping states or observations to actions.
Reinforcement learning differs from supervised learning because the correct action is not always provided directly. Rewards may be delayed, and exploration can be necessary.
The training set is used to fit model parameters.
The validation set is used to select settings, compare models and tune hyperparameters.
The test set estimates performance on unseen data after development decisions are complete.
Using test results repeatedly to tune a model leaks information and makes the test set less trustworthy.
Data leakage occurs when information unavailable at real prediction time enters training or evaluation. It can create unrealistically high scores.
Parameters are values learned from data, such as neural-network weights or linear-regression coefficients.
Hyperparameters are choices set by the developer or tuning process, such as learning rate, tree depth, regularisation strength or number of clusters.
A large language model’s “parameter count” refers to learned numerical values, not the length of its prompt or the number of users.
Overfitting occurs when a model learns training details or noise so closely that it performs poorly on new data.
Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple, poorly trained or insufficiently expressive to capture important patterns.
High bias means the model makes overly simple assumptions and may underfit.
High variance means the model is highly sensitive to the training sample and may overfit.
The bias–variance trade-off describes the balance between these error sources. It is not the same as social or demographic bias, although the word “bias” appears in both contexts.
Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct. It can mislead when classes are imbalanced.
• Precision = true positives divided by all predicted positives.
• Recall, or sensitivity = true positives divided by all actual positives.
• Specificity = true negatives divided by all actual negatives.
• F1 score = harmonic mean of precision and recall.
A confusion matrix records true positives, true negatives, false positives and false negatives.
In cancer screening, missing a true case can be especially costly, so recall may matter greatly. In a system that automatically blocks legitimate transactions, false positives also matter.
A receiver operating characteristic, or ROC, curve plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate as the decision threshold changes.

Area under the ROC curve, or AUC, summarises ranking performance across thresholds. An AUC closer to 1 generally indicates better separation; about 0.5 resembles random ranking in a balanced binary setting.
AUC does not choose the operational threshold and does not replace analysis of real costs, class imbalance or calibration.
A feature is an input variable used by a model. Feature engineering creates, selects or transforms useful inputs.
Deep learning often learns representations automatically, but data preparation and domain knowledge remain important.
K-fold cross-validation divides data into K parts. The model trains K times, each time using one part for validation and the rest for training. Results are averaged.
Stratified cross-validation preserves class proportions where appropriate.
Time-series data should normally respect chronological order. Randomly mixing future observations into past training can create leakage.
PART III — NEURAL NETWORKS, GENERATIVE AI AND LANGUAGE MODELS
An artificial neuron combines inputs with weights, adds a bias and applies an activation function.
A neural network is organised into layers:
Training adjusts weights to reduce a loss function. Backpropagation efficiently computes how each parameter contributed to error, and an optimiser updates the parameters.
Frank Rosenblatt developed the perceptron in the late 1950s. It was an early trainable artificial-neuron model.

A single-layer perceptron can solve linearly separable classification problems but cannot represent XOR. Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert analysed important limitations of simple perceptrons in their 1969 book.
Multilayer networks with nonlinear activation functions can represent far richer relationships.
Backpropagation applies the chain rule of calculus to compute gradients through a network.
The method has a long history, but the 1986 paper by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams strongly popularised backpropagation for multilayer neural networks.
Quiz trap: backpropagation computes gradients; gradient descent or another optimiser uses those gradients to update parameters.
• ReLU: returns zero for negative input and the input itself for positive input.
• Softmax: converts a vector of scores into a probability-like distribution summing to one.
Without nonlinear activations, stacking ordinary linear layers still behaves like one linear transformation.
A convolutional neural network, or CNN, applies learned filters across local regions. It is especially associated with images but can also process audio and other grid-like data.

LeNet, associated with Yann LeCun and collaborators, was influential in handwritten-character recognition. AlexNet, created by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, won the 2012 ImageNet competition by a large margin and accelerated the deep-learning boom.
26. Recurrent networks, LSTM and sequence modelling
A recurrent neural network, or RNN, processes sequences while carrying information from earlier steps.
Long short-term memory, or LSTM, networks were introduced by Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber to address difficulties in learning long-range dependencies.

RNNs and LSTMs were widely used for language, speech and time series. Transformers later displaced them in many large-scale language applications because transformers train in parallel more effectively and capture long-range relationships through attention.
The transformer architecture was introduced in the 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need” by Ashish Vaswani and colleagues at Google.
Its core idea is attention: each token can assign different importance to other tokens when building a representation.
• Multi-head attention: several attention patterns learned in parallel.
• Positional encoding: information about token order.
BERT is an encoder-focused transformer family. GPT models are decoder-style autoregressive transformers. The original Transformer used both encoder and decoder.
Natural language processing, or NLP, covers computational work with human language.
• Speech-to-text and text-to-speech when combined with speech systems.
A token may be a word, part of a word, punctuation mark or byte-like unit depending on the tokenizer.
A large language model, or LLM, is trained on large text or multimodal datasets to model token sequences.
During generation, an autoregressive model repeatedly predicts a probability distribution for the next token and samples or selects from it.
• Context window: amount of input and generated context the model can consider.
• System prompt: high-level instruction setting behaviour.
• Inference: using a trained model to produce outputs.
• Fine-tuning: additional training for a narrower behaviour or domain.
An LLM does not retrieve a stored sentence for every answer. It generates from learned statistical representations, although some systems also use search or databases.
Generative AI creates new content such as text, images, audio, video, code or 3D assets.
• Autoregressive models generate one element after another.
• Generative adversarial networks, or GANs, use a generator and discriminator in competition.
• Variational autoencoders, or VAEs, learn a structured latent space.
• Diffusion models learn to reverse a noise-adding process.
Ian Goodfellow and colleagues introduced GANs in 2014. Diffusion models became central to modern image generation.
Prompt engineering shapes the instruction and context supplied at inference time. It does not change the model’s trained weights.
Fine-tuning updates model weights using additional examples.
Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, first retrieves relevant documents or data and then gives them to a generative model as context.
RAG can improve freshness and traceability, but retrieval can fail, sources can be wrong and the model can still misinterpret evidence.
An embedding is a numeric vector representing meaning or other features. Similar items are often located near one another in the embedding space.
Vector search finds nearby embeddings using a similarity measure.
A vector database is optimised to store and search embeddings. It is commonly used for semantic search, recommendation and RAG.
Quiz trap: an embedding is not human-readable text, and vector search is not identical to keyword search.
A hallucination is an output that is unsupported, fabricated or inconsistent with reliable evidence while often sounding fluent.
• Asking the model to abstain when uncertain.
A model stating an answer confidently does not make the answer correct.
An AI agent is a system that combines a model with goals, memory, tools and an action loop.
Observe → reason or plan → act through a tool → inspect result → continue or stop.
Agents can search, call APIs, use software and coordinate subtasks. Their risks include cascading errors, excessive permissions, prompt injection, cost, nondeterminism and failure to stop.
Multimodal AI processes or generates more than one data type, such as text, images, audio and video.
• Generating an image from a text description.
• Controlling a robot from vision and language instructions.
Multimodal does not necessarily mean all modalities are processed by one identical neural network; systems may combine specialised encoders, decoders and tools.
Responsible AI aims to make systems lawful, safe, fair, transparent, accountable, privacy-preserving and aligned with human goals.
Fairness has multiple mathematical definitions that can conflict. There is no single metric that guarantees fairness in every context.
Explainable AI, or XAI, seeks to make model behaviour understandable.
Global explanations describe broad model behaviour. Local explanations explain one prediction.
An explanation method can itself be approximate or misleading. Interpretability must be tested rather than assumed.
An adversarial example is an input deliberately modified to cause incorrect model behaviour while remaining similar to a normal input.
Prompt injection targets the instructions and connected tools of an AI system. It is not the same as SQL injection, although both exploit improperly trusted input.
PART IV — DATA, DATABASES AND ANALYTICS
Data consists of recorded observations or symbols. Information is data organised to convey meaning. Knowledge combines information with context, interpretation and experience.
Metadata is data about data, such as file creator, timestamp, schema, location or camera settings.
A dataset is an organised collection of data. A schema defines its structure and relationships.
Structured data follows a fixed schema, commonly rows and columns in a relational database.
Semi-structured data has tags or keys but flexible structure. JSON and XML are common examples.
Unstructured data lacks a predefined tabular schema. Documents, images, audio and video are typical examples.
“Unstructured” does not mean random or useless. It means the structure is not directly represented in a fixed relational form.
A relational database organises data into tables.
• Row or record: one entity or event.
• Primary key: uniquely identifies a row.
• Foreign key: links one table to another.
• Index: data structure that speeds selected queries.
• Transaction: a logical unit of work.
Edgar F. Codd proposed the relational model in 1970 while at IBM.
SQL means Structured Query Language. It is used to define, query and modify relational data.
SQL is a language and standard family, not one database product. MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server and SQLite are different systems that support SQL dialects.
• Atomicity: all or none of a transaction’s operations complete.
• Isolation: concurrent transactions behave according to an isolation model.
• Durability: committed results survive failures within the system’s guarantees.
ACID does not mean a database can never lose data under any conceivable disaster. Backups, replication and operational design still matter.
NoSQL broadly refers to non-relational database models, often designed for flexible schemas or distributed scale.
NoSQL does not mean “no query language” or “never use SQL.” The phrase is often expanded as “not only SQL.”

The CAP theorem, associated with Eric Brewer and formalised by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch, states that a distributed data system facing a network partition cannot simultaneously guarantee both complete consistency and complete availability for every request.
• Consistency: every read sees the latest successful write or an error.
• Availability: every non-failing node returns a response.
• Partition tolerance: system continues despite lost or delayed network messages between parts.
Quiz trap: CAP is about choices during a partition, not a claim that every database permanently chooses exactly two of three under all conditions.
46. Data warehouse, data lake and lakehouse
A data warehouse stores curated, structured data for reporting and analytics. It commonly applies schema-on-write.
A data lake stores large volumes of raw or lightly processed structured, semi-structured and unstructured data. It commonly applies schema-on-read.
A lakehouse attempts to combine the openness and scale of a lake with management, reliability and query features associated with a warehouse.
A poorly governed data lake may become a “data swamp.”
ETL means extract, transform, load. Data is transformed before entering the destination.
ELT means extract, load, transform. Raw data is loaded first and transformed using the destination platform’s compute.
Neither is universally superior. The choice depends on scale, governance, latency, destination capability and compliance.
Big data refers to datasets or data flows that challenge conventional processing methods.
• Velocity: speed of creation and processing.
The phrase became popular through industry analysis; different sources use different numbers of Vs.
Batch processing handles accumulated groups of data at intervals.
Stream processing handles events continuously or with very low delay.

Apache Hadoop became famous for distributed batch processing. Apache Spark supports fast distributed processing and multiple workloads. Apache Kafka is strongly associated with event streaming and durable logs.
Diagnostic analytics asks: Why did it happen?
Predictive analytics asks: What is likely to happen?
Prescriptive analytics asks: What action should be taken?
A dashboard showing last month’s sales is descriptive. A churn model is predictive. An optimiser recommending delivery routes is prescriptive.
Business intelligence, or BI, uses data integration, reporting, dashboards and analysis to support decisions.
Common BI products include Microsoft Power BI, Tableau and Qlik.
A key performance indicator, or KPI, is a measurable value linked to an objective. A metric becomes a useful KPI only when it connects clearly to performance and decisions.
• Consistency: values agree across sources and rules.
• Validity: conforms to format and constraints.
“Garbage in, garbage out” means poor input data can produce poor output even with sophisticated algorithms.
Data governance defines ownership, policies, standards, access, quality and accountability.
Data lineage records where data came from, how it changed and where it moved.
A data steward helps maintain definitions, quality and proper use. A data owner is accountable for a data domain or asset.
Master data management maintains authoritative records for key entities such as customers, products and suppliers.
Anonymisation attempts to remove or transform identifying information so individuals are not reasonably identifiable.
Pseudonymisation replaces direct identifiers with artificial identifiers but may allow re-linking with additional information.
Encryption protects data using keys but does not anonymise it.
Differential privacy adds carefully calibrated randomness to limit what can be inferred about one individual while preserving aggregate usefulness.
Federated learning trains across decentralised devices or organisations without centralising all raw data, but it does not automatically solve every privacy or security risk.

Cloud computing provides on-demand access to shared computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, networking and software over a network, commonly with rapid provisioning and usage-based charging.
Cloud does not mean the data exists “nowhere.” It runs in physical data centres operated by cloud providers or private organisations.
Infrastructure as a Service, or IaaS, supplies virtual machines, storage and networking. The customer manages more of the software stack.
Platform as a Service, or PaaS, provides a managed application platform, runtime or database so developers manage less infrastructure.
Software as a Service, or SaaS, delivers a complete application through the internet.
• Deploying code to a managed application runtime: PaaS.
• Using webmail or an online CRM: SaaS.
The boundaries can overlap; classify according to what the provider manages and what the customer controls.
Public cloud uses shared provider infrastructure offered to many customers.
Private cloud is dedicated to one organisation, on its premises or hosted.
Hybrid cloud connects private infrastructure with public cloud services.
Multi-cloud uses services from more than one cloud provider.
Hybrid describes a mix of private and public environments. Multi-cloud describes multiple providers. A strategy can be both.
Virtualisation allows one physical machine to run multiple isolated virtual machines.
• Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware.
• Type 2 hypervisor runs on a host operating system.
Each VM normally includes a guest operating system. This gives strong isolation but adds overhead.
VMware, Microsoft Hyper-V, KVM and Xen are major virtualisation names.
A container packages an application with its libraries and configuration while sharing the host operating-system kernel.
Containers are generally lighter and start faster than full virtual machines.
Docker popularised modern application containers. Kubernetes, originally developed at Google and donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, orchestrates containers across clusters.
• Docker is strongly associated with building and running containers.
• Kubernetes schedules and manages containerised workloads.
• A container is not a miniature physical machine and normally does not contain a full independent kernel.
Serverless computing lets developers run functions or managed services without provisioning individual servers.
“Serverless” does not mean no servers exist. The provider manages server allocation, scaling and much of the operations.
Function as a Service examples include AWS Lambda, Azure Functions and Google Cloud Functions.
A cloud region is a geographic area containing cloud infrastructure.
An availability zone is an isolated location within a region, designed to reduce correlated failures.

Deploying across zones improves resilience to a local data-centre failure. Deploying across regions can protect against wider regional disruption but adds cost, latency and data-governance complexity.
Scalability is the ability to handle growth by adding resources.
Vertical scaling adds capacity to one machine. Horizontal scaling adds more machines or instances.
Elasticity automatically increases or decreases resources in response to demand.
High availability aims to keep a service accessible despite failures.
Reliability is the probability that a system performs correctly over time. Resilience is the ability to withstand and recover from disruption.
A load balancer distributes traffic across multiple healthy servers or services.
Auto-scaling changes the number or size of resources based on metrics, schedules or demand.
Load balancing alone does not create unlimited capacity. The application, database and network must also scale.
Object storage stores objects in buckets and is suited to media, backups, logs and data lakes.
Block storage presents raw storage volumes and is suited to virtual-machine disks and databases.
File storage presents a shared hierarchical file system.
Equivalent services exist across other cloud providers.
A backup is a separate recoverable copy of data.
Disaster recovery, or DR, is the broader plan for restoring systems and operations.
Recovery point objective, RPO, is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time.
Recovery time objective, RTO, is the target time to restore service.
A low RPO requires frequent replication or backups. A low RTO requires rapid recovery capability.

In cloud security, the provider secures parts of the cloud infrastructure while the customer remains responsible for areas such as identities, access policies, data, application code and configuration, depending on the service model.
Moving to SaaS shifts more operational responsibility to the provider than using IaaS, but the customer still controls users, permissions and data use.
Misconfigured storage or excessive privileges remain customer-side risks.
Cloud computing centralises large-scale resources in data centres.
Edge computing processes data near the device or data source.
Fog computing distributes processing across intermediate nodes between edge devices and central cloud.
Examples include factory control, autonomous vehicles, smart cameras and telecom networks.
Cloud-native systems are designed to exploit automation, elasticity, managed services, containers and continuous delivery.
A microservices architecture divides an application into independently deployable services.
Benefits can include team autonomy and independent scaling. Costs include network failures, distributed data, observability, versioning and operational complexity.
A monolith is not automatically bad, and microservices are not automatically more scalable.
69. Major cloud providers and quiz associations
Amazon Web Services, launched publicly in the mid-2000s, helped popularise utility cloud computing. Key names include EC2, S3 and Lambda.
Microsoft Azure is closely integrated with Microsoft enterprise software, identity, developer and productivity ecosystems.
Google Cloud is associated with data analytics, Kubernetes heritage, machine learning and global infrastructure.
IBM Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Alibaba Cloud are also major names.
Salesforce is a landmark SaaS company and helped popularise cloud-delivered customer relationship management.
FinOps is a collaborative discipline for managing cloud value and cost across engineering, finance and business teams.
Cloud is not automatically cheaper than owned infrastructure. Its value may come from speed, flexibility, global reach and reduced capital expenditure as well as cost.
Automation uses technology to perform tasks with reduced manual effort.
Automation follows defined processes. AI may add perception, prediction or language ability, but automation does not require AI.
A workflow defines the sequence of tasks, decisions and hand-offs needed to complete work.
Business process management, or BPM, analyses, designs, executes, monitors and improves end-to-end processes.
A workflow engine routes tasks and applies rules. BPM focuses on the full process, including people, policies, systems and performance.
Robotic process automation, or RPA, uses software bots to imitate repetitive user actions across applications.
The “robot” in RPA is normally software, not a physical machine.
Attended bots run alongside a user and are triggered during a task.
Unattended bots run independently on servers or virtual machines according to schedules, events or queues.
A call-centre assistant that fills fields while an employee speaks to a customer is attended. A nightly invoice-reconciliation bot is unattended.
Intelligent automation combines workflow or RPA with AI technologies such as document recognition, language models, prediction and computer vision.
Hyperautomation is a broad strategy of discovering, automating and managing as many suitable business processes as practical using multiple tools.
Hyperautomation is not one specific product.
Process mining reconstructs real processes from event logs. It identifies common paths, delays, deviations and bottlenecks.
Task mining records or analyses user-level interactions to understand how individual tasks are performed.
Process discovery should precede automation. Automating a broken or unnecessary process can make waste occur faster.
An API exposes a defined machine-to-machine interface.
Screen automation controls an application through its user interface.
APIs are usually more stable and efficient when available. Screen automation is useful for legacy systems but can break when buttons, layouts or timing change.
Human-in-the-loop systems send selected decisions to people for review.
The goal is not always to remove people. Good automation assigns machines repetitive work and keeps humans responsible for judgement, escalation and accountability.
Major RPA companies include UiPath, Automation Anywhere and SS&C Blue Prism. Microsoft Power Automate is prominent in low-code workflow and automation.
A robot is a programmable physical system that senses its environment, processes information and acts through mechanical or other physical outputs.
A machine that repeats a fixed motion can be a robot, but greater autonomy requires sensing and decision-making.
Sensors measure the world or the robot itself.
A sensor measures; an actuator acts.
Industrial robots perform manufacturing tasks such as welding, painting, assembly, machine tending, inspection and packaging.
Degrees of freedom describe independent motions. A common articulated arm has six degrees of freedom, but robot designs vary.
A collaborative robot, or cobot, is designed to work in a shared space with people under defined safety conditions.
“Collaborative” does not mean harmless in every situation. The tool, payload, speed and application still require risk assessment.
An automated guided vehicle, or AGV, typically follows predefined paths or markers.
An autonomous mobile robot, or AMR, builds or uses a map and plans routes dynamically around obstacles.
Autonomous vehicles combine perception, localisation, prediction, planning and control.

The Society of Automotive Engineers defines levels 0 to 5 of driving automation. Level 2 still requires continuous driver supervision. Level 5 means full automation under all roadway and environmental conditions a human driver could manage.
2. Estimate the robot and object states.
Control answers “How should motors move to do it?”
SLAM means simultaneous localisation and mapping.
A robot in an unknown environment estimates its own position while building a map.
SLAM is difficult because localisation requires a map while mapping requires a position estimate. Loop closure recognises a previously visited place and corrects accumulated drift.
Computer vision enables machines to interpret images or video.
Machine vision commonly refers to industrial vision systems used for inspection, measurement and guidance.
An unmanned aerial vehicle, or UAV, is an aircraft without an onboard human pilot.
A quadcopter changes motor thrust to control roll, pitch, yaw and altitude.
A humanoid robot resembles aspects of the human body, often with a torso, head, arms or legs.
Service robots perform useful tasks outside traditional industrial automation. Examples include hospital delivery, warehouse transport, cleaning, inspection and hospitality.

Boston Dynamics is known for robots including Spot and Atlas. SoftBank Robotics is associated with Pepper and NAO. Hanson Robotics created Sophia. These systems differ greatly in autonomy and purpose.
The da Vinci Surgical System, developed by Intuitive Surgical, is a famous robot-assisted surgery platform.
It does not perform surgery independently. A trained surgeon controls instruments through a console.
Other medical robots support rehabilitation, imaging, pharmacy operations, logistics and prosthetics.
The word “robot” entered popular use through Karel Čapek’s 1920 play R.U.R., from a Czech word related to forced labour. Čapek credited his brother Josef with suggesting the word.
Isaac Asimov popularised the term “robotics” and formulated the Three Laws of Robotics in science fiction.
Unimate, created by George Devol and developed commercially with Joseph Engelberger, became the first widely recognised industrial robot. It began work at a General Motors plant in 1961.
Joseph Engelberger is often called the father of industrial robotics.
A digital twin is a digital representation of a physical asset, process or system that is updated using data.
A static 3D model is not automatically a digital twin. A twin usually maintains a meaningful relationship with the real system and its state.
Swarm robotics coordinates many relatively simple robots using local rules and distributed interaction.
It is inspired by ants, bees, fish and other collective systems.
Risks include collision, unexpected behaviour, cybersecurity, surveillance, job displacement, unclear liability and military misuse.
A highly accurate perception system can still fail in rare conditions, so safety should not depend on one model alone.
Biometrics uses measurable human characteristics for recognition.
Voice includes physiological and behavioural information, so classifications may vary.
7. Compare and calculate a match score.
8. Apply a threshold and return a decision.
A biometric template is a mathematical representation of features, not necessarily a stored photograph or raw fingerprint image.
Verification asks: “Am I the person I claim to be?” It is a one-to-one, or 1:1, comparison.
Identification asks: “Who is this person?” It is a one-to-many, or 1:N, search against a database.
Unlocking a phone with a registered face is usually verification. Searching a watchlist for a matching face is identification.
Authentication factors are commonly grouped as:
• Something you know: password or PIN.
• Something you have: phone, token or smart card.
• Somewhere you are: location, in some schemes.
• Something you do: behaviour, in some schemes.
Multi-factor authentication uses factors from different categories. A password plus a PIN is normally not true two-factor authentication because both are knowledge factors.
False acceptance rate, or FAR, measures how often an unauthorised person is incorrectly accepted.
False rejection rate, or FRR, measures how often an authorised person is incorrectly rejected.
False match rate and false non-match rate are closely related terms used in standards and testing.

Equal error rate, or EER, is the operating point where false-accept and false-reject rates are equal. Lower EER generally indicates better separability, but real systems choose thresholds according to risk rather than automatically using EER.
A stricter threshold generally reduces false accepts but increases false rejects.
A looser threshold generally reduces false rejects but increases false accepts.
High-security access may prefer a stricter threshold. A low-risk convenience feature may accept more false-match risk to reduce user frustration.
There is no single threshold that simultaneously minimises both error types in all situations.
Fingerprint recognition uses ridge endings, bifurcations and other features called minutiae.
Fingerprints are widely used but can be affected by cuts, dirt, moisture, worn ridges and poor capture.

Sir Francis Galton studied fingerprint individuality and classification. Edward Henry developed the Henry Classification System used in policing. Juan Vucetich developed an early practical fingerprint classification system and was involved in a landmark criminal identification in Argentina.
Face recognition extracts features from a face image and compares them with templates.
Face detection finds a face. Face verification compares two identities. Face identification searches a database. These are different tasks.
Iris recognition analyses the coloured ring around the pupil. John Daugman developed highly influential iris-recognition algorithms and IrisCode methods.
Retinal scanning analyses blood-vessel patterns at the back of the eye.

Quiz trap: iris and retina are not the same structure. Iris systems generally capture the visible eye pattern using a camera; retinal systems examine internal blood-vessel patterns and are less common for everyday authentication.
Voice recognition for identity, also called speaker recognition, analyses vocal characteristics.
Speaker verification checks a claimed identity. Speaker identification searches among speakers.
Speech recognition converts spoken words into text. It is not the same as identifying the speaker.
Voice biometrics can be affected by illness, background noise, microphones, replay attacks and synthetic speech.
Behavioural systems analyse patterns such as:
They can support continuous authentication and fraud detection.
Unlike a password, behaviour varies naturally, so systems use probability and thresholds.
A presentation attack attempts to fool a sensor using an artefact or reproduced biometric, such as a photograph, mask, fingerprint mould or replayed voice.
Presentation attack detection, often called liveness detection, attempts to distinguish a live genuine subject from an attack.
Liveness reduces risk but is not perfect.
Multimodal biometrics combines more than one biometric source, such as face plus voice or fingerprint plus iris.
• Greater robustness when one modality is unavailable.
Multimodal biometrics is not the same as multi-factor authentication if every modality still belongs to “something you are.” Policies may treat them differently.
Biometrics are difficult to replace after compromise. A person can reset a password but cannot easily reset a face or fingerprint.
• Use cancellable biometrics or protected transformations.
• Apply access control and audit logs.
A hash designed for passwords cannot always be applied directly to noisy biometric measurements because two genuine captures are rarely bit-for-bit identical.
Aadhaar authentication can use demographic information, OTP or biometric modalities. UIDAI supports fingerprint, iris and face authentication.
Aadhaar biometric authentication is a verification process against UIDAI records; it is not a public reverse-search service that reveals a person’s full biometric data.
• UIDAI is the Unique Identification Authority of India.
• Aadhaar is a 12-digit identity number, not proof of citizenship.
• Fingerprint, iris and face are biometric modalities.
• OTP is a possession-based mechanism, not a biometric.
An electronic passport stores data in a secure chip and may include biometric information. The ICAO e-passport symbol resembles a small rectangle with a circle.
Modern phones commonly use face or fingerprint verification. Secure designs may store protected templates in isolated hardware rather than sending raw biometrics to a remote server for every unlock.
Convenience biometrics should be combined with device encryption, fallback credentials and anti-spoofing.
PART IX — LANDMARK AI SYSTEMS, COMPANIES AND INDIA CONNECTIONS
IBM Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match in 1997.
IBM Watson defeated champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter on the quiz show Jeopardy! in 2011.
DeepMind’s AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol in a five-game Go match in 2016.
AlphaZero later learned chess, shogi and Go from self-play and rules rather than human game records in the same style as earlier supervised systems.
Quiz trap: Deep Blue was primarily specialised search and evaluation, Watson was a question-answering system, and AlphaGo combined neural networks with tree search.
ImageNet is a large labelled image dataset initiated by Fei-Fei Li and collaborators.
The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge became a benchmark for computer vision.
AlexNet’s 2012 victory demonstrated the power of deep CNNs trained with GPUs and helped accelerate modern deep learning.
DeepMind landmarks include AlphaGo, AlphaZero and AlphaFold.
AlphaFold transformed protein-structure prediction by producing highly accurate predictions for many proteins. It does not replace every laboratory experiment or solve all of biology.
Google is also associated with the Transformer paper, TensorFlow, TPUs and the Gemini model family.
It is associated with GPT language models, ChatGPT, DALL·E image generation and reinforcement learning from human feedback in deployed conversational systems.
GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer.
ChatGPT is an application or service built around language models; “GPT” refers to a model family and architecture lineage. They are related but not identical terms.
Microsoft is a major investor and infrastructure partner in OpenAI and integrates generative AI into products under the Copilot name.
GitHub Copilot assists software development by suggesting and generating code.
Microsoft’s cloud platform is Azure. Azure AI services and Azure Machine Learning support AI development and deployment.
Quiz trap: “Copilot” is a broad brand used in several Microsoft products, not one single model.
Amazon Web Services provides cloud infrastructure and managed AI services.
• Bedrock: managed access to foundation models and generative-AI building blocks.
Amazon Robotics grew partly from Amazon’s acquisition of Kiva Systems in 2012.
• IBM Research contributions to AI and quantum computing.
IBM acquired Red Hat in 2019. Red Hat is strongly associated with enterprise open-source software and OpenShift, a Kubernetes platform.
Nvidia began as a graphics-chip company and became central to AI computing through GPUs, CUDA, high-speed networking and integrated systems.
CUDA is Nvidia’s parallel-computing platform and programming model.
Tensor cores accelerate matrix operations used in AI.
Nvidia designs chips and systems but generally relies on external foundries for leading-edge fabrication.
119. TCS and AI, data and cloud
Tata Consultancy Services is an Indian multinational IT services, consulting and business-solutions company within the Tata Group.
• F. C. Kohli is widely called the father of the Indian software industry and was TCS’s first general manager.
• TCS works across cloud, data, AI, cybersecurity, enterprise software, engineering and business-process transformation.
• TCS BaNCS is associated with financial-services software.
• TCS iON is associated with digital learning, assessments and business services.
• TCS Research traces its major research heritage to the Tata Research Development and Design Centre, established in Pune in 1981.

BHASHINI is India’s National Language Translation Mission under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. It supports digital services and language technologies for Indian languages.

• ISRO uses robotics and autonomous systems in space missions and research.
• DRDO works on unmanned systems, defence robotics and autonomy.

PART XI — COMMON TRAPS TO ELIMINATE
1. AI is broader than machine learning.
2. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning.
3. Classification predicts categories; regression predicts continuous values.
5. Validation tunes; testing estimates final unseen performance.
6. Accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced data.
7. High precision does not automatically mean high recall.
8. Backpropagation computes gradients; an optimiser updates weights.
9. A transformer is not the same thing as a chatbot.
10. An LLM predicts tokens; fluent language is not guaranteed truth.
11. RAG retrieves context but does not eliminate hallucination.
12. Prompting does not update model weights; fine-tuning does.
13. An embedding is a vector representation, not a database row or prompt.
14. SQL is a language family, not one database product.
15. NoSQL does not mean no structure or no queries.
16. A warehouse, lake and lakehouse are related but not identical.
17. ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads before transformation.
18. A KPI is tied to an objective; not every metric is a useful KPI.
19. SaaS is a complete service; IaaS exposes more infrastructure control.
21. Containers usually share the host kernel; VMs normally include guest operating systems.
22. Kubernetes orchestrates containers; Docker popularised container build and runtime workflows.
23. Hybrid cloud and multi-cloud are different dimensions.
24. Backup is not the whole disaster-recovery plan.
25. RPO concerns acceptable data loss; RTO concerns restoration time.
26. RPA robots are software bots, not physical robots.
27. An API is usually more stable than screen scraping.
28. Process mining uses event logs; task mining studies user-level actions.
29. A sensor measures; an actuator acts.
30. AGVs commonly follow fixed routes; AMRs plan more dynamically.
31. SLAM means localisation and mapping at the same time.
33. Robot-assisted surgery is not autonomous surgery.
35. FAR accepts an impostor; FRR rejects a genuine user.
36. A stricter biometric threshold usually lowers FAR but raises FRR.
38. Speaker recognition identifies the person; speech recognition identifies the words.
39. Liveness detection reduces spoofing risk but is not infallible.
40. Multiple biometric modalities are not always treated as different authentication factors.
41. Biometrics cannot be reset as easily as passwords.
42. Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship.
44. Deep Blue, Watson and AlphaGo solved different problems.
45. AlphaFold predicts protein structures; it does not replace all biological research.
46. OpenAI created ChatGPT; GPT is the model-family term.
47. AWS, Azure and Google Cloud are providers; cloud is the computing model.
48. TCS is separate from Tata Elxsi, Tata Technologies and Tata Communications.
49. IndiaAI and BHASHINI are different government initiatives.
50. UPI is a payments system, not a biometric identity system.

A conductor permits electric charge to move readily. Copper and aluminium are common interconnect materials. An insulator resists charge movement; silicon dioxide has historically been crucial as an insulating and gate material. A semiconductor lies between these extremes and, more importantly, can have its conductivity deliberately controlled.

Silicon dominates mainstream electronics because it is abundant, forms a useful native oxide, supports mature manufacturing and can be doped precisely. Germanium was important in early transistors and has returned in specialised high-mobility structures. Gallium arsenide is useful for high-frequency and optoelectronic devices. Gallium nitride and silicon carbide are increasingly important in high-power, high-voltage and high-temperature electronics.
• Gallium arsenide, gallium nitride and silicon carbide are compound or wide-bandgap materials.
• A semiconductor is not simply a weak conductor; its electrical behaviour can be engineered.
Pure silicon is intrinsic. Adding carefully selected impurities creates extrinsic material.
• N-type material has extra mobile electrons as majority carriers.
• P-type material has holes as majority carriers.
• Joining P-type and N-type material creates a PN junction.

The depletion region at a PN junction contains few mobile carriers and creates an internal electric field. Forward bias reduces the barrier and permits substantial current. Reverse bias enlarges the barrier and normally permits only small leakage until breakdown.
The diode is the simplest major PN-junction device. It conducts mainly in one direction and is used for rectification, switching, protection, light emission and sensing.
3. From vacuum tubes to solid state
Vacuum tubes enabled amplification and switching but were large, fragile, hot and power-hungry. The transistor made electronic systems smaller, more reliable and more efficient.

The first working point-contact transistor was demonstrated at Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1947 by John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, with William Shockley leading the group and subsequently developing the junction transistor. Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Quiz trap: Shockley is often casually called the transistor’s sole inventor. The historically safer answer recognises the Bell Labs team and distinguishes the point-contact device from Shockley’s junction-transistor work.
A bipolar junction transistor, or BJT, uses both electrons and holes and has emitter, base and collector terminals. A small base current can control a larger collector current.

A field-effect transistor controls current through an electric field. The metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, MOSFET, is the foundation of modern digital integrated circuits. Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng demonstrated the first working MOSFET at Bell Labs in 1959.

MOSFET terminals are gate, source, drain and body. Gate voltage controls a channel between source and drain. Because the gate can be insulated, MOS technology can achieve low steady-state control power and very high device density.

CMOS means complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor. It combines complementary N-channel and P-channel MOS transistors. In ideal static logic, one network is off while the other is on, so little direct current flows between supply rails except during switching and through leakage.
Frank Wanlass is associated with the invention of CMOS at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1963. CMOS became dominant because it offered high density and comparatively low power.

PART II — INTEGRATED CIRCUITS AND THE SILICON VALLEY FAMILY TREE

Early transistor circuits still required many separate components and wires. Large systems suffered from the “tyranny of numbers”: as component count rose, assembly complexity, size, cost and failure probability also rose.
An integrated circuit fabricates multiple electronic components and their connections on one piece of semiconductor material.

Jack Kilby demonstrated an integrated circuit at Texas Instruments in 1958 using germanium and fine-wire connections. Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor independently developed a practical silicon integrated-circuit approach using the planar process and deposited interconnections. Kilby received part of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics; Noyce had died and Nobel Prizes are not awarded posthumously.
Quiz rule: Kilby and Noyce are both central. Kilby produced the early working demonstration; Noyce’s silicon planar approach was more directly suited to scalable manufacture.

Jean Hoerni of Fairchild developed the planar process. It used silicon dioxide to protect the surface and photolithography to define regions. Noyce recognised that metal interconnections could be deposited on the protected surface, helping turn the integrated circuit into a manufacturable technology.
The Fairchild family tree is quiz gold:
• William Shockley established Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory.
• Eight employees left and became known as the “traitorous eight.”
• Fairchild alumni later founded or helped create Intel, AMD and many other Silicon Valley firms.
The term Silicon Valley was popularised by journalist Don Hoefler, although the region’s electronics history predates the phrase.
A microprocessor places the central processing unit’s core functions on one integrated circuit or a small chip set.

The Intel 4004, released in 1971, is widely described as the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor. It was a 4-bit processor created for a Busicom calculator project. Key contributors included Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor and Masatoshi Shima.
• Intel 8080: highly influential in early microcomputers.
• MOS Technology 6502: inexpensive processor used in systems including the Apple II, Commodore machines and game hardware.
• Zilog Z80: designed under Federico Faggin and widely used in computers and embedded systems.
• Motorola 68000: influential 16/32-bit family used in early Macintosh, Amiga and Atari ST systems.
• Intel 8088: powered the original IBM PC; internally related to the 8086 but with an 8-bit external data bus.
Quiz trap: Intel 4004 was not the first CPU design, first electronic computer or first programmable machine. Its claim is the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor.
PART III — HOW A CHIP IS MADE
Silicon is abundant in silica, but chipmaking requires extraordinary purity. A simplified chain is:
8. Wafer testing, dicing, packaging and final testing.

The Czochralski process grows a single-crystal ingot by drawing a seed crystal from molten material while rotating it. Float-zone silicon is another high-purity method used for specialised applications.

A wafer is the circular slice on which many dies are fabricated. A die is one rectangular chip before packaging. A packaged chip combines one or more dies with mechanical protection and electrical connections.
Modern chip fabrication is not a single printing operation. Hundreds or thousands of process steps build structures layer by layer.
• Deposition: adding material through methods such as chemical vapour deposition, physical vapour deposition or atomic layer deposition.
• Photolithography: transferring a pattern from a mask or reticle to light-sensitive photoresist.
• Etching: removing selected material, either wet or dry.
• Annealing: heating to repair crystal damage and activate dopants.
• Chemical-mechanical planarisation: polishing the surface flat.
• Inspection and metrology: measuring features and finding defects.
The front end of line generally forms transistors. The middle end connects contacts close to devices. The back end of line creates the larger interconnect stack that wires devices into circuits.

Feature dimensions can be far smaller than ordinary dust particles. Fabs therefore use cleanrooms, filtered air, strict clothing, chemical controls and vibration management. Coloured light often seen in lithography areas helps prevent accidental exposure of photoresist to wavelengths that could affect it.

A fab means semiconductor fabrication plant. A modern leading-edge fab can cost tens of billions of dollars because it requires specialised buildings, ultrapure water, enormous power infrastructure, gas and chemical systems, and fleets of precision tools.
A chip design is decomposed into geometric layers. Masks or reticles carry patterns used during lithography. Leading-edge designs require many masks, and mask sets are extremely expensive.

Optical proximity correction intentionally modifies mask shapes so diffraction and process effects produce the desired wafer pattern. Computational lithography uses intensive calculation to optimise these patterns.

Yield is the fraction of manufactured dies that meet requirements. A wafer can contain many dies, but a single defect may ruin a die. Larger dies generally expose more area to possible defects, making high yield harder.

Manufacturers improve yield through process control, defect reduction, redundancy and binning. Binning sorts chips according to tested performance, power and functional characteristics. Two products may come from similar silicon but be sold at different speed grades because testing shows different safe operating points.
• Process node does not equal a single physical measurement on every transistor.
• Smaller node labels broadly represent a technology generation, not a universal gate-length ruler.
• A “5 nm” chip does not mean every feature measures exactly five nanometres.
Photolithography uses light to define patterns. Resolution depends on wavelength, optical system and process techniques. Shorter wavelengths can support smaller features.
• Deep ultraviolet, including 248 nm krypton-fluoride and 193 nm argon-fluoride systems.
• 193 nm immersion lithography, where water between lens and wafer increases numerical aperture.
• Extreme ultraviolet, using approximately 13.5 nm radiation.
Multiple patterning allowed 193 nm lithography to create features smaller than a single exposure could resolve, but at the price of more masks, steps, cost and alignment risk.
Extreme ultraviolet light is strongly absorbed by air and ordinary optical materials. EUV systems therefore operate in vacuum and use mirrors rather than conventional transmissive lenses.

A high-power laser strikes tiny molten tin droplets to create plasma that emits EUV radiation. Multilayer mirrors collect and direct the light. The system must synchronise droplets, lasers, mirrors, masks, wafer stages and metrology with extreme precision.

ASML of the Netherlands is the only commercial supplier of leading-edge EUV lithography scanners. It relies on a specialised international supplier network. Carl Zeiss SMT provides crucial optical systems; light-source expertise came through Cymer, which ASML acquired.
Quiz trap: ASML does not manufacture the world’s chips. It supplies critical lithography equipment used by manufacturers such as TSMC, Samsung and Intel.

Numerical aperture describes an optical system’s ability to collect light and resolve detail. High-NA EUV raises numerical aperture compared with first-generation EUV, supporting smaller features but also requiring new optics, masks, resists and process integration.
High-NA does not eliminate every other challenge. Pattern roughness, defects, stochastic effects, overlay, resist chemistry, throughput and cost remain important.
PART V — THE SEMICONDUCTOR BUSINESS MODEL
17. Integrated device manufacturer, foundry and fabless firm
An integrated device manufacturer, or IDM, designs and manufactures chips. Intel and Samsung are major examples, although both also participate in foundry services.
A pure-play foundry manufactures chips designed by customers. TSMC, founded by Morris Chang in 1987, pioneered the dedicated foundry model at global scale.
A fabless company designs chips but contracts manufacturing to a foundry. Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm, Broadcom and many startups use this model.

A design-house licence supplier may create architectures or processor cores for others. Arm is the most famous example: it licenses instruction-set architectures and core designs rather than primarily selling its own mass-produced general-purpose chips.
OSAT means outsourced semiconductor assembly and test. Companies such as ASE and Amkor package and test chips after wafer fabrication.
• Electronic design automation: Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens EDA.

• System companies: server, phone, automobile, network and consumer-device manufacturers.

No single country or company controls every link. This interdependence explains why export controls, natural disasters, power shortages, logistics disruptions and geopolitical tension can affect global electronics.

Morris Chang founded Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company with support from Taiwan’s government and industrial institutions. TSMC’s key strategic idea was neutrality: manufacture designs for customers without competing against them through a broad branded-chip business.

Intel was founded in 1968 by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore; Andy Grove became its defining operational leader. “Intel” derives from integrated electronics.
