Samsung and SK hynix are central to global memory supply. Memory leadership is not identical to logic-foundry leadership; a quiz may deliberately mix the two.

Not every important chip uses the newest node. Automobiles, industrial controllers, power-management chips, radio-frequency products and many sensors may prioritise reliability, analogue performance, long availability and cost.

GlobalFoundries, UMC and other manufacturers remain strategically important even without competing at every leading-edge logic node. The 2020–2022 chip shortage demonstrated that shortages of mature-node devices can stop production of expensive finished products.

As planar transistors shrank, the gate struggled to control the channel, increasing leakage and short-channel effects. A FinFET raises the channel into a fin so the gate can wrap around multiple sides, improving electrostatic control.
Intel introduced its Tri-Gate commercial implementation at scale in the early 2010s. Foundries subsequently adopted FinFETs broadly for advanced nodes.
A gate-all-around transistor surrounds the channel more completely. Nanosheet and nanoribbon structures stack horizontal channels, offering designers flexibility in balancing current and area.
• Samsung uses MBCFET for its multi-bridge-channel implementation.
• TSMC’s N2 family uses nanosheet transistors.
• Intel uses RibbonFET terminology for its gate-all-around implementation.

Traditional chips route both signals and power through interconnect layers above the transistors. Backside power delivery separates much of the power network to the rear side of the wafer, potentially improving voltage delivery and freeing front-side routing resources.
Intel calls its approach PowerVia. The important concept is separation of power and signal routing, not merely memorising a brand name.
26. Dennard scaling and the power wall

Dennard scaling described an era in which shrinking transistor dimensions and voltages allowed density and clock frequency to rise without proportional growth in power density. This trend broke down as voltage scaling slowed and leakage increased.
• Power efficiency became as important as raw transistor count.
• Dark silicon describes transistors that cannot all be active simultaneously within power limits.
An instruction-set architecture, ISA, defines the programmer-visible interface: instructions, registers, data types, memory model, privilege levels and related behaviour.
A microarchitecture is a particular internal implementation of an ISA. Two processors can execute the same x86 or Arm program while using different pipelines, caches and execution units.
Quiz trap: x86, Arm and RISC-V are instruction-set families. Zen, Core, Cortex, Neoverse and specific Apple CPU designs are microarchitectures or core families.
1. Fetch an instruction from memory or cache.
Real high-performance processors overlap many instructions through pipelining.
A pipeline divides work into stages. Like an assembly line, it increases throughput even though one item still passes through multiple steps.
• Data hazards: an instruction needs a result not yet ready.
• Control hazards: the next instruction depends on a branch.
• Structural hazards: two operations need the same resource.
Forwarding, scheduling, branch prediction and duplicated resources reduce stalls.

A superscalar processor can issue multiple instructions per clock cycle. Out-of-order execution allows independent instructions to proceed while another waits, while retirement preserves required architectural order.
• Register renaming to eliminate false dependencies.

Speculation improves performance but created security concerns highlighted by attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown. Those vulnerabilities belong primarily to Module 7, but the architectural cause belongs here.
A branch predictor guesses the outcome and target of control-flow instructions so the pipeline can continue. A correct prediction saves time; a misprediction requires wrong-path work to be discarded.
Deep pipelines and wide processors make branch accuracy valuable. Modern predictors use complex histories and pattern-recognition structures.
CPU speed greatly exceeds main-memory access speed. Caches store recently or frequently used data closer to execution units.
• L1 cache: very small and very fast, often split into instruction and data caches.
• L3 or last-level cache: shared or semi-shared, larger again.
Temporal locality means recently used data may be reused. Spatial locality means nearby data may soon be used.
• Miss: data must be fetched from a lower level.
• Cache line: unit transferred between cache levels.
• Coherence: maintains a consistent view across cores.
• MESI: a well-known family of coherence states—Modified, Exclusive, Shared and Invalid.
Virtual memory gives each process an address space and maps virtual addresses to physical memory through page tables. A translation lookaside buffer caches recent address translations.

Benefits include isolation, convenient memory layout, controlled sharing and the ability to use secondary storage as backing when necessary. A page fault occurs when required mapping or data is not currently available in the needed form.

A multicore processor contains multiple processing cores. Simultaneous multithreading allows one core to maintain architectural state for more than one thread and use otherwise idle execution resources.
Intel’s brand name Hyper-Threading is one implementation; SMT is the general term.
Amdahl’s Law limits speedup when part of a program remains serial. Adding cores cannot make a fundamentally serial section disappear.
PART VIII — x86, ARM AND RISC-V
The x86 lineage begins with Intel’s 8086. The IBM PC used the 8088, strengthening the architecture’s ecosystem. Backward compatibility helped later processors run large bodies of existing software.
• 80486: integrated floating-point unit in major versions and deeper integration.
• x86-64/AMD64: 64-bit extension introduced commercially by AMD.

CISC means complex instruction set computer, but modern x86 processors often translate complex instructions into simpler internal micro-operations. Therefore, “CISC versus RISC” is not a complete description of modern implementation.
Advanced Micro Devices was founded in 1969 by Jerry Sanders and colleagues. Important milestones include:
• AMD64, which became the dominant 64-bit x86 extension.
• Acquisition of ATI, strengthening graphics capability.
• Zen architecture, central to AMD’s modern revival.
• Ryzen consumer CPUs, EPYC server CPUs and Instinct accelerators.
Lisa Su became CEO in 2014 and is strongly associated with AMD’s strategic and technical revival.
Arm grew from Acorn Computers’ search for an efficient processor for its computers. ARM originally meant Acorn RISC Machine and later Advanced RISC Machines. The company is now styled Arm.
Its business model centres on licensing:
• Architecture licences permit a company to design its own compatible cores.
• Core licences provide ready-designed Arm cores such as Cortex families.

Arm strengths include energy efficiency, a large embedded ecosystem and widespread mobile use. It expanded into servers through Neoverse and into PCs through custom designs and Windows-on-Arm systems.
• Qualcomm Snapdragon families, including Oryon CPU designs derived from Nuvia expertise.
Quiz trap: Apple Silicon uses the Arm ISA but Apple designs its own high-performance CPU cores; it does not merely rebadge a standard Cortex core.

RISC-V is an open standard instruction-set architecture originating from research at the University of California, Berkeley. The name follows earlier Berkeley RISC projects and is pronounced “risk-five.”
• Modular base instruction sets plus extensions.
• Implementers may create proprietary or open-source microarchitectures.
• Used in education, microcontrollers, storage controllers, embedded devices and increasingly higher-performance systems.
The RISC-V ISA being open does not mean every RISC-V chip design is open source, free of patents, or fabricated without cost.
RISC traditionally emphasises simple, regular instructions, many registers, load/store organisation and pipeline-friendly encoding. CISC traditionally includes richer, more variable instructions.
• Arm and RISC-V designs can use advanced out-of-order execution.
• Performance depends on microarchitecture, memory, manufacturing, software and workload—not ISA label alone.
PART IX — CPUS, GPUS, TPUS, NPUS AND OTHER ACCELERATORS

A CPU is optimised for flexible control flow, low-latency execution and a broad range of tasks. It usually has a modest number of sophisticated cores, large caches and strong branch-handling capability.
A GPU contains many arithmetic resources designed for high-throughput parallel work. It originated in graphics but became crucial for scientific computing, machine learning and AI.
Graphics workloads process many vertices, pixels and fragments with related operations. This data parallelism also suits matrix and vector computation.

Nvidia popularised general-purpose GPU computing through CUDA, introduced in 2006. CUDA’s software ecosystem—compilers, libraries, developer tools and trained users—became a major competitive advantage.
Nvidia was founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The founders are famously associated with an early meeting at a Denny’s restaurant.
• RTX professional families: workstation and rendering uses.
• CUDA: parallel-computing platform and programming model.
• Blackwell and Rubin: major recent AI-computing platform generations.
The term GPU was popularised commercially by Nvidia around the GeForce 256, although graphics processors existed earlier.

Google’s Tensor Processing Unit is an application-specific integrated circuit designed for machine-learning workloads, especially tensor operations. TPUs are used in Google’s infrastructure and cloud offerings.
A TPU is not a generic name for every AI accelerator; it is Google’s product family and trademarked term.

Neural processing unit is a broad industry term for hardware optimised for neural-network inference or related AI operations. NPUs increasingly appear in phones and PCs to run AI locally with lower power and reduced dependence on cloud processing.

TOPS means trillions of operations per second, often quoted for low-precision AI arithmetic. TOPS figures are not directly comparable unless precision, sparsity assumptions, workload and utilisation are known.
• DSP: digital signal processor, optimised for repeated numeric operations in audio, communications, control and sensing.
• FPGA: field-programmable gate array, reconfigurable after manufacture.
• ASIC: application-specific integrated circuit, custom-designed for a particular purpose.

An FPGA offers flexibility but may use more area or power than a purpose-built ASIC. An ASIC offers efficiency at scale but has high design cost and cannot normally be fundamentally reconfigured after manufacture.
PART X — SYSTEM-ON-CHIP AND HETEROGENEOUS COMPUTING
A system-on-chip integrates multiple functions that once required separate chips:
Smartphone processors are usually SoCs. Integration can reduce power, board area and latency.
Different processors excel at different workloads. A heterogeneous system assigns work accordingly:
• CPU for control and serial logic.
• Fixed-function engines for video or encryption.

The programming challenge is moving data efficiently and selecting the right engine. An accelerator that is theoretically fast can be limited by memory bandwidth, transfer overhead or poor software support.
A chiplet design partitions a system into smaller dies connected in one package. Benefits may include:
• Better yield than one enormous monolithic die.
• Ability to combine different process nodes.
• Reuse of standard I/O or cache dies.
Challenges include interconnect latency, power, package cost, thermal design, testing and standards.

AMD’s Ryzen and EPYC families helped popularise chiplets in mainstream high-performance processors. UCIe, Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express, aims to standardise die-to-die connections across an ecosystem.
Volatile memory loses stored information when power is removed. Non-volatile memory retains it.
• SRAM: fast, expensive per bit, typically used for caches.
• DRAM: dense and relatively inexpensive, used for main memory; must be refreshed.
• NAND flash: non-volatile, used in SSDs and memory cards.
• NOR flash: supports random read access and is commonly used for firmware and embedded code.
• ROM: broad term for memory intended primarily for reading; implementations vary.

Static random-access memory stores a bit using a bistable circuit, often a six-transistor cell. It does not require periodic refresh while powered, but occupies more area than DRAM. CPU caches commonly use SRAM because latency matters more than maximum density.
Dynamic random-access memory stores charge in a tiny capacitor controlled by a transistor. Charge leaks, so rows must be refreshed.
• DIMM: memory module format used in many computers.
• LPDDR: low-power DDR for mobile and energy-sensitive systems.
• HBM: high-bandwidth memory, using stacked dies and very wide interfaces.

High-bandwidth memory stacks DRAM dies and places them close to processors through advanced packaging. Through-silicon vias connect layers vertically. HBM offers high bandwidth and energy efficiency per transferred bit, making it important in AI accelerators and high-performance computing.

HBM supply links memory makers, foundries, packaging capacity and accelerator designers. This is why an AI-chip shortage may actually involve packaging or memory rather than only logic-wafer fabrication.
NAND flash stores charge or related electrical state in non-volatile cells. Modern 3D NAND stacks many layers vertically.
• MLC: commonly two bits per cell.
More bits per cell increase density but generally reduce endurance and make sensing more difficult. Controllers use error correction, wear levelling, bad-block management and over-provisioning.
An HDD stores data magnetically on spinning platters and uses moving heads. An SSD uses flash memory and has no moving read/write head.
SSDs usually offer lower latency, greater shock resistance and higher random-access performance. HDDs can remain cost-effective for high-capacity bulk storage.

NVMe is a storage protocol designed for non-volatile memory over interfaces such as PCI Express. SATA is an older interface/protocol family originally designed around disks. An NVMe SSD is not simply a faster version of the same protocol as SATA.

Technologies explored beyond conventional DRAM and NAND include MRAM, phase-change memory, resistive RAM and ferroelectric memory. Each balances speed, endurance, density, retention and manufacturability differently.
PART XII — PACKAGING, INTERCONNECTS AND TESTING
• Provides a standard form for system assembly.
• Can connect multiple dies and memory stacks.
Package types evolved from dual in-line packages to pin-grid arrays, ball-grid arrays, land-grid arrays, flip-chip arrangements, wafer-level packages and sophisticated 2.5D/3D systems.
Wire bonding uses fine wires to connect die pads to package leads or substrate. Flip-chip mounting turns the die face-down and connects it with bumps, shortening connections and supporting more I/O.
• 2.5D packaging places dies side by side on an interposer.
• Through-silicon vias can provide vertical electrical connections.
• Hybrid bonding can connect surfaces with very fine pitch.
TSMC CoWoS, Intel Foveros and EMIB, and Samsung advanced-packaging families are common quiz names. Do not treat them as identical: they represent different implementations and product families.
• Burn-in or stress testing for some products.

Automatic test equipment, probe cards and test programs are specialised parts of the industry. Packaging and testing are not low-skill afterthoughts; advanced integration makes them central to performance and yield.
Electrical power becomes heat. Excess temperature reduces reliability and can force frequency reduction, called thermal throttling.
• Immersion cooling in specialised data centres.
Thermal design power is a design guideline rather than a universal statement of exact maximum electrical consumption.
PART XIII — INTERFACES AND SYSTEM INFRASTRUCTURE

PCI Express is a high-speed serial interconnect used for GPUs, SSDs, networking and accelerators. It uses lanes; a device may have x1, x4, x8 or x16 connections. Each generation broadly increases per-lane transfer capability. Actual application throughput is lower than raw signalling rate because of encoding and protocol overhead.
Compute Express Link builds on the PCIe physical layer to support coherent connections among processors, memory and accelerators. It can enable memory expansion, pooling and sharing in data centres.
Modern computing performance is increasingly limited by data movement. Moving a value from distant memory can consume more time and energy than performing a simple arithmetic operation.
PART XIV — COMPUTING LAWS AND QUIZ-FAVOURITE FORMULATIONS

Gordon Moore observed in 1965 that the number of components on an economical integrated circuit was increasing rapidly; he later revised the cadence. The popular modern shorthand is that transistor count on integrated circuits roughly doubles about every two years.
It is an empirical industry observation, not a law of physics. Transistor density can continue improving even when clock frequency or user-visible performance does not double at the same pace.

Robert Dennard and colleagues described scaling relationships that once allowed smaller transistors to operate at lower voltage while maintaining approximately constant power density. Its breakdown contributed to the power wall.

Gene Amdahl’s law limits the speedup from parallelisation according to the fraction that remains serial. If 10% of a workload cannot be parallelised, unlimited processors cannot produce more than a tenfold speedup under the simple model.

John Gustafson argued that larger systems often solve larger problems rather than merely running a fixed problem faster. Scaled speedup can therefore be more optimistic than fixed-workload Amdahl analysis.
Koomey’s Law describes a long-term trend of increasing computations per unit of energy. It concerns energy efficiency, not transistor count.
Niklaus Wirth’s aphorism says software becomes slower more rapidly than hardware becomes faster. It is a warning about software complexity and bloat, not a quantitative physical law.
Kryder’s Law refers to historical growth in magnetic-storage areal density. Like Moore’s Law, it describes a trend rather than a guaranteed physical rule.

Rock’s Law, associated with Arthur Rock, observes that semiconductor-fabrication plant costs rise dramatically over time. It helps explain industry consolidation and the difficulty of competing at the leading edge.
PART XV — CHIP SUPPLY CHAINS, ECONOMICS AND GEOPOLITICS

A finished processor may depend on architecture IP from one country, design teams distributed worldwide, EDA software from a few firms, EUV equipment assembled in the Netherlands, optics from Germany, chemicals and wafers from Japan and elsewhere, fabrication in Taiwan, South Korea or the United States, and packaging through an Asian manufacturing network.
A disruption at one specialised stage cannot always be replaced quickly.

During the pandemic-era shortage, demand shifted, companies placed protective orders, automobile demand recovered faster than expected, and capacity was difficult to reassign. Long manufacturing lead times amplified forecasting errors.
A car can require hundreds or thousands of chips, many built on mature nodes. The absence of one inexpensive microcontroller can stop shipment of an entire vehicle.

Advanced-computing and semiconductor-manufacturing export controls aim to restrict access to selected capabilities. Quiz questions may ask which technologies are controlled, which companies dominate supply, or why leading-edge equipment is strategically significant.

Avoid simplistic claims that one restriction instantly stops all chipmaking. Firms can redesign products, use older nodes, develop substitutes or obtain capabilities through alternate routes, but specialised bottlenecks can still have major effects.

India has long had strength in semiconductor design, embedded software and engineering services. Current policy aims to expand fabrication, assembly, testing, compound semiconductors and supply-chain capacity.
Quiz-relevant Indian names and concepts include:
• SHAKTI processors from IIT Madras, based on RISC-V.
• AJIT, an Indian processor initiative associated with IIT Bombay.
Do not confuse designing an indigenous processor core with manufacturing it entirely in a domestic leading-edge fab.

A classical bit takes a definite logical value, 0 or 1. A qubit is a two-level quantum system whose state can be represented as a superposition of basis states α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where the squared magnitudes of the amplitudes sum to one.
Measurement produces a classical outcome according to probabilities determined by the amplitudes. A qubit is not simply “both 0 and 1” in the ordinary classical sense.
Superposition means quantum states can be combined linearly. Quantum algorithms manipulate amplitudes so that useful answers are amplified and unwanted possibilities interfere destructively.
The power does not come from reading all possible answers simultaneously; measurement returns limited classical information.
Entanglement creates correlations that cannot be described by assigning each qubit an independent local state. Measuring one part constrains correlations with the other, even when separated.
Entanglement does not permit faster-than-light communication. The local measurement result is random, and classical communication is still required to compare outcomes.

Quantum amplitudes have phase. Amplitudes can reinforce or cancel. Algorithm design uses interference to increase the probability of desired outcomes. Superposition without controlled interference would not by itself produce useful quantum speedup.
Quantum computation applies reversible unitary gates before measurement.
• X gate: analogous to a bit flip.
• H or Hadamard gate: creates and recombines superpositions.
• CNOT: controlled operation that can create entanglement.
• Rotation gates: change qubit state by specified angles.
A quantum circuit is a sequence of gates and measurements. Unlike many classical gates, ideal quantum gates must be reversible.
The no-cloning theorem states that an arbitrary unknown quantum state cannot be copied perfectly. This affects communication, error correction and cryptography.
Quantum error correction does not violate no-cloning because it encodes logical information across entangled physical qubits rather than making an independent perfect copy of an unknown state.
Qubits interact with their environment and lose quantum information. Sources include thermal noise, control errors, material defects, crosstalk and imperfect measurement.
Coherence time is the period over which useful quantum information persists under specified conditions. Gate fidelity describes how closely an operation matches the intended one.
A physical qubit is an actual device. A logical qubit is error-protected information encoded across many physical qubits.
Useful fault-tolerant machines may require very large numbers of physical qubits for each logical qubit. Therefore, comparing machines only by raw physical-qubit count is misleading.
Quantum error-correcting codes detect and correct errors without directly measuring the encoded quantum information. Ancilla qubits and syndrome measurements reveal error information.
The surface code is a leading approach. The error threshold is crucial: if physical error rates fall below a threshold, increasing code size can reduce logical error rates.

Google’s Willow announcement highlighted below-threshold error-correction behaviour in a surface-code scaling experiment. This is not the same as a complete general-purpose fault-tolerant quantum computer.
• Superconducting qubits: used by IBM, Google and others; fast gates but cryogenic operation.
• Trapped ions: excellent fidelity and connectivity, with slower gates; used by IonQ, Quantinuum and research groups.
• Neutral atoms: atoms trapped with lasers; pursued by QuEra, Pasqal and others.
• Photonic quantum computing: uses photons and optical components; pursued by PsiQuantum, Xanadu and others.
• Spin qubits: encode information in electron or nuclear spin.
• Topological approaches: seek intrinsically protected states; technically challenging and still developing.
No platform has yet won every dimension of scalability, fidelity, speed, connectivity, manufacture and error correction.

Quantum advantage means a quantum computer performs a useful or well-defined task better than a classical alternative under stated criteria. Quantum supremacy was the earlier term for demonstrating a quantum computation infeasible for leading classical machines, even if the task lacked immediate practical value.
Claims depend on the precise benchmark and classical comparison. Improved classical algorithms can narrow an earlier claimed gap.
PART XVII — QUANTUM ALGORITHMS AND APPLICATIONS

Peter Shor developed a quantum algorithm for integer factorisation and discrete logarithms with major asymptotic speedup. A sufficiently large fault-tolerant quantum computer could threaten widely deployed public-key systems based on RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography.
Today’s noisy machines are far too small and error-prone to factor cryptographically significant RSA keys using full Shor execution.
Lov Grover’s search algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for unstructured search. Searching N possibilities takes on the order of √N quantum queries rather than N classical queries under the model.
For symmetric cryptography, Grover’s algorithm does not make all keys instantly useless; increasing key length can compensate for the quadratic reduction in effective search complexity.

These early algorithms demonstrate separations between quantum and classical query complexity and helped establish quantum-algorithmic ideas. They are common quiz names even though their direct commercial value is limited.

Richard Feynman argued that quantum systems are difficult to simulate efficiently on classical computers and proposed quantum computation as a natural approach. Chemistry, materials and many-body physics remain major target applications.

Variational quantum eigensolver and quantum approximate optimisation algorithm combine parameterised quantum circuits with classical optimisation. They were proposed for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices, but practical advantage remains an open engineering and scientific question.

Quantum annealing addresses optimisation through a physical process related to energy landscapes. D-Wave is the company most associated with commercial quantum annealers. A quantum annealer is not equivalent to a universal gate-based quantum computer.
Quantum teleportation transfers an unknown quantum state using shared entanglement plus classical communication. It does not transport matter and cannot transmit information faster than light.
QKD uses quantum states to detect eavesdropping under specified assumptions. BB84, proposed by Charles Bennett and Gilles Brassard in 1984, is the best-known protocol.
QKD is different from post-quantum cryptography:
• QKD requires quantum communication hardware or channels.
• Post-quantum cryptography runs on conventional computers using algorithms believed resistant to quantum attacks.

A cryptographically relevant quantum computer does not exist today, but sensitive data may need protection for decades. An attacker can collect encrypted information now and attempt to decrypt it later: “harvest now, decrypt later.”
Cryptographic migration also takes years because protocols, hardware, certificates and embedded devices must change.
The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology selected and standardised post-quantum algorithms after an international competition.
• ML-KEM, derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber, for key encapsulation.
• ML-DSA, derived from CRYSTALS-Dilithium, for digital signatures.
• SLH-DSA, derived from SPHINCS+, for hash-based signatures.
Post-quantum does not mean “uses a quantum computer.” It means designed to resist known attacks from both classical and quantum computers.
Crypto agility is the ability to replace algorithms and keys without rebuilding an entire system. Hybrid approaches may combine classical and post-quantum methods during transition.
PART XIX — CURRENT DEVELOPMENTS SNAPSHOT: JULY 2026

TSMC states that its N2 process entered volume production in the fourth quarter of 2025. N2 introduces nanosheet gate-all-around transistors in TSMC’s leading logic line. TSMC unveiled A14 in 2025 and targets production in 2028; it describes performance, power and density improvements over N2.
Quiz distinction: N2 is the near-term production family; A14 is the later announced generation.

Intel’s Panther Lake, sold as Core Ultra Series 3, is the first major client platform built on Intel 18A. Intel 18A combines RibbonFET gate-all-around transistors with PowerVia backside power delivery.

Nvidia announced its Rubin platform for 2026 as the successor generation after Blackwell. Rubin is a platform rather than only one GPU: it combines processors, networking, memory, systems and software for large-scale AI infrastructure.

AMD launched the Instinct MI350 series in 2025 using its CDNA 4 accelerator architecture. The family targets AI training, inference and high-performance computing and competes with Nvidia’s data-centre accelerators.

Qualcomm announced Snapdragon X2 Elite and X2 Elite Extreme for Windows PCs in 2025, using third-generation Oryon CPU cores and stronger on-device AI capability. Their importance is the continuing expansion of Arm-based custom CPUs in PCs.

Google announced the 105-qubit Willow superconducting processor in December 2024. Its central research claim was that increasing surface-code size reduced errors, an important below-threshold error-correction milestone.

Microsoft announced Majorana 1 in February 2025 as a processor based on its topological-core approach. For quiz purposes, remember the company, product and claimed hardware direction. Do not confuse an announced scaling path with an already demonstrated million-qubit fault-tolerant computer.

IBM’s roadmap targets demonstrations of near-term quantum advantage by the end of 2026 and a large-scale fault-tolerant system named Starling in 2029. IBM also marks 2016 as the year it first made a quantum computer publicly accessible through the cloud.

A silicon wafer is circular and often shows rainbow-like interference colours. Repeated rectangular dies fill most of the surface, with incomplete dies around the edge.
• Exposed square die: often a bare processor or accelerator.
• Heat spreader: metal cap over a CPU package.
• Land-grid array: flat contact pads on package underside.
• Pin-grid array: pins on package underside.
• Ball-grid array: solder balls used for board attachment.

• Ion-trap system: vacuum and laser apparatus.

• IBM Quantum System One: enclosed integrated quantum-computing system.
PART XXI — COMMON TRAPS TO ELIMINATE
1. A fabless company designs chips; it does not mean the company has no laboratories or hardware expertise.
2. A foundry manufactures customer designs; it may also develop process technology and packaging.
3. Arm licenses architectures and cores; it is not primarily a mass-market chip foundry.
4. RISC-V is an ISA, not one processor model or one company.
5. x86-64 was introduced commercially by AMD and is also called AMD64.
6. A GPU is not automatically faster than a CPU for every task.
7. TOPS cannot be compared without precision and workload context.
8. HBM is stacked DRAM, not NAND storage.
9. NVMe is a protocol; M.2 is a physical form factor and connector specification.
10. Process-node names are generational labels, not exact dimensions for every feature.
11. EUV uses mirrors in vacuum because 13.5 nm radiation is absorbed by air and ordinary lenses.
12. ASML makes lithography systems, not consumer processors.
13. Moore’s Law concerns component or transistor density, not guaranteed clock-speed doubling.
14. Superposition does not allow all answers to be read out at once.
15. Entanglement does not permit faster-than-light messaging.
16. Physical-qubit count is not the same as useful logical-qubit count.
17. Quantum annealers are not identical to universal gate-model computers.
18. Post-quantum cryptography runs on classical hardware.
19. Shor threatens public-key cryptography at sufficient scale; Grover offers quadratic search speedup.
20. Quantum advantage depends on a defined task and classical baseline.
