MODULE 12 — ENGINEERING MARVELS, ENERGY SYSTEMS & SUSTAINABLE TECHNOLOGY

This module covers the ideas, people, structures, machines, energy systems and sustainability technologies that repeatedly appear in technology, science, business and current-affairs quizzes. The goal is not merely to memorize names. You should be able to identify an answer from a clue about a design principle, material, engineer, company, country, record, failure, nickname, diagram or historical first.

The module follows the roadmap through structural engineering, landmark infrastructure, major engineers, power generation, electricity grids, batteries, hydrogen, carbon capture, desalination, waste management and the circular economy. It includes India-specific material wherever quiz relevance is high.

Engineering is the application of scientific and mathematical principles to design systems that satisfy a human need under constraints. A scientist may ask, “Why does this happen?” An engineer asks, “How can this principle be used reliably, safely and economically?”
• Function: What must the system do?
• Safety: How can failure be prevented or contained?
• Cost: Can it be built, operated and maintained affordably?
• Energy: What power source and efficiency are possible?
• Environment: What are the emissions, waste and ecological effects?
• Time: How quickly must it be built or delivered?
• Reliability: How consistently must it perform?
• Maintainability: Can components be inspected, repaired and replaced?
• Scalability: Can a prototype become a mass-deployed system?
Design load: The load a structure or component is expected to carry in service.
Factor of safety: The ratio between the failure strength and the permitted working stress. A factor of safety greater than one provides a margin for uncertainty.
Redundancy: Inclusion of alternative load paths or backup systems so that one failure does not cause total collapse.
Fail-safe design: A failure causes the system to move into a safer condition.
Fault tolerance: The ability to continue operating despite faults.
Resilience: The ability to withstand disruption and recover.
Life-cycle assessment: Evaluation of environmental impact from raw-material extraction through manufacture, use and disposal.
Embodied energy: Energy consumed in producing and transporting a material or product.

“Strongest” is not the same as “best engineering material.” Engineers choose materials by balancing strength, stiffness, density, corrosion resistance, cost, manufacturability, fatigue behaviour and temperature tolerance.
Tension: A pulling force that stretches a member. Cables in a suspension bridge primarily carry tension.
Compression: A pushing force that shortens a member. Stone columns and bridge piers primarily carry compression.
Shear: Opposing forces acting parallel to a cross-section, tending to make one layer slide past another.
Bending: A combination of tension on one side and compression on the other.
Stress describes internal force intensity. Its SI unit is the pascal.
Strain = Change in length / Original length
Young’s modulus = Stress / Strain within the elastic region
A high Young’s modulus means a material is stiff. Stiffness is resistance to deformation. Strength is resistance to failure. These are not identical.
Elastic deformation disappears when the load is removed. Plastic deformation remains. The yield point marks the transition to significant permanent deformation.
Dead load: Permanent weight of the structure itself and fixed components.
Live load: Variable load from people, vehicles, furniture and movable equipment.
Wind load: Pressure and suction caused by wind.
Seismic load: Inertial forces generated during an earthquake.
Snow load: Weight of accumulated snow.
Thermal load: Stress caused by expansion or contraction when movement is restrained.
Impact load: Sudden load, such as collision or dropped weight.
Dynamic load: Load that changes with time and may cause vibration or resonance.

A triangle keeps its shape unless the lengths of its sides change. A four-sided frame can deform into a parallelogram unless braced. Trusses therefore use triangular units to distribute forces efficiently.
A truss is a framework of members joined at nodes. In an ideal pin-jointed truss, members carry mainly axial tension or compression rather than bending.
• Pratt truss: Diagonal members generally slope toward the centre and typically carry tension under gravity loading.
• Howe truss: Diagonals slope away from the centre and generally carry compression.
• Warren truss: Repeating equilateral or near-equilateral triangles.
• K truss: Vertical members and diagonals form K shapes.
An arch transfers load largely through compression toward its supports. The wedge-shaped central stone that locks a masonry arch is the keystone. The outward force at the supports is called thrust.

A dome is essentially an arch rotated around a vertical axis. Domes can enclose large spaces without internal columns. Important dome forms include hemispherical, onion, geodesic and tensile membrane domes.
A vault extends an arch through space. A barrel vault resembles a continuous tunnel. A groin vault is formed by intersecting barrel vaults.
A simply supported beam rests on supports at its ends.
A cantilever is fixed at one end and free at the other.
A continuous beam spans more than two supports.
An I-beam places most material in the upper and lower flanges, far from the neutral axis, where it contributes strongly to bending resistance. The vertical web resists shear.

Long slender compression members can fail by sudden sideways bending before the material itself crushes. This instability is buckling. Buckling risk increases with length and decreases with greater stiffness and an efficient cross-section.

Every structure has natural frequencies. If repeated forcing occurs near one of them, oscillations may grow through resonance. Engineers reduce this risk through stiffness changes, damping devices and tuned mass dampers.
A tuned mass damper is a large auxiliary mass designed to oscillate out of phase with a building and reduce motion. Taipei 101 is famous for its visible tuned mass damper.
Materials expand when heated and contract when cooled. Bridges, rails and pipelines use expansion joints or flexible supports to prevent thermal stress and buckling.
• Sudden sideways instability of a column → buckling
• Repeated forcing at natural frequency → resonance
• Large moving counterweight in a skyscraper → tuned mass damper

Stone performs well in compression but poorly in tension. Ancient pyramids, temples, arches and aqueducts exploited this property. Brick is modular, fire-resistant and durable but similarly depends on mortar and geometry to manage loads.
Concrete is made from cement, fine aggregate, coarse aggregate and water. Cement is the binder. Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension.

Reinforced concrete embeds steel bars so concrete carries compression and steel carries tension. Steel and concrete work well together because they bond effectively and have broadly compatible thermal expansion.

Prestressed concrete introduces compressive stress before service loading. This reduces tensile cracking. In pretensioning, steel tendons are tensioned before concrete is cast. In post-tensioning, tendons are tensioned after the concrete hardens.
Portland cement was patented by Joseph Aspdin in 1824. The name referred to its resemblance to Portland stone.
Cement production is carbon-intensive because fuel is used for heating and because limestone releases carbon dioxide during calcination.
Cast iron contains more carbon than most steels. It is hard and strong in compression but relatively brittle.
Wrought iron has low carbon content and is tough and workable.
Steel is primarily iron alloyed with carbon and often other elements.
Stainless steel contains enough chromium to form a protective passive oxide layer. Nickel, molybdenum and other elements may be added for specific grades.
Weathering steel, often associated with the trademark COR-TEN, forms a stable rust-like protective layer under suitable conditions.

Aluminium is lightweight, corrosion-resistant and highly recyclable. Although abundant in Earth’s crust, it was historically expensive because extracting it from ore requires substantial electricity. The Hall–Héroult process, independently developed by Charles Martin Hall and Paul Héroult in 1886, enabled large-scale aluminium production.

A composite combines materials to obtain improved properties. Fibreglass combines glass fibres with polymer resin. Carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer offers high strength-to-weight ratio but can be expensive and difficult to recycle.
Reinforced concrete is itself a composite.
Shape-memory alloys can return toward a pre-set shape when heated. Nitinol is a nickel-titanium shape-memory alloy.
Piezoelectric materials generate electric charge under mechanical stress and deform when an electric field is applied.
Aerogels are extremely low-density, highly porous solids with excellent insulation properties.
Graphene is a one-atom-thick sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice.
Self-healing concrete may use bacteria, capsules or chemical agents to seal cracks.
• Graphene isolation associated with Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov
• Stainless steel’s corrosion resistance → chromium-rich passive layer
The simplest bridge type. A horizontal deck rests on supports. Suitable for relatively short spans unless supported by many piers.
Loads travel through compression along the arch to abutments. Ancient Roman stone bridges and aqueducts are classic examples.
Uses triangular frameworks. Trusses can carry substantial loads efficiently and were central to the expansion of railways.
Projecting arms extend from piers and may support a suspended central span. The Forth Bridge in Scotland is a famous steel cantilever railway bridge.

The deck is hung from vertical suspenders attached to main cables draped over towers and anchored at both ends. Main cables carry tension; towers carry compression. Suspension bridges are ideal for very long main spans.
• Brooklyn Bridge: Designed by John A. Roebling; completed under Washington Roebling, with Emily Warren Roebling playing a crucial coordinating role.
• Golden Gate Bridge: Connects San Francisco and Marin County; chief engineer Joseph Strauss, with major design contributions from Leon Moisseiff, Charles Alton Ellis and architect Irving Morrow.
• Akashi Kaikyō Bridge, Japan: Famous long-span suspension bridge linking Kobe and Awaji Island.
The deck is supported directly by inclined cables connected to towers. Unlike a suspension bridge, it generally does not require massive end anchorages for the main cables.
• Fan: Cables converge near the tower top.
• Bandra–Worli Sea Link, Mumbai: Cable-stayed sections; officially Rajiv Gandhi Sea Link.
• Signature Bridge, Delhi: Asymmetrical cable-stayed bridge over the Yamuna.
• Sudarshan Setu in Gujarat: Cable-stayed bridge connecting Okha mainland and Beyt Dwarka.
• Atal Setu, Mumbai Trans Harbour Link: A major sea bridge linking Mumbai and Navi Mumbai; not principally known as a cable-stayed landmark, but highly quiz-relevant as infrastructure.
Bascule bridge: Deck pivots upward, often counterweighted.
Swing bridge: Rotates horizontally around a central pivot.
Vertical-lift bridge: Entire span rises vertically.
London’s Tower Bridge is a combined bascule and suspension bridge, not the same as London Bridge.
Tacoma Narrows Bridge, 1940: Nicknamed “Galloping Gertie.” Its dramatic collapse involved wind-induced aeroelastic flutter. It transformed understanding of bridge aerodynamics.
Silver Bridge, 1967: Collapse over the Ohio River linked to failure of an eyebar and highlighted fracture, inspection and redundancy.
I-35W Mississippi River Bridge, 2007: Collapse in Minneapolis focused attention on gusset-plate design and infrastructure inspection.
Morandi Bridge, 2018: Collapse in Genoa intensified scrutiny of ageing prestressed-concrete infrastructure and maintenance.
• Suspension bridge cables pass over towers and reach anchorages; cable-stayed cables connect tower directly to deck.
• Tacoma Narrows is associated with aeroelastic flutter, not simply resonance in the narrow textbook sense.
5. TUNNELS, CANALS, DAMS AND TRANSPORT MEGAPROJECTS
Cut-and-cover: A trench is excavated, the tunnel built, and the surface restored.
Drill-and-blast: Holes are drilled, explosives used, and broken rock removed.
Tunnel boring machine: A large rotating cutter head excavates a circular tunnel while support segments may be installed behind it.
New Austrian Tunnelling Method: Uses the surrounding rock mass as part of the load-bearing system, with monitoring and flexible support.
Immersed tube: Prefabricated tunnel sections are floated, sunk into a trench and joined underwater.
Channel Tunnel: Rail tunnel beneath the English Channel connecting the United Kingdom and France. Often called the Chunnel.
Gotthard Base Tunnel: Swiss rail tunnel through the Alps, designed as a low-gradient base tunnel.
Seikan Tunnel: Rail tunnel in Japan linking Honshu and Hokkaido beneath the Tsugaru Strait.
Lærdal Tunnel: Long road tunnel in Norway.
Atal Tunnel: Highway tunnel beneath Rohtang Pass in Himachal Pradesh, improving all-weather connectivity to Lahaul-Spiti.
Chenani–Nashri Tunnel: Also known as Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee Tunnel, in Jammu and Kashmir.
Suez Canal: Connects the Mediterranean Sea and Red Sea. It is a sea-level canal without locks along the main transit route.
Panama Canal: Connects the Atlantic and Pacific through a system of locks that raises ships to Gatun Lake and lowers them again.
Kiel Canal: Connects the North Sea and Baltic Sea through Germany.
Corinth Canal: Cuts through the Isthmus of Corinth in Greece.
Suez saves ships from sailing around Africa. Panama saves ships from sailing around South America.
Gravity dam: Resists water pressure mainly through its own weight.
Arch dam: Curves upstream and transfers load to canyon walls.
Buttress dam: Upstream face supported by triangular buttresses.
Embankment dam: Built from compacted earth or rockfill.
• Hoover Dam: Concrete arch-gravity dam on the Colorado River, between Nevada and Arizona.
• Three Gorges Dam: Massive hydroelectric project on the Yangtze River in China.
• Itaipu Dam: Hydroelectric project on the Paraná River between Brazil and Paraguay.
• Bhakra Dam: Concrete gravity dam on the Sutlej River.
• Tehri Dam: Earth and rockfill embankment dam on the Bhagirathi River in Uttarakhand.
• Hirakud Dam: Across the Mahanadi in Odisha.
• Sardar Sarovar Dam: On the Narmada River in Gujarat.

Railways reduce rolling resistance by using steel wheels on steel rails. High-speed rail requires smooth alignment, large curve radii, advanced signalling, grade separation and carefully engineered tracks.
Maglev trains use magnetic forces for levitation and propulsion. Major approaches include electromagnetic suspension and electrodynamic suspension.
Shinkansen: Japan’s high-speed rail network, inaugurated in 1964 between Tokyo and Osaka.
Shanghai Maglev: Commercial high-speed magnetic-levitation line using Transrapid technology.
• First passenger train in India: 1853, Bombay to Thane.
• First metro railway in India: Kolkata Metro.
• Delhi Metro: Associated prominently with E. Sreedharan, often called the “Metro Man of India.”
• Konkan Railway: Major engineering achievement across difficult Western Ghats terrain.
• Chenab Rail Bridge: Steel arch railway bridge over the Chenab River in Jammu and Kashmir, notable for its exceptional height.
Runway numbers represent the runway’s magnetic heading rounded to the nearest ten degrees with the final zero omitted. A runway aligned roughly 90° is numbered 09; the opposite direction is 27.
Taxiways connect runways, aprons, terminals and maintenance areas. Instrument Landing Systems provide lateral and vertical guidance for aircraft approach.
As buildings rise, wind effects become more important. Engineers must control:
Rigid frame: Beams and columns resist lateral loads through bending.
Shear wall: Vertical walls resist lateral forces.
Braced frame: Diagonal members provide stiffness.
Tube system: Closely spaced perimeter columns and beams act like a hollow tube.
Bundled tube: Multiple tubes connected together.
Diagrid: Diagonal grid carries gravity and lateral loads efficiently.
Core-and-outrigger: Central core connected to perimeter columns through outriggers.

Fazlur Rahman Khan, a Bangladeshi-American structural engineer at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, revolutionized skyscraper design through tubular structural systems. He is associated with buildings such as the John Hancock Center and Sears Tower, now Willis Tower.

Eiffel Tower: Designed for the 1889 Exposition Universelle by Gustave Eiffel’s company. Principal engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier developed the concept, with architect Stephen Sauvestre contributing refinements.
Burj Khalifa: Dubai skyscraper designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill; Adrian Smith was the design architect and Bill Baker the structural engineer. It uses a buttressed-core structural system.
Taipei 101: Taiwan skyscraper known for its tuned mass damper and pagoda-inspired form.
Petronas Towers: Kuala Lumpur twin towers designed by César Pelli; once the world’s tallest buildings and still famous as twin towers.
Shanghai Tower: Twisting supertall skyscraper in Shanghai designed by Gensler.
Canton Tower: Slender observation and broadcasting tower in Guangzhou.
Tokyo Skytree: Broadcasting tower in Japan, inspired partly by traditional Japanese structural ideas.
Shallow foundations transfer loads near the surface. Deep foundations use piles or drilled shafts to reach stronger soil or rock.
Raft or mat foundation: Large slab supporting many columns and walls.
Pile foundation: Slender members driven or bored into the ground.
Caisson: Watertight retaining structure used for underwater foundation work.
Tensile membrane: Fabric or cable surface held in tension.
Geodesic dome: Network of triangles approximating a sphere, popularized by Buckminster Fuller.
Shell structure: Thin curved surface carrying loads through membrane action.
7. ENGINEERS AND INVENTORS YOU MUST KNOW

British engineer associated with the Great Western Railway, steamships Great Western and Great Britain, and the Great Eastern. Worked on the Thames Tunnel project begun by his father, Marc Isambard Brunel. Known for ambitious Victorian engineering.
French civil engineer associated with the Eiffel Tower and the internal structural framework of the Statue of Liberty. Also worked on bridges and aerodynamics.
Often called the father of civil engineering. Designed the third Eddystone Lighthouse and helped establish civil engineering as a profession.
Scottish civil engineer associated with roads, bridges, canals and the Menai Suspension Bridge. Nicknamed the “Colossus of Roads.”
Railway and civil engineer, son of George Stephenson. Associated with the Rocket locomotive and major railway bridges.
Known as the “Father of Railways.” Developed early practical locomotives and engineered the Stockton and Darlington Railway and Liverpool and Manchester Railway.
Designed London’s major sewer network after the Great Stink, helping reduce waterborne disease by moving sewage away from central London.
Indian civil engineer associated with the Konkan Railway and Delhi Metro. Known as the “Metro Man of India.”

Indian civil engineer, statesman and Diwan of Mysore. Associated with automatic sluice gates, flood-protection and irrigation works. His birthday, 15 September, is celebrated as Engineers’ Day in India.
Pioneer of tubular structural systems for skyscrapers.
Engineer and founder of Arup, closely associated with the structural realization of the Sydney Opera House.
Danish architect who designed the Sydney Opera House. Its shell geometry was ultimately rationalized using sections of a sphere.
Architect, designer and futurist who popularized the geodesic dome. Also coined or promoted ideas such as “Spaceship Earth.”
Associated with scientific management and time-and-motion-oriented industrial efficiency studies.
Pioneers of motion study. “Therbligs” are basic units of motion; the term is “Gilbreth” roughly reversed.
Developed the Gantt chart for project scheduling.
Quality-management thinker influential in postwar Japanese manufacturing. Associated with statistical process control and the Plan–Do–Study–Act cycle.
Associated with the cause-and-effect diagram, also called the fishbone or Ishikawa diagram.
Key architect of the Toyota Production System and just-in-time manufacturing.
• Engineers’ Day in India → M. Visvesvaraya
• Father of civil engineering → John Smeaton
• Metro Man of India → E. Sreedharan
• Tube skyscraper systems → Fazlur Rahman Khan
8. ELECTRICITY: FROM GENERATION TO THE SOCKET
Voltage: Electric potential difference, measured in volts.
Current: Rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.
Resistance: Opposition to current, measured in ohms.
Power: Rate of energy transfer, measured in watts.
Energy: Power multiplied by time, commonly measured in joules or kilowatt-hours.
For a resistor: P = I²R = V²/R
Direct current flows in one direction. Batteries supply DC.
Alternating current periodically reverses direction. Most power grids use AC because transformers allow efficient voltage conversion.
The late nineteenth-century “War of the Currents” involved Thomas Edison’s DC systems and the AC approach championed by George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla.
8.3 Why electricity is transmitted at high voltage

For a given power, raising voltage reduces current. Since line losses are proportional to I²R, lower current greatly reduces heating losses. Transformers step voltage up for transmission and down for distribution and use.
A transformer transfers AC energy between circuits through electromagnetic induction.
where V is voltage and N is number of turns.
Step-up transformer: Secondary voltage greater than primary voltage.
Step-down transformer: Secondary voltage lower than primary voltage.
Generation → step-up transformer → high-voltage transmission → substations → distribution → consumers.
A grid must continuously balance supply and demand. Frequency deviations reveal imbalance. Grid operators use reserves, dispatchable generation, storage, demand response and interconnections.
Load factor: Average load divided by peak load.
Capacity factor: Actual energy generated divided by maximum possible energy over a period.
Smart grids combine sensors, digital communications, automated controls and advanced metering. They can integrate distributed renewables, electric vehicles, storage and demand response.
Microgrid: Local group of loads and generators capable of operating connected to or separated from the larger grid.
Demand response: Consumers alter electricity use in response to prices or grid needs.
Virtual power plant: Aggregates distributed resources such as batteries, rooftop solar and controllable loads so they can be coordinated like a power plant.
High-voltage direct current transmission is useful for very long distances, undersea cables and connecting asynchronous grids. Converter stations change AC to DC and back.
Notable technology companies include Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy and GE Vernova, among others.
Coal, gas, oil, nuclear heat or concentrated solar heat can produce steam that drives a turbine connected to a generator.
Combined-cycle gas turbine: Gas turbine generates electricity and its hot exhaust produces steam for a second turbine, improving efficiency.
Generator principle: Mechanical rotation changes magnetic flux through coils, inducing voltage according to Faraday’s law.
Coal is burned to heat water and produce steam. Major concerns include carbon dioxide, particulate matter, sulfur oxides, nitrogen oxides, mercury and ash.
• Electrostatic precipitator: Removes particles using electric charge.
• Flue-gas desulfurization: Removes sulfur dioxide, often using limestone.
• Selective catalytic reduction: Reduces nitrogen oxides using ammonia or urea with a catalyst.
Gas turbines can start and ramp faster than traditional coal or nuclear plants. Methane leakage is a major climate concern because methane is a potent greenhouse gas.
Potential energy of stored or flowing water drives turbines.
• Pelton: High head, low flow; impulse turbine.
• Kaplan: Low head, high flow; propeller-like reaction turbine.
Pumped-storage hydropower moves water uphill when electricity is abundant and releases it through turbines when needed. It is an energy-storage system, not a net energy source.
Fission splits heavy nuclei such as uranium-235, releasing energy and neutrons. A controlled chain reaction provides heat.
• Moderator to slow neutrons in many reactor types
Pressurized Water Reactor: Primary water remains under high pressure and transfers heat to a secondary loop.
Boiling Water Reactor: Water boils directly in the reactor vessel.
Pressurized Heavy Water Reactor: Uses heavy water as moderator and coolant; important in India’s nuclear programme.
Fast breeder reactor: Uses fast neutrons and can produce more fissile material than it consumes under designed conditions.
India’s three-stage nuclear programme is associated with Homi J. Bhabha and aims ultimately to exploit India’s thorium resources.
Fusion combines light nuclei, such as isotopes of hydrogen, releasing energy. Deuterium–tritium fusion is a major research focus. The reaction requires extremely high temperature and confinement.
Inertial confinement: Powerful lasers compress tiny fuel pellets.
ITER is a major international tokamak project in southern France. A tokamak is a toroidal magnetic-confinement device originally developed in the Soviet Union.
Photovoltaic cells convert light directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect. Most commercial cells use silicon.
Monocrystalline silicon: High efficiency, cut from single-crystal ingots.
Polycrystalline silicon: Made from multiple crystal fragments.
Thin-film: Includes cadmium telluride and CIGS technologies.
Perovskite solar cells: Emerging high-efficiency technology, often researched in tandem with silicon.
An inverter converts solar-panel DC into AC suitable for the grid or appliances.
Mirrors concentrate sunlight to produce heat, which can drive a turbine. Thermal storage, often using molten salts, may allow generation after sunset.
Types include parabolic trough, solar power tower and dish systems.
Wind turns rotor blades connected through a drivetrain or direct-drive generator.
Horizontal-axis wind turbine: Dominant commercial form.
Vertical-axis designs include Darrieus and Savonius turbines.
Betz’s law states that no ideal wind turbine can capture more than 59.3% of the kinetic energy in wind passing through its swept area.
Offshore wind benefits from stronger, steadier winds but faces harder installation and maintenance.
Uses heat from Earth. Dry steam, flash steam and binary-cycle plants are common types. Iceland is strongly associated with geothermal energy, though geothermal deployment exists worldwide.
Tidal barrages exploit water-level differences. Tidal-stream turbines use moving currents. Wave-energy devices capture surface-wave motion. Tides are predictable but suitable sites are limited.

Biomass energy uses organic material. Anaerobic digestion produces biogas rich in methane. Ethanol is commonly produced by fermenting sugars or starches. Biodiesel can be made from oils and fats through transesterification.
A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy through redox reactions.
In a discharging galvanic cell, electrons flow through the external circuit from anode to cathode.
Separator: Prevents direct electrical contact while allowing ion transport.
Primary battery: Non-rechargeable in normal use.
Invented by Gaston Planté in 1859. Uses lead dioxide, sponge lead and sulfuric acid. Common in vehicle starter batteries and backup systems. Heavy but inexpensive and highly recyclable.
Nickel–cadmium: Durable and capable of high power but cadmium is toxic and memory-effect concerns are famous.
Nickel–metal hydride: Replaced cadmium with a hydrogen-absorbing alloy and was widely used in early hybrid vehicles.
Commercialized by Sony in 1991. The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry honoured John B. Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino for lithium-ion battery development.
During discharge, lithium ions move through the electrolyte from anode to cathode while electrons travel through the external circuit.
Common anode: Graphite. Silicon-rich anodes are being developed for higher capacity. Lithium-metal anodes are pursued in next-generation cells.
LFP advantages: Strong thermal stability, long cycle life, no nickel or cobalt in the cathode.
NMC/NCA advantages: High energy density, useful for longer-range vehicles.
Energy density: Energy stored per unit mass or volume.
Power density: How quickly energy can be delivered.
Cycle life: Number of charge-discharge cycles before major capacity loss.
State of charge: Remaining charge percentage.
State of health: Condition relative to a new battery.
C-rate: Charge or discharge rate relative to capacity.
A 1C discharge theoretically empties a battery in one hour; 2C in half an hour.

An uncontrolled rise in battery temperature can trigger exothermic reactions, gas release and fire. Battery management systems monitor voltage, current and temperature. Pack design also uses cooling, fuses, contactors and physical barriers.

Replace conventional liquid electrolyte with a solid electrolyte. Potential benefits include improved safety and compatibility with high-energy anodes, but challenges include interfaces, manufacturing and dendrite control.

Use sodium rather than lithium. Sodium is abundant and potentially lower-cost. Energy density is generally lower than leading lithium-ion cells, but sodium-ion may suit stationary storage and lower-cost mobility.

Electrolytes are stored in external tanks and pumped through an electrochemical stack. Energy capacity can be increased by enlarging tanks, while power depends on stack size. Vanadium redox flow batteries are a prominent type.
Pumped hydro: Water moved between reservoirs.
Compressed-air energy storage: Air compressed and later expanded.
Flywheel: Energy stored in a rapidly rotating mass.
Gravity storage: Raises a mass and later lowers it to recover energy.
Molten-salt storage: Stores heat, often in concentrated solar plants.
Store energy electrostatically rather than mainly through bulk chemical reactions. They charge rapidly, deliver high power and survive many cycles, but store less energy than batteries.
• Battery capacity in ampere-hours is not the same as energy in watt-hours; voltage matters.
• Pumped hydro is storage, not a primary fuel.
• Anode is oxidation and cathode is reduction in both galvanic and electrolytic terminology, though electrode signs change by operating mode.
Hydrogen is an energy carrier, not a primary energy source. Energy must be used to produce it.
Colour labels are informal industry shorthand:
• Grey hydrogen: Usually natural gas without carbon capture.
• Blue hydrogen: Fossil-based production with carbon capture.
• Green hydrogen: Electrolysis powered by renewable electricity.
• Brown or black hydrogen: Coal-based production.
• Pink hydrogen: Electrolysis powered by nuclear energy.
• Turquoise hydrogen: Methane pyrolysis producing solid carbon.
Electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Fuel cells reverse the broad logic of electrolysis: hydrogen reacts electrochemically with oxygen to produce electricity, water and heat.
Proton-exchange membrane fuel cells operate at relatively low temperature and are common in vehicle research.
Solid-oxide fuel cells operate at high temperature and can use a wider range of fuels after processing.
• Low volumetric energy density at ambient conditions
• Need for compression, liquefaction or chemical carriers
• Direct reduced iron for lower-carbon steel
• Shipping fuels such as ammonia or methanol derivatives
Ammonia, NH₃, contains no carbon and can carry hydrogen, but it is toxic and produces nitrogen-oxide concerns when burned.
12. CARBON CAPTURE, CLIMATE ENGINEERING AND INDUSTRIAL DECARBONISATION
Carbon capture and storage: Captures carbon dioxide and stores it underground.
Carbon capture, utilisation and storage: Uses some captured CO₂ in products or processes before storage or release.
Direct air capture: Removes CO₂ directly from ambient air.
Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage: Biomass absorbs CO₂, is used for energy, and resulting emissions are captured; potentially net-negative under strict conditions.
Post-combustion capture: Removes CO₂ from flue gas after fuel is burned.
Pre-combustion capture: Converts fuel into a gas mixture, separates CO₂ before combustion.
Oxy-fuel combustion: Burns fuel in nearly pure oxygen, producing exhaust rich in CO₂ and water.
Solvents such as amines can chemically absorb CO₂. Other approaches use solid sorbents, membranes and mineralisation.
Captured CO₂ is compressed and transported to geological formations such as deep saline aquifers or depleted oil and gas reservoirs. Monitoring is essential to verify containment.
Cement: Emissions from fuel and limestone calcination.
Steel: Traditional blast furnaces use coke both as fuel and reducing agent.
Shipping and aviation: Require high-energy-density fuels.
Chemicals and fertilisers: Depend on carbon- and hydrogen-intensive feedstocks.
Electric arc furnace: Melts scrap using electricity.
Direct reduced iron: Removes oxygen from iron ore using a reducing gas, potentially hydrogen.
Carbon capture: Can reduce emissions from some conventional routes.

Carbon dioxide removal addresses greenhouse-gas concentration. Solar radiation modification aims to reflect a small fraction of sunlight or alter Earth’s radiation balance. These categories differ in mechanisms, risks and governance.
Examples studied under solar radiation modification include stratospheric aerosol injection and marine cloud brightening. These remain controversial and are not substitutes for emissions reduction.
A conventional drinking-water plant may include:
Coagulation destabilises tiny suspended particles. Flocculation gently mixes them into larger flocs. Sedimentation allows flocs to settle.
Disinfection methods include chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet light.
Primary treatment: Physical removal of solids.
Secondary treatment: Biological breakdown of dissolved organic matter.
Tertiary treatment: Advanced removal of nutrients, pathogens or specific contaminants.
Activated-sludge process: Aerated microorganisms consume organic matter, followed by settling.
Anaerobic digestion can stabilise sludge and produce biogas.
Reverse osmosis: Pressure forces water through a semi-permeable membrane, leaving most salts behind.
Multi-stage flash distillation: Seawater flashes into steam in successive low-pressure stages.
Multiple-effect distillation: Uses heat repeatedly across stages.
Electrodialysis: Electric potential moves ions through selective membranes, more suited to brackish water than very salty seawater in many applications.
Reverse osmosis is now the dominant modern seawater-desalination technology in many regions because of major efficiency improvements.
Roman aqueducts used carefully controlled gravity gradients.
The London sewer system is associated with Joseph Bazalgette.
Singapore’s NEWater programme treats reclaimed water using advanced membranes and ultraviolet disinfection.
Israel is strongly associated with large-scale desalination and drip irrigation.
Drip irrigation is closely associated with Israeli engineer Simcha Blass and the company Netafim.
Rainwater harvesting captures runoff for storage or recharge.
Aquifer recharge allows water to infiltrate underground.
A watershed is the land area draining to a common outlet.
14. WASTE, RECYCLING AND THE CIRCULAR ECONOMY
Prevent or refuse → reduce → reuse → repair → refurbish → remanufacture → recycle → recover energy → dispose.
Recycling is valuable but usually comes after avoiding and reusing materials.
The linear model is take–make–use–dispose. A circular economy aims to design out waste, keep products and materials in use and regenerate natural systems.
Extended producer responsibility makes producers responsible for collection or end-of-life management of products.
Aluminium recycling uses far less energy than producing primary aluminium from bauxite.
Steel is widely recycled using electric arc furnaces.
Copper retains value because of high electrical conductivity and recyclability.
1 PET or PETE: Beverage bottles and polyester.
7 Other: Mixed category including polycarbonate and some bioplastics.

Mechanical recycling sorts, cleans, melts and reforms plastic. Chemical recycling breaks polymers into smaller molecules or feedstocks. Pyrolysis heats material without oxygen to produce oils and gases, though economics and environmental performance vary.
Thermoplastics soften when heated and can generally be remoulded. Thermosets form cross-linked structures and do not simply remelt.

Electronic waste contains valuable metals such as copper, gold, silver, cobalt and palladium, along with hazardous substances. Urban mining means recovering useful materials from discarded products and infrastructure.
Printed circuit boards are especially metal-rich. Informal burning and acid leaching can create severe health and environmental harm.
Lead–acid batteries have a mature recycling system. Lithium-ion recycling methods include:
• Direct recycling: Attempts to recover cathode material while preserving more of its structure.
Composting converts organic waste into soil amendment under aerobic conditions.
Anaerobic digestion produces biogas without oxygen.
Landfills generate methane as organic waste decomposes anaerobically.

Incineration can reduce waste volume and generate energy but requires emissions control and still produces ash. Gasification uses limited oxygen or steam to make synthesis gas. Waste-to-energy does not eliminate the need for waste reduction and recycling.
One industry’s waste becomes another’s input. Kalundborg in Denmark is a famous industrial-symbiosis example involving exchanges of steam, water and by-products among facilities.
Fatigue: Damage from repeated cyclic loading, often below the material’s static strength.
Creep: Slow deformation under sustained load, especially at high temperature.
Fracture: Crack growth leading to separation.
Corrosion: Chemical or electrochemical material degradation.
Wear: Surface loss through friction or contact.
Thermal shock: Stress caused by rapid temperature change.

The de Havilland Comet airliner disasters in the 1950s revealed the danger of metal fatigue and stress concentration around window corners. Later aircraft adopted more rounded window geometry and improved fatigue testing.
The Liberty ships of the Second World War experienced brittle fractures, helping advance fracture mechanics and understanding of notch sensitivity and low-temperature behaviour.
Cathodic protection makes the protected structure the cathode of an electrochemical cell.
Sacrificial anodes use a more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium.

MODULE 11 — SCIENCE, MEDICINE AND MATHEMATICS THROUGH INNOVATION

This module links discovery with problem-solving. It is built around the roadmap’s central instruction: never learn a breakthrough as an isolated fact. Connect the idea, the innovator, the practical application, the route to adoption, and the long-term effect on society.
